2step.description: 2 step is UK garage with the second and fourth kick removed: the groove becomes limping, sensual and unpredictable. Between 1998 and 2001, its absolute golden age, it ran everywhere from the pop charts to pirate radio, with Craig David as its voice, MJ Cole as its craftsman, and El-B representing its darker side. 2 step is proof that silence placed in exactly the right spot can make a floor dance harder than any kick drum could. That missing pulse forces the ear to fill the gap itself, and it is that tension between what is played and what is left out that gives the style its off kilter sway.
2step.production: Sit between 130 and 138 BPM, most classics at 134 or 136, and define the groove by what you remove: strip the kicks off beats two and four so the pattern limps and sways, with a heavier swing than 4/4 garage, around 60 to 66 percent. The skeleton is kick on beat one and the and of two, a bright, snappy snare or rimshot on two and four with a ghost note late in beat three, and swung hats alternating loud and soft velocities. Bass fills the spaces the missing kicks left: a sine or triangle sub playing short, syncopated notes on the offbeats, with El-B style darker tracks adding a filtered, gliding sawtooth. Over it sit chopped female vocal phrases turned into rhythmic motifs, Rhodes stabs, and light bell or marimba color, softer than 4/4 UK garage.

acidhouse.description: In 1985, Phuture repurposed the Roland TB-303, a commercially unloved bass machine, and discovered that its squelching filter was an instrument in its own right. That acid squelch became a voice: hypnotic, liquid, faintly unsettling. Chicago invented it, and England turned it into the banner of the Second Summer of Love in 1988, with the smiley face as its flag. Few machines have defined a genre as completely as the 303 defined acid house.
acidhouse.production: Work between 118 and 128 BPM, a touch slower than the acid techno that follows it. The 303 sets its own feel, playing sixteenths with an internal swing and sliding notes into a glissando, so keep the drum machine dead straight and let the acid line be the only thing that wavers. Early records lean on the 808: long open decay kick, dry snare on two and four, accented closed hats, syncopated cowbell and claves. The bass is the whole track: a 16 step line, one or two notes, hand placed accents and slides, fundamental repeated, an octave jump, a slide down a semitone. Automate cutoff and resonance live over dozens of bars, opening suddenly on accents. Keep everything else minimal: a second, higher 303 answering the first, and a short delay on the line.

acidtechno.description: Acid techno replants the TB-303 in techno soil, harder and faster than its Chicago house origins. London's squats and free parties turned it into a subculture in its own right during the 1990s, embracing a deliberately dirty sound, while Hardfloor delivered its widescreen version. Here the 303 screams rather than coos, often with two machines trading lines against each other.
acidtechno.production: Acid techno runs 130 to 145 BPM; Hardfloor stays near 130 for the widescreen version while London's squat scene pushes to 140 or 145, with a light swing on the sixteenths applied to the hats and the 303, never the kick. A hard 909 kick holds every beat, the closed hat plays only three hits per bar in a velocity pyramid, and the open hat runs all the sixteenths. The TB-303 is the bass and the whole point: a sixteenth-note sequence of four or five notes with accents and slides, cutoff around 30 to 50 percent and high resonance. The genre's real signature is two 303s trading lines, a low one laying the pattern and a higher, distorted one answering, run through overdrive and EQ.

acidtrance.description: Acid trance puts the TB-303 to work in the service of ecstasy rather than grime: long acid lines, resonance rising with the track, straight kicks and background pads. Between 1993 and 1996 it sat at the heart of the Harthouse sound and the German rave scene. Hardfloor wrote the genre's monument with Acperience 1, a track claimed equally by acid techno and trance, exactly the kind of hinge point between styles that this map favors. Its long, patient builds turned the 303's raw squelch into something closer to a slow, hypnotic euphoria than a purely dirty acid workout.
acidtrance.production: Work between 135 and 145 BPM with no swing: the pulse comes from the TB-303 itself, its accents and slides doing what quantization cannot. Keep drums fully quantized and let the acid line breathe over 16 or 32 bar spans, since the real tempo is the slow rise of the filter resonance. A 909 provides the carpet, kick on every beat, clap on two and four, open hats on the offbeats, its kick slightly shorter to leave room for the 303 in the low end. Write the 303 line as 16 steps on tonic and octave with two or three accents and a slide per bar, cutoff opening slowly over 32 to 64 bars while resonance climbs toward a whistle. Add slow filtered pads holding a static minor chord and a dotted eighth delay on the acid line.

afrohouse.description: Afro house is house music rewritten from South Africa and its diaspora, where kwaito, traditional percussion and deep house all meet. Its rhythms are polyrhythmic and patient, its vocals often sung in local languages, and its spirituality is embraced rather than hidden. It went global through the 2010s and shifted house music's center of gravity toward Johannesburg and Lisbon, reshaping the genre's sound worldwide.
afrohouse.production: Afro house sits between 118 and 124 BPM, slower and more patient than the tribal house it descends from, its feel coming from polyrhythm: a straight four-beat kick underneath percussion written in 6/8 or 12/8, giving a ternary sway over a binary base. Build the drums from a round, not-too-loud kick, very little clap, a rim or wood percussion instead, and a heart of sampled African percussion, djembe, dundun, shekere, udu, in triplet motifs with a continuous sixteenth-note shaker and a discreet log drum answering the kick. Keep phrases long, sixteen or thirty two bars, over tracks running seven to nine minutes that settle in like a ceremony. The bass is a supple deep house tone, filtered to 200 or 300Hz, placing notes on the triplets as well as the eighths, often just one or two notes per phrase.

aggrotech.description: Aggrotech is the dancefloor hardening of dark electro in the 2000s: shouted, vocoder-processed vocals, club-ready kicks, minor-key trance melodies and apocalyptic imagery. It runs on the fuel of gothic festivals like Hellfest and cyber clubs, with Combichrist and Hocico as its leading acts. The style openly embraces excess, since that is its very definition, piling distortion, speed and volume on top of dark electro's already grim template. Where its parent genre still leans on atmosphere and dread, aggrotech is built first for the dancefloor, trading some of that slow-burning menace for an immediate, pounding club impact.
aggrotech.production: Aggrotech runs 130 to 150 BPM, usually settling at 140, on a fully quantized, unswung grid built for the dancefloor from the first bar, faster than the dark electro it hardens. Build a heavy, saturated club kick with a pitch envelope and strong compression, a layered snare and clap on 2 and 4 with white noise, sixteenth hats at alternating velocities, and kick rolls into a snare buildup before each drop. The bass is deliberately distorted and rolling, a wavetable sawtooth through a resonant filter and internal distortion, heavily sidechained to the kick, its minor-key lines leaning on the minor second and tritone until it rivals the kick rather than supporting it. The shouted, vocoder vocal is the genre's emblem, pushed through overdrive into a robotic growl, joined by bright unison leads.

amapiano.description: South Africa, 2015 to 2020: a slow hybrid of deep house, kwaito and local jazz, instantly recognizable for its log drum, that hollow, bouncing percussive bass under the pads. Tracks run long and patient, carried by real pianos and welcoming vocals. Now the dominant popular music of the continent, it is redrawing the map of global club music, one patient introduction at a time.
amapiano.production: Sit between 110 and 115 bpm, slow for house, giving the log drum room to bounce between hits, with a marked shuffle on shakers and hats over a straight kick, percussion often laid in triplets over the 4/4. Build a round, short kick, a discreet rim or clap on 2 and 4, and a driving layer of shuffled shakers at different speeds, sampled African percussion, bells, whistles, keeping the intro nearly complete except for the missing log drum. The log drum is bass, percussion and melody in one, a pitch-dropping sine or triangle played in syncopated patterns on root, third and fifth. Layer played jazz piano chords, Rhodes, soft deep house pads, welcoming vocals in call and response, sampled saxophone, and long reverb on piano and voice.

ambientdub.description: Dub dissolved into ambient: endless echoes, submarine bass, pads that breathe at the tempo of the delay. The Orb and Beyond's Ambient Dub series fix the name in the early 1990s, Banco de Gaia and Dreadzone take it traveling. It is the chill room of English rave turned into a lasting genre, one where the mixing console itself becomes the lead instrument.
ambientdub.production: Here, finally, a pulse: sit between 70 and 100 bpm, a slowed reggae dub tempo, or 120 played in half time, kick landing once every bar and a half. The delay defines the feel, synced to a dotted eighth with heavy feedback, becoming the track's real grid, pads breathing on the same subdivision. Build a soft, buried kick, one drop style, kick and rimshot together on beat 3, with sporadic percussion sent into a Space Echo, drums appearing and vanishing as if mixed live. For bass, use a deep, round sub following the reggae pattern, silence on beat 1, root and fifth, only a chord or two over many bars. Layer delays pushed near self-oscillation, spring reverb on percussion, slow-chorused pads, and traveling samples, radio dialogue, flutes, voices.

ambientgenre.description: Brian Eno named the genre in 1978 with Music for Airports: music meant to be as easy to ignore as to listen to, an environment rather than an event. Ambient is really a listening contract more than a fixed sound, built from pads, patience and the absence of any clear goal or destination. Every style that follows in this family declines that same contract in different ways, from dark to bright. Eno's earlier Discreet Music and the opening track 1/1 of Music for Airports remain the genre's cornerstones. It treats music as something to inhabit a room with, changeable in importance depending on how closely you choose to listen.
ambientgenre.production: Ambient has no tempo in the club sense: what replaces pulse is duration, notes lasting 10 to 30 seconds in cycles that never quite land back on their feet, following Eno's method of tape loops of different lengths slowly drifting out of phase. In Ableton, loop clips of 7, 11 and 13 bars, each carrying a held note, and let them wander; a BPM, if needed, is only around 60 to 70, to sync delays. There is no drum kit: rhythm comes instead from the slow beating of two close notes, a piano attack surfacing every twenty seconds, or a slow LFO breathing on a pad's volume. The low end comes only from pad fundamentals, a tonic note held below the chords, a pedal rather than a bassline. Long reverbs and layered textures complete a sound built to be inhabited.

ambienthouse.description: England, 1989 to 1991: house music set adrift, pads and travel samples floating over discreet kicks, the invention of the chill-out back room as an art form in itself. The Orb built its floating monuments here, the KLF wrote its pastoral counterpart. The genre died young commercially, but its DNA keeps resurfacing in every balearic and progressive house revival since.
ambienthouse.production: This is the one branch of the family that keeps a real house tempo, 110 to 125 BPM in a straight 4/4, though the kick is present but never leads, pulsing quietly under the pads. Keep the swing faint, around 50 to 53 percent, a steady pulse that lets the journey happen above it, The Orb's tracks often run past ten minutes with tempo serving as a thread rather than an engine, aim for something like 118 BPM and a kick the listener could almost forget.

ambienttechno.description: Ambient techno is the contemplative side of 1990s techno, the machinery of the dancefloor put to the service of listening rather than dancing. Wide synthetic pads, softened drum machines and patient melodies sit somewhere between the chill out rooms of English raves and the most atmospheric end of the Detroit school. Acts like B12, Black Dog and the early Aphex Twin built it into a lasting repertoire that labels have kept reissuing ever since.
ambienttechno.production: Ambient techno runs 100 to 125 BPM, often near 115, because the kick is not the point: groove is minimal or absent, and long delays on a dotted quarter or half note create the sway. A softened TR-909 kick, attack faded and lowpass filtered, sits low in a short plate reverb, snare or clap drowns in a lush 1980s reverb, and closed hats play gentle eighths on the offbeats. The bass is warm analog, a triangle or filtered sawtooth with a long release, playing one note per bar or soft eighths on the chord roots, a sine sub doubling it an octave down and resting during breaks. Wide detuned analog pads, sampled strings, patient four or five note melodies on a minor scale, and long filtered delays with reverbs stretching five to ten seconds complete the atmosphere.

anthemtrance.description: Anthem trance is the trance of the turn of the millennium's anthems: a simple, enormous theme, repeated until it becomes unforgettable. Greece 2000 in 1998, For an Angel: tracks that became common touchstones of rave memory, where the chorus matters more than everything else combined. The border with uplifting trance is thin, often the same record seen from two different summers apart. Both styles share the same drums and structure, but anthem trance organizes the entire track around one immense, instantly recognizable theme rather than a staged climb toward a climax, making the hook itself the reason the track exists.
anthemtrance.production: Anthem trance sits in the same 136 to 140 BPM zone as uplifting trance on a straight grid, but organizes the arrangement around one enormous, memorable theme that arrives complete and repeats, rather than climbing toward a climax; count how many times the theme returns, at least six, filtered, bare, then full power. Drums follow the uplifting template, a clean 909 kick, clap and snare on two and four, open hats on the offbeats, but stay restrained, shorter snare rolls marking the breakdown, since the theme builds the tension. The offbeat bass, a sidechained sawtooth on a JP-8000 or Virus, stays simple, following the theme's chords and dropping out during the breakdown before returning on the drop. The lead is a monophonic supersaw theme, first filtered, then opened wide, doubled in octaves, wrapped in reverb and delay.

balearic.description: Balearic is less a genre than a DJ doctrine: at Amnesia in Ibiza between 1985 and 1988, Alfredo played everything, languid rock, dub, italo, strange pop, as long as the sunset agreed with it. Balearic is the art of eclecticism set to the tempo of the sea, reactivated by every generation of diggers since. It is the anti genealogy of this map: proof that a state of mind can itself become a genre. It resists being pinned to any single sound or era, defined instead by mood, pacing and a DJ's instinct for what belongs together, which is why later generations keep reinventing it on their own terms.
balearic.production: Balearic sits at sea tempo, 95 to 115 BPM, with a light, straight 4/4 groove and only mild swing, around 52 to 55 percent, treating tempo as a DJ's doctrine more than a rule: almost anything, a slowed rock record, a stretched italo track, works if it lands near 100. A soft, low mixed 808 or LinnDrum kick and open eighth note hats sit under hand played latin percussion, congas in tumbao, bongos, shaker and a bell on the offbeat, humanized in velocity. Bass is round and played, an electric bass or a chorused Juno 106 square wave filtered near 400 Hz, moving through root, octave and fifth with chromatic passing tones, sharing the low end with the soft kick. On top, tape delayed guitar carries the sound, joined by piano, saxophone or flute, and soft reverbed vocals.

balearictrance.description: Trance music with its eyes on the sea: languid guitars, open piano chords, and held-back tempos carrying the spirit of Ibiza over rave song structures. Chicane fixed its image in 1996 with Offshore, turning a sunset into a genre of its own. This is the trance of the small hours and hotel terraces, closer to a holiday memory than a strobe light, gentler and more song-like than its club-facing cousins.
balearictrance.production: Keep the tempo relaxed, between 120 and 130 BPM, often around 126, the one trance style where a little swing, 8 to 12 percent on hats and shakers, belongs. The kick stays straight, but think in eight-bar phrases that breathe, with a silent bar or a beat where the kick drops away. Soften the 909 kick with a lowpass around 8 kHz, add a light rimshot on 2 and 4, and build the groove from congas with ghost notes and a swung shaker rather than aggressive drums, drums that could back a song. The bassline is round and singing, closer to pop than to trance's off-beat pulse: a Juno-106 saw and square with the cutoff near 400 Hz following the chord roots, held with gentle compression rather than pumping sidechain.

baltimoreclub.description: Baltimore club is house music taken to the blowtorch, born in Baltimore in the 1990s: the Sing Sing and Think breaks hammered in an eight four four pattern, shouted samples looped endlessly, all at around 130 beats per minute without a pause. It was a raw, direct local music that stayed within its own clubs for thirty years before the Jersey and Philly scenes turned it into the root of today's club music. K-Swift and Rod Lee remain its living memory.
baltimoreclub.production: Baltimore club runs 125 to 135 BPM with 130 as its historic center, straight with no programmed swing, the groove coming from looping the Think and Sing Sing breaks with their own recorded shuffle. The sampled breaks sit under a huge, muffled 808 kick in a syncopated pattern, kick on beat one, beat two and two offbeat sixteenths, with an 808 clap on two and four, breaks cut, stopped and relaunched. The 808 kick doubles as the bass, a long, muffled hit with a 400 to 600 millisecond decay occupying the sub alone; many tracks add nothing else. The identity lives in its samples, a shouted rap phrase or crowd scream looped relentlessly, alongside sirens, funk horn stabs, whistles and DJ shouts, all grabbed raw and played fast.

bangintechno.description: Banging techno is 1990s English warehouse techno at its most direct: hard, fast and stripped of melodic detour, sitting between the acid sound of free parties and continental hard techno. The term stuck in British raver slang for this beating, no-frills core of the techno sound, the soundtrack to nights that ask no questions. It favours raw drive over songwriting, built from a driving kick, layered reverb and a looping acid line rather than melody or arrangement tricks. It remains a DJ tool as much as a genre: functional, relentless and built for warehouses rather than concert halls.
bangintechno.production: Banging techno runs 135 to 145 BPM with no swing on a dead-straight grid, its energy from pumping compression rather than groove: tune the kick's reverb tail to die out just before the next hit. Build the kick in three layers, a compressed 909 sample, a heavily sidechained reverb bed, and a click transient, then add 909 hats in sixteenths at fixed velocities, an open hat on the offbeats, a dry clap on 2 and 4, and a snare roll every two bars. The bass is really the kick's own rumble, a sidechained, low-passed reverb tail, joined by a short looping 303 acid line, both tuned to the kick and kept mono below 120 Hz. The palette stays narrow: a saturated 909, one acid loop, one rave stab, and aggressive compression.

basshouse.description: The meeting of house music with the bass sound design inherited from dubstep, formalized in the mid-2010s: a four-on-the-floor house structure carrying modulated, metallic basslines that are played like dubstep drops rather than continuous riffs. The style now rules the big festival stages and the North American club scene, sitting somewhere between G-house and the drier, more clipped current of UK bass music.
basshouse.production: Work between 125 and 130 BPM, like the electro house it descends from, but treat the bass like a dubstep drop, played in heavy quarter and eighth notes with rests and accents rather than a continuous riff, with no swing and a short, hard sidechain. Structure the track in 16-bar sections with a drop around bar 33 or 65, building like a piece of bass music: rise, drop, and a second, different drop. Keep the kick short and heavily compressed with a sharp click and little sustain, layer a snappy clap on 2 and 4, and closed hats or metallic percussion with accents, adding noise-fueled snare rolls before each drop.

bassline.description: Bassline is the sound of northern England keeping speed garage alive and pushing it harder: warping basslines pushed to the front, pitched-up R&B vocals and club euphoria around 140 beats per minute. Niche in Sheffield is the genre's matrix club, giving it its other name, niche. T2's Heartbroken carried it into the charts in 2007. Repeatedly targeted by police licensing crackdowns but never extinguished, it has enjoyed a strong revival since 2015. It keeps speed garage's tempo and swagger but strips away its subtlety, putting a single distorted, modulating bassline at the centre of every track rather than a full arrangement.
bassline.production: Bassline runs 135 to 142 BPM, faster than the speed garage it descends from, with a mandatory four-on-the-floor kick, giving it its other name, 4x4, and only a weak swing on the hats since the bounce comes from the bassline landing on the offbeats, kick on the beats, vocal on the sixteenths. Keep the drums simple, a dry short kick with no sub, a clap on 2 and 4 doubled with a 909 snare, an open hat on every offbeat and a snare roll closing each phrase. That bass is the whole point: a square-and-saw blend, medium attack, long decay, pitch and filter modulated by an envelope for the classic wah, playing offbeat eighths with octave jumps, and a separate sine sub sidechained under it. Pitched-up R&B vocal chops, M1 organ stabs and orchestra hits complete a fast, direct sound.

belgiantechno.description: Between 1990 and 1992, Belgium invented a kind of stadium techno: gloomy organ stabs, siren-like hoover sounds and heavy kicks inherited from the new beat sound it had just buried. The R&S label in Ghent was its command center, and tracks like Energy Flash and Anasthasia became monuments that both techno and hardcore scenes still claim as their own. For roughly two years, the whole of European rave culture spoke with this Belgian accent. It is massive and spacious rather than fast, built for huge rooms rather than intimate clubs, trading speed for weight and letting every hit carry room to breathe.
belgiantechno.production: Belgian techno sits between 118 and 128 BPM, a slowed legacy of new beat, Energy Flash at 123 and staying under 130 to avoid the hardcore invented right after, with no swing anywhere: a straight 909 kick and bass, the rolling weight from a continuous sub and heavy, spaced-out hits. Build a straight four-on-the-floor 909 kick with closed and open hats, then claps rather than snares, a first clap on 2 and 4 with fills, and a second, higher clap panned hard right with a delayed reverb, plus a dry rimshot appearing once. Two basses stack, a sub holding a single fundamental throughout and, later, the famous hoover riff, a pulsing note from a mean filter synth with its cutoff moving in phrases, cut above 100 Hz. The Alpha Juno hoover completes the sound.

bigbeat.description: Big beat took England's breakbeat scene and turned it into stadium rock between 1995 and 1999: huge, compressed breaks, sampled riffs, chorus hooks built like advertising jingles, all drunk on excess and proud of it. The Chemical Brothers, Prodigy and Fatboy Slim sold millions of records and put electronic music into every commercial on the planet. It burned out in three years and came back as nostalgia.
bigbeat.production: Big beat runs 115 to 140 BPM, with faster exceptions near 153, centered around 125 to 130 with a rock feel: breaks sit heavy and ahead of the beat with an MPC-style hip-hop swing around 58 to 62 percent that drags just enough. A huge funk or rock break, sampled on an Akai S1000 or MPC, plays almost whole at 128 BPM with a 909 kick on 1 and 3 and a 909 snare on 2 and 4 layered on top for extra weight. The bass is a riff rather than a line, either lifted from a distorted rock record or played raw on an analog synth through heavy overdrive, mixed loud and dirty enough to fight the kick. On top, sampled rock riffs, pitched vocal hooks, sirens, rave stabs and turntable scratches, run through Vinyl Distortion and Beat Repeat.

birminghamtechno.description: Birmingham techno is the city's 1990s school: grey, hammering, with no melodic concession, sitting between the city's industrial heritage and an almost monastic radicalism. Surgeon and Regis, working around the Downwards label, made a sound recognizable in an instant, short loops, metallic textures, an obstinate groove. Its influence on 2010s industrial techno is direct and openly claimed. Nothing here courts a melody; the reward is in the friction itself.
birminghamtechno.production: Birmingham techno runs from 123 to 140 BPM, with 1990s Downwards records often climbing to 135 or 140, on a dead straight grid with no applied groove, the style deliberately grey and obstinate. What moves is the friction between two-beat loops and the four-beat bar, a one-and-a-half-beat loop that only realigns after three bars, and the tradition dares odd signatures like 5/4 or 9/8 with a kick on every beat. A shaved TR-909 or 808 plays a dry, straight kick with no reverb, while the percussion comes from short loops, usually just two beats isolated from an eight-bar sample and looped, processed through a multiband shaper so only the lows and mids pump against the kick. There is almost no separate bass, the loops themselves supplying the low-mid. The effect chain stays austere: dry distortion, EQ, and a volume shaper.

bleeptechno.description: Bleep techno is Britain's first properly homegrown techno, born in Sheffield and Leeds in 1989 around the Warp label. Crystalline, almost naive synth bleeps sit over enormous sub bass lines inherited from the Yorkshire reggae soundsystem scene. It is a music of space and contrast: tiny high frequencies set against seismic lows, with little in between. That stark pairing makes bleep techno the direct ancestor of the entire English bass music lineage, from bass-heavy techno through to jungle, garage and dubstep. It stayed a local phenomenon at first before becoming one of the most influential blueprints in British electronic music.
bleeptechno.production: Bleep techno runs 118 to 135 BPM, LFO and Nightmares on Wax staying under 125 while club versions climb to 135, with an MPC-style swing of around 55 percent on hats and shaker but never the kick, which lands dead on the grid with the sub. Build a short, dry 909 kick on the four, a snare placed a sixteenth ahead of the beat, two hi-hats alternating strictly, and shortened 707 toms as dry accents. The bass is the real subject: a pure sine sub, mono, one or two notes on the root, with no filter or distortion, thickened only by a quiet octave-up layer. Bleeps are short square or sine notes played high on a pentatonic scale through a ping-pong delay, joined by pitched vocal snippets and a tight, dark reverb, with pads left out entirely.

boogie.description: Boogie is what American disco became after the backlash of 1979: slower, funkier, more electronic. The bass line moved from live players to keyboard synthesizers, drum machines took over from real drummers, and the lush orchestral arrangements of disco disappeared. The groove tightened around 110 beats per minute. Record diggers coined the name boogie long after these records were made, and the style became one of the foundations of the West Coast sound and of the warmest strains of house music.
boogie.production: Boogie runs 100 to 118 BPM, centered on 108 to 112, with a funky 56 to 60 percent swing on the sixteenths, everything lagging behind the beat except the kick. A LinnDrum or TR-808 plays it funky: kick on one, the upbeat of two and sometimes beat three, snare doubled with a clap on two and four, sixteenth hats accented on the eighths with an open hat late in the bar, plus rimshots and cowbell. The bass moves to a keyboard, a Minimoog or Prophet-5, sawtooth through a resonant filter opening on the attack, short release, some glide, playing a syncopated, almost slapped sixteenth note line that trades with the kick. Rhodes chords, wah clavinet, a talkbox line, synth horns and strings, and warm stacked R&B vocals complete the sound.

bouncytechno.description: Bouncy techno came out of Scotland and the north of England between 1993 and 1996, sitting between happy hardcore and gabber: a bouncing four on the floor beat, simple stabs, and a working class, stadium sized euphoria. It was an intense regional scene built around events like Rezerection and the Scottish clubs, with Ultra-Sonic and Q-Tex as its local heroes. Barely documented outside its own borders, it remained essential within them.
bouncytechno.production: Bouncy techno sits between 160 and 180 BPM, mostly around 170; unlike happy hardcore at the same tempo it drops the piano and sung vocal for just a kick, an offbeat bass and stabs. A saturated 909 kick with a short decay plays every beat to leave room for the bass, backed by a dry snare on two and four, open hats on the offbeats and closed hats in sixteenths. The bass is the real center, a fat, distorted saw or square note through a resonant lowpass filter hitting on every offbeat, alternating with the kick to create the bounce, usually staying on the tonic for eight bars before rising. Simple rave stabs, a softened hoover riff, and a short repeated vocal sample round out a sparse palette where every sound is instantly identifiable.

braindance.description: Braindance is the counter name coined by Rephlex, the label run by Aphex Twin and Grant Wilson Claridge, to poke fun at the IDM label: music that makes the brain dance. Twisted acid, prankish electro, naive melodies and knowing breaks, it is more a house spirit than a strict style. The term outlived the label and today describes the whole playful acid IDM lineage. It deliberately resists definition, favoring surprise, humor and virtuosity over any single formula, and its refusal to settle into a fixed sound is arguably the one consistent trait shared by everyone who has ever claimed the name.
braindance.production: Braindance lives at two tempos, 130 to 150 BPM for twisted acid lines and 100 to 115 for prankish electro in the DMX Krew mold, jumping to jungle speeds near 165, on a straight grid ambushed with odd step counts, sudden tempo jerks or breaks that double speed for two bars. Keep the kick largely in 4/4, danceable but jostled, over an 808 electro or 909 acid base, then edit playful breaks on top, a repeated slice, a pitched snare roll, a missing hit, changing the pattern every four bars. The real voice is a TB-303 off the rails, sequenced in sixteenths with slides and out of scale notes, driven hard until it screams, paired with a rounder SH-101 bass. Add detuned keyboard melodies, DX7 bells, joke samples, and toy effects for a broken but precise sound.

breakbeat.description: Breakbeat is the root term: building music on a sampled drum break rather than a programmed grid. The Winstons' Amen break and James Brown's Funky Drummer, a few seconds of drumming recorded in 1969 and 1970, became, twenty years later, the DNA of hardcore, jungle and everything syncopated that England would go on to build. This node documents that raw material itself, the handful of breaks that British producers looped, sliced and pitched into an entirely new lineage of dance music, long before the genres that carry the breakbeat name today had even taken shape.
breakbeat.production: Breakbeat has no fixed tempo of its own, only the tempo of whatever break you sample, Funky Drummer around 100 BPM, Amen Brother around 136, late 1980s British producers settling around 110 to 130 before The Prodigy pushed toward 140. The feel comes from the original drummer, not your grid: hats never land exactly on the sixteenth, the snare drags, keep that blur rather than quantizing it away. Load a break into a sampler in slice mode, then replay it: kick on beat one and the and of two, snare on two and four, ghost notes kept low, doubled with a short 909. Bass is a single sine or a Moog sub on root notes with passing tones, lightly sidechained to the kick. Downsample or grain warp for old grain, and layer a few horn, piano and vocal samples.

breakbeatgarage.description: Breakbeat garage is the 2000 to 2003 variant of garage that puts breaks back under warp basslines, sitting between late 2 step and early dubstep. Menta, Agent X and the Stanton Warriors held the decks for it. It occupies a narrow slot in the genealogy, but it is through this style that the garage lineage relearned the syncopation of breaks before passing it on to dubstep. Though short lived, it functioned as a crucial relay point, carrying rhythmic ideas from 1990s jungle and breakbeat culture forward into the bass heavy, warp driven productions that would come to define UK dance music through the following decade.
breakbeatgarage.production: Breakbeat garage sits at garage tempo, 132 to 138 BPM, keeping UK garage's heavy swing, 58 to 62 percent, carried through a full breakbeat rather than programmed hats, festive and bouncy, closer to nu skool breaks than the darker dubstep just emerging. A funk break, chopped in slice mode and looped with a grainy timestretch, reorders every four bars while a 909 kick on beat one and the and of two and a snare on two and four keep a garage foot, the break filtered to clear the kick. The bass is intact speed garage warp, sawtooth and square with a falling pitch envelope and an enveloped low pass filter, on the break's offbeats, holding when it rolls and filling when it stops. MC hooks from pirate radio, Korg M1 stabs, sirens and rave stabs keep the club ready energy.

breakbeathardcore.description: England's raves of 1990 to 1992: speeded-up house collides with hip-hop breaks, Belgian rave stabs, and reggae basslines. Euphoric pianos, pitched-up vocals, and sirens define hardcore as the music of a generation dancing outdoors, pressed onto white labels that sold out within a week. Its eventual split would give birth to jungle on one side and happy hardcore on the other, making it one of the most consequential forks in dance music history.
breakbeathardcore.production: The tempo climbed year by year between 1990 and 1992, from 125 BPM to 140 in 1991 and 150 by early 1992, so start around 145 BPM with the feel of a hip-hop break sped up by roughly 30 percent, its swing coming from the sample rather than the sequencer. Layer a steady four-on-the-floor 909 kick under a pitched-up hip-hop break, Funky Drummer, Amen, or Think, sped up without time-stretching so it turns brighter and more nervous. Add a 909 clap on 2 and 4, closed hats in alternating velocities, and an open hat on every off-beat, replacing the break with a rising snare roll on the last four bars.

breakcore.description: Breakcore is the punk escalation of the breakbeat: the Amen break saturated to the point of fusion, wild collages mixing ragga, metal and gabber in the same grinder, running between 180 and 220 beats per minute. The scene grew out of squats and netlabels in the late 1990s, with Venetian Snares as its genius of odd time signatures. It aims to be violent, funny and virtuosic, all three at once or nothing at all.
breakcore.production: Breakcore runs from 180 to 220 BPM and the tempo can shift mid phrase, its violence and odd time signatures, Venetian Snares writing in seven four or five four. The crushed Amen break is chopped into 32 slices written into patterns of seven or fourteen lines, using tracker commands like retrigger and pitch slide on the snare slices for bursts, stacking two or three Amens at different pitches. The bass is secondary and brutal, often just the saturated gabber kick stretched down to 50 Hz, or a distorted square and pitched ragga sample fused with the kick through the same distortion and compressor into a single mass. The tracker is the real instrument, its per line commands producing the retriggered bursts, while unlicensed samples, cartoons, metal, ragga, film dialogue, get pitched and saturated alongside screamed vocals and hoover stabs.

breakstep.description: Breakstep is the 2000 to 2002 link between garage and dubstep: 2 step that borrows breaks, jungle basslines and a darker tone, before halfstep would go on to impose its slowness. Zinc with 138 Trek, Zed Bias and early Plastician marked out the territory. It was short lived and transitional, yet indispensable to the genealogy of British bass music, a brief window in which garage's swing collided with jungle's syncopation and dubstep's weight before any of those later genres had fully crystallized into the forms that would come to define the next decade of UK bass.
breakstep.production: Breakstep sits between 135 and 140 BPM, keeping 2 step's heavier swing, 58 to 62 percent, but pushing the tone dark: a chopped breakbeat runs fast on top while kick and bass stay slow underneath. The skeleton is 2 step, kick on beat one and the offbeat 2.5, a heavy snare on two and four, but a funk break sliced into sixteenths, high pass filtered to stay clear of the kick, adds jungle syncopation, run through crunchy, downsampled processing for a grainy texture. The bass pairs a deep sub with a jungle Reese, two detuned sawtooths through a slow low pass filter, alternating with the kick, arriving on the offbeat and holding until 2.5, with just two or three notes. Dark synth stabs, dub sirens, sampled MC shouts and tape delayed percussion complete a grey sound for a sound system.

bristolsound.description: The local root of trip hop: the Wild Bunch collective in the 1980s, sound systems, dub, punk and soul in the same port city. Smith and Mighty lay down its first recorded translations, Massive Attack would grow out of it. This entry documents the mother scene, the one before the word trip hop existed, when Bristol invented its own slowness, years before the genre had a name.
bristolsound.production: 1980s Bristol is faster and brighter than the trip hop that followed, 90 to 105 bpm, a hip hop breakbeat or lovers rock tempo. The swing comes from the sampled breaks themselves rather than any setting, so program straight and let the break carry its own feel, with a straight kick on every beat like digital reggae. Build it from two layers, a looped funk drum break, and a dry drum machine kick underneath, a spring-reverbed snare cracking on 2 and 4, an offbeat rimshot like a reggae skank, and a dub-style wood block running through a delay. For bass, play deep sound system lines on electric bass, a lovers rock model, mixed loud and heavily compressed. Layer reworked soul samples, a softly sung vocal, spring reverb, tape delay, and cassette hiss standing in for the tape.

brokenbeat.description: Broken beat is the jazz and soul answer to quantized dance music, born in west London around the year 2000. Its rhythms sway in ways almost impossible to count, wrapped around rich chords and a direct heritage of jazz-funk and the Reinforced scene. Bugz in the Attic and IG Culture ran its laboratory, and the club Co-Op gave it a home. It is musicians' music for demanding dancers, reevaluated by a new generation every decade.
brokenbeat.production: Broken beat runs between 120 and 130 BPM, but the tempo matters less than the sway, which comes from an extreme MPC3000 swing, 65 to 70 percent on the sixteenths, and kick and snare placements landing beside the beat: the snare a sixteenth late on two or early on four, the kick shifting bar to bar. Program the kick on beat one, the sixteenth before three, and the and of four, snare on the sixteenth after two and on four, reversing next bar, wrapped in congas and agogo bells with their own swing. The bass should sound played, an electric bass or Moog line running root, fifth, sixth, minor seventh and octave in syncopated sixteenths, with glissandi and ghost notes. Center it on a played Fender Rhodes voicing ninth chords, the contrast between hand and machine being the point.

brokentechno.description: Broken techno refuses the four-on-the-floor kick without ever leaving the dancefloor: displaced kicks, smashed-up breaks, and a swing digested from electro and UK bass. From the experiments of Blawan and Objekt to the broken anthems of Overmono, it is the liveliest corner of recent British techno, where rave heritage keeps returning in fragments. The term stays deliberately vague, even as the approach itself is perfectly clear.
brokentechno.production: Broken techno runs 125 to 140 BPM, Overmono nearer 130 to 135, Blawan and Objekt pushing to 140, with swing as the central ingredient, an MPC groove of 55 to 62 percent filled out by low-velocity ghost notes. The grid is present but the kick refuses to follow it: place hits on beat one, the offbeat of two, beat three and the last sixteenth of the bar, changing every two bars, while a snare anchors two and four. Build twin basses on the same motif, a clean sub close to an organ tone, and a howling main bass, two detuned saws through a resonant filter, pushed through heavy saturation, grouped with the sub. Source the top layer from resampling, chopping a recorded sequence into slices and replaying them shifted, alongside wobbling basses and pitched metallic impacts.

brostep.description: The American mutation of dubstep around 2010: the bass moved out of the subwoofer and into the midrange, metallic growls, rollercoaster drops, video game aggression. Rusko started it, Skrillex made it global and became the lightning rod for the debate that followed. Despised by Croydon purists, it nonetheless trained an entire generation of producers in aggressive, detailed sound design work.
brostep.production: Hold 140 BPM as in the dubstep it comes from, snare on beat three, but the half time feel becomes a pretext: the drop fills up with sixteenths, triplets and sudden silences in the bass, swing all but disappears, and everything quantizes tight for fills. Layer the kick with a 909 click and a short sub, and the snare with a clap, white noise and an acoustic snare, with syncopated ghost kicks answering the bass in between. Build snare rolls that move from eighths to sixteenths to triplets over sixteen bars with a riser before the drop. The growl is the heart of the genre: a rich wavetable in Serum or Massive, light FM from a second oscillator, a formant filter, and several LFOs synced to shifting rates modulating cutoff and wavetable position, with the sub a separate mono sine.

chicagohouse.description: In Chicago's early 1980s, DJs at the Warehouse and the Music Box stretched disco out with drum machines, and their regulars eventually moved into the studio themselves. The TR-909 and synthetic basslines replaced the orchestra, turning the track into a mixing tool as much as a song. Jack, the trance of the body, became the watchword. Everything the word house means today traces back to these records pressed on Trax and DJ International, the raw blueprint the entire genre grew from.
chicagohouse.production: Aim for 120 to 124 BPM on a TR-909 or TR-707, straight with no swing, or only a light 52 to 54 percent. The groove comes from contrast rather than humanization: a steady kick against hats and claps that land off the grid, and a bass that pushes on the off-beat. Layer a boomy 909 kick near 50 to 60 Hz, a clap on 2 and 4 nudged a sixteenth late for the jacking feel, closed hi-hats in eighths, and a syncopated cowbell. Keep it to four or five elements, with simple tom fills every eight bars. The bass is a short, monophonic Juno-106 or Poly-61 sawtooth, lowpass filtered around 300 to 600 Hz, bouncing an octave between root and off-beat, between 80 and 250 Hz.

chillout.description: Chill-out was born in the back rooms of English raves around 1990, when the KLF released Chill Out and clubs began opening separate rooms where dancers could catch their breath: soft pads, radio samples and slowed-down beats. It later grew into an industry of poolside compilation albums, but the original chill-out sound remains an art of decompression, ambient music with a smile rather than a straight face. It keeps a foot on the dancefloor even while resting, letting a beat drift in and out rather than disappearing altogether. Acts such as the KLF and, later, Zero 7 shaped its warm, unhurried, slightly wistful character.
chillout.production: Chill-out treats time as more important than tempo: 80 to 100 BPM when there is a beat at all, often none for minutes, its freedom to let rhythm appear, fade and return slower sets it apart from downtempo. Pick around 92 BPM as a delay reference and let pads float unquantized; when a beat arrives keep it simple and unswung, like a machine left running next door. Build it from a softened 808, kick filtered low, snare swapped for a reverb-drowned rimshot, low-velocity eighth hats, through a filter opening slowly so the beat seems to arrive from afar. The bass is soft and sparing, a fingered electric line or a long-release sine Moog holding notes over two bars, quieter than in downtempo since it accompanies rather than leads. Wide detuned pads and field recordings complete the sound.

chillwave.description: The summer of 2009 blogosphere: bedroom pop veiled in reverb and VHS nostalgia, detuned synths, drowned vocals, memories of summers never lived. Washed Out, Neon Indian and Toro y Moi form its founding triangle. Mocked in its time as a microwave genre, chillwave won in the end: half of indie pop still sounds like it, and its washed-out palette became a permanent color in the wider genre.
chillwave.production: Sit between 85 and 110 bpm with a slowed 1980s pop feel: chillwave is a proper song, verse and chorus, sung, with a straight drum machine groove, though the whole track wobbles because a cassette wow on the master bends pitch and time together. Build the drum machine from cheap, lo-fi sources, the simplest possible pattern, kick on 1 and 3, snare or clap on 2 and 4, a tambourine drowned in reverb, the whole kit low-passed. For bass, use a square filtered around 500Hz with chorus, playing 1980s pop lines, cut low since chillwave has little sub by nature. Layer detuned, chorused synths through a low-pass and reverb, a doubled, drowned vocal, slowed pop samples, and a chorused guitar, all run through simulated cassette hiss and saturation.

clickscuts.description: A laboratory of micro sound applied to rhythm, built around Mille Plateaux's Clicks and Cuts label at the turn of the 2000s. The glitch became raw material: digital clicks, CD reading errors, silences cut with a scalpel, assembled into spectral grooves. More radical than the microhouse it later fed, it marks a pivotal moment when German electronic music turned to examine its own raw material and process.
clickscuts.production: Tempo swings further than in microhouse, from around 100 BPM for Pole's dub pieces up to 130 for Akufen. The feel is often deliberately irregular: a grid exists, but some clicks fall off it, shifted by a few milliseconds like reading errors. Use moderate swing, or none at all with everything placed by hand, and treat silence as a rhythmic element. Build the kick from a short sine or a raw digital pop, and the snare from a fragment of error, a skipping CD or a dropout, cut with no fade so the click becomes the material. Keep the loop at four beats but fragmented, kick only on one and three, irregular clicks, an empty eighth in the middle. The bass stays sparse, a round sine sub, or a barely present low drone.

coldwave.description: France and Belgium between 1979 and 1984 answered English post-punk with poorer means and a drier kind of gloom: cheap drum machines, basslines pushed to the front, and blank, deadpan vocals sung in the artists' own languages. Long a confidential scene, cold wave has since been reassessed as a major source, and its lo-fi grain now haunts half of today's dark productions.
coldwave.production: Work between 100 and 140 BPM, most often 120 to 130, with the flat, nuance-free energy of a cheap drum machine pushed by punk urgency and no swing. Set the project around 126 BPM, quantize the drums, but play the bass and guitar by hand, the contrast between the rigid box and the human instruments is the heart of the sound. Use a cheap preset drum machine like a CR-78, TR-606, or DR-55, barely processed beyond light downsampling and soft tape saturation, with no fills and no variation from start to finish. The electric bass is the lead instrument, played with a pick in eighth notes through a slow chorus, carrying the main melody, mixed almost as loud as the vocal with light overdrive and compression.

cosmic.description: Cosmic Disco is less a production style than a way of spinning records, born at the Afro-Cosmic Club near Verona in the late 1970s. Daniele Baldelli slowed everything down, blending funk disco, German electronic music and African percussion, often by playing records at the wrong speed. The result is hypnotic and slow, sitting between 90 and 110 beats per minute, and its influence reaches far beyond the small number of records actually released under the name. It began as a DJ practice, built on pitch and patience, before becoming a recognizable studio sound, one that still shapes slow, dubby dance floors today.
cosmic.production: Set the project at 100 bpm, in the slow 90 to 110 range, with samples pitched down 20 to 30 percent and a 55 percent swing on sixteenths. Slow a funk or disco drum break with warp off, or in Re-Pitch mode, so the tone drops with the tempo, giving a round kick and a thickened snare. Layer loose African percussion, congas, shakers, bells, through a tape echo with 40 percent feedback. For bass, hold long root notes through a filtered Moog, low-pass near 200Hz, release around 300ms, cutting below 40Hz so the kick owns 50 to 80Hz. Add slow, repeating arpeggios with the filter drifting over 32 bars.

crossbreed.description: Crossbreed is the formalized pact between hard drum and bass and industrial hardcore, struck around 2010: gabber kicks driving underneath neurofunk-style breaks at 175 to 180 BPM. The Outside Agency and the PRSPCT label turned it into a solid bridge between two audiences that had previously ignored each other. The name says it all: a deliberate, effective crossbreeding of two hard-edged scenes rather than a subtle fusion. Tracks typically alternate between the two engines within the same drop, switching from a rolling breakbeat to a pounding four-on-the-floor gabber kick and back, built above all to be mixed and played loud in a club.
crossbreed.production: Crossbreed runs 175 to 180 BPM, above drum and bass so its gabber kicks keep their violence, built in square 4/4 bars for mixing, alternating two drum engines: a hardened two-step neurofunk pattern, kick on beat 1 and the and of 3, snare on 2 and 4, and a straight 4/4 gabber kick whose decay is pushed to 400 ms and distorted until the tail becomes a note. In the drop, alternate four bars of two-step with four of the 4/4 kick, then combine both, the hardcore kick on the beats with the break on top. The bass, a resampled Reese or FM bass, works around the tuned kick tail, high-passed in the midrange during two-step, falling silent once the 4/4 kick takes over, heavily sidechained. A synthesized gabber kick and industrial screeches round out a palette built for impact.

darkambient.description: Dark ambient is ambient music that chooses the night: low drones, crypt-like resonances, industrial textures slowed down to near stillness. Lustmord set the reference point with Heresy in 1990, recorded inside real underground spaces. It is a music of total immersion, cousin to horror cinema, sustained by a faithful worldwide scene and a handful of devoted labels. There is no dancefloor here, only a room built entirely out of sound.
darkambient.production: Dark ambient has no tempo, and moves even slower than classic ambient: a drone can take 45 seconds to rise, with an event every couple of minutes, and a BPM, if set at all, only serves to line up the delays. Nothing sings here, everything rumbles, movement coming from free, unsynced LFOs at 0.03 to 0.05 Hz on filter, pitch and pan, so nothing ever repeats exactly. There is no regular percussion, only isolated impacts, a dull thud every 20 to 40 seconds, set against field recordings from underground spaces, cisterns and parking garages, the way Lustmord recorded Heresy. The bass is the low drone and it dominates everything, aimed at 30 to 60 Hz, a sine for weight plus a filtered sawtooth for body, two oscillators detuned to produce a slow beating that vibrates the room.

darkcore.description: The winter of 1992 to 1993 in English hardcore: the euphoria fades, pianos disappear, and breaks get wrapped in anxious pads and horror samples. Mr Kirk's Nightmare set the tone, as rave discovered its dark side. Darkcore is the passage through which hardcore became jungle, and Goldie's Reinforced period is its beating heart, not to be confused with the modern gabber darkcore, a different world entirely and a separate lineage.
darkcore.production: Darkcore keeps the 1992 hardcore tempo but pushes further, 150 to 160 BPM, the zone where the break starts running on its own. The feel changes completely: where hardcore bounces, darkcore slides, with breaks time stretched rather than pitched up, sometimes pitched down, giving a cold, dragging edge, and no continuous kick under the break, which appears only in sections for weight. Time stretch the break the old way, warping rather than transposing it, which creates grain and metallic artefacts on the cymbals, and reinforce it with a 909 kick on beat one and scattered rimshots. The sub is menacing because it barely moves, a sine held over long notes with a slight glide between distant notes. Replace the pianos with a held minor chord, and layer horror samples, dialogue, screams, creaking doors, with long reverb.

darkdisco.description: Dark disco is a slow chug between 115 and 125 beats per minute, built on organic, often live played basslines and cold synths inherited from cold wave and italo, without the euphoric build of indie dance. The movement was born between France and Germany around 2017, and it recognizes one founding track: Damon Jee's remix of Power To The People, released on Roam Recordings. The scene lives through its labels and podcasts, moving between dark clubs and festivals that have since claimed it as their own. It favors mood and tension over release, staying low and heavy rather than lifting toward a euphoric peak.
darkdisco.production: Set the tempo at 120 BPM, heavy and steady with little or no swing: the track should advance on a hypnotic plateau rather than build to a euphoric peak. An 808 clone kick, round and slightly long, holds all four beats, with a dry clap or snare on two and four and closed hi hats in eighths opening on the offbeat for a marching feel. 808 toms hammer eighth note patterns through the second half of each bar, the genre's tribal signature. The bass, often a real electric bass or a Korg MS-20, sawtooth, low pass filtered near 400 Hz, compressed hard, chorused and saturated, repeats a minor riff for bars at a time and doubles the kick. On top sit an acid MS-20 lead, unchorused Juno-106 pads, spoken low reverbed vocals, and long delayed guitars.

darkelectro.description: Dark electro is the European school of the 1990s that pushed electro-industrial music toward horror: whispered, saturated vocals, icy minor-key melodies, and atmospheres modeled on the autopsy room. Labels such as Zoth Ommog and Off Beat published its canon during the decade. The scene remains alive today in gothic-industrial clubs, where the style still functions almost as a liturgical language, its rituals intact.
darkelectro.production: Dark electro sits between 120 and 140 BPM, straight and metronomic with no swing, some tracks dropping to 100 for liturgical passages; keep the kick perfectly regular and let irregularity come from off-grid noise samples, a slamming door, a medical instrument, a breath. The kick is drier and tighter than its electro-industrial parent, a short 909 with no reverb, while the snare is thin but drenched in a long, dark reverb around 3 seconds that builds the autopsy-room feel, and hats alternate cleanly between two velocities. The bass is a minor-key arpeggio rather than a repeated note, a sawtooth with a lowpass filter opening slowly over 8 bars, descending root, fifth, minor third, minor second for the chill. The voice is whispered then pushed through heavy overdrive with the formant lowered, set against icy pads and horror-film samples.

darkpsy.description: Dark psy is the nocturnal, high speed side of psytrance, formalized in the mid 2000s across Russia, Germany and Brazil at 148 to 160 beats per minute and beyond. It is built from grating textures, horror movie voice samples, black humor and an abrasive kind of trance. It is the music of a festival's deepest hours, when the dancefloor has thinned to the people who still know why they are there.
darkpsy.production: Dark psy starts at a minimum of 148 BPM, most tracks between 150 and 158, some past 160; at that speed a rolling bass turns to vibration, so the genre leans on triplet figures. The kick is dry and short with no tail, tuned high around 65 to 70 Hz so the low end stays clean, paired with a thin, sharp snare or metallic hit, irregular sixteenth hats, and micro percussion. The bass follows the same triplet logic, kick on the first triplet of each beat and bass on the other two. FM8 and Absynth supply metallic, talking textures and anxious granular pads, short horror film samples run through filtered delays and pitch shifts, and leads stay rare, resonant blips bouncing in a ping pong delay.

darkstep.description: Darkstep is the darkest, fastest side of drum and bass: breaks fired in bursts, hostile basslines, apocalyptic imagery, right at the border with breakcore. Panacea embodied it from 1997 on the German side, and Technical Itch and Limewax hardened it further afterward. This is drum and bass built for caves, and it wears that image proudly. Where its cousins chase euphoria, darkstep chases dread.
darkstep.production: Darkstep plays between 175 and 185 BPM, the highest tempo in drum and bass before breakcore, distinguished from its techstep parent by density: where techstep leaves silence, darkstep fills everything with Amen bursts and doubled kicks, the feel closer to a chase than a groove, no swing. A base two-step kick on 1 and the and of 3 gets doubled with a second hit a sixteenth later for a hammering effect, while a saturated Amen break at full tempo fires in two-bar bursts, thirty-second cuts and a beat of silence. The bass is a Reese pushed harder than techstep's, distorted in series and resampled, growling under a fast filter LFO, playing long root notes with descending fifth glissandi, sidechained hard so the hammering cuts through. On top, screaming resonant leads and horror-film samples drowned in reverb build the claustrophobic atmosphere.

darkwave.description: Darkwave is the dark, synthetic side of 1980s European new wave: deep vocals, funereal pads and black romanticism, sitting somewhere between guitar-driven gothic rock and pure electronics. The term gathered up dispersed scenes after the fact, from Clan of Xymox to the current revival that made Lebanon Hanover a late-arriving icon. It overlaps in part with cold wave, a border that is as much linguistic as musical.
darkwave.production: Darkwave sits between 90 and 130 BPM, most dance tracks around 110 to 125, driven by a straight 1980s drum machine, a LinnDrum or TR-707, but rounder and fuller than the cold wave it descends from, since reverb and pads slow how the tempo is perceived. Build the kick on the beats with an extra hit on the offbeat of three, a snare on two and four wrapped in gated reverb, the sound of the decade, and eighth-note hats opening on the last offbeat, with clean tom fills every eight bars and no distortion. Layer two basses, an electric bass with chorus playing melodic lines, and a Juno-106 saw bass an octave below, both forward in the mix, almost level with the vocal. The Juno-106 carries chorused saw pads on minor chords, answered by arpeggios and a deep, baritone vocal.

deconstructedclub.description: Deconstructed club shatters the dancefloor into fragments: signifiers of rave, reggaeton and grime cut apart and reglued without a stable grid, a post-internet aesthetic mixing violence and fragility. PC Music on one side, NON and Janus collectives on the other, the style served as a laboratory for the decade's experimental pop, from Arca to SOPHIE. It treats the club track less as a functional tool than a piece meant to be listened to as much as danced to.
deconstructedclub.production: Deconstructed club has no fixed tempo, and that is the point: start from a base of 130 to 140 BPM to converse with grime and dembow, then break it with tempo automation, sections dropping to 90 or jumping to 160, rhythmic fragments from rave, reggaeton, grime and ballroom never holding for more than four bars. A saturated gabber kick might run four bars, a dembow pattern for two, an isolated grime snare for one, followed by silence, with metallic impacts and slamming doors placed off-grid as drums. The sub works as an impact rather than a line, a sine explosion at 40 Hz with the pitch envelope dropping an octave in 200 milliseconds, kick and sub ignoring or colliding rather than sidechaining cleanly. On top, granular synthesis stretches voices into clouds and hyperreal textures snap like plastic and latex.

deeptech.description: The London crossover of minimal and tech house in the 2010s: dark sub bass inherited from UK garage, rolling grooves, a basement mood rather than a festival one. A scene of residencies and intimate clubs, driven by FUSE and its offshoots, where the flow of the set matters more than any single track, and continuity between records is prized above drama.
deeptech.production: Sit at 125 to 128 bpm, with a groove inherited from UK garage: 55 to 58 percent swing on the sixteenths, accents landing on the off eighths, while kick and bass stay straight. Build a dry, short 909 kick with a marked click, a thin clap or rimshot on 2 and 4, tight closed hats on every sixteenth, and rolling percussion, a tom or conga with gaps, plus a shaker and a block pattern that drops a step every 4 bars. The sub bass carries the track: a low sine with light saturation, holding two beats then a short note, joined by a triangle an octave up, gliding to the minor seventh, sidechained from the kick. Keep textures sparse, a fading minor chord, a pitched-down vocal fragment, and low club recordings for atmosphere.

detroitelectro.description: Detroit electro emerged after techno, with Drexciya inventing an underwater mythology and a maniacally precise sound, and Dopplereffekt bringing a theoretical coldness to the same lineage. The school continues through Ectomorph and finds its European relay in the Clone label. It treats electro as serious science fiction, machine funk without nostalgia, and remains one of the most respected lineages on the whole electronic music map. Where much electro leans on retro-futurist charm, this strain is deliberately clinical and forward-looking, built from tightly sequenced analogue synths rather than samples, and prizes precision and concept as much as groove.
detroitelectro.production: Detroit electro runs 125 to 140 BPM, Drexciya often around 130 to 135, Dopplereffekt slower, on a rigorously quantized grid with zero swing, its patterns built as 16-step loops, sometimes odd-numbered so they drift against the grid and realign after several bars. Build a precise 808 kick with a short decay, an 808 snare on 2 and 4, closed hats ramping in velocity, and tuned 808 toms playing a three-note motif on even bars. The bass is analogue and constantly moving, a mixed saw and square tone through a filter with a slow eight-bar cutoff sweep, playing octave and fifth jumps on a chromatic minor scale, sometimes split into a held low root and a higher line. Cold, detuned pads, a mono lead with portamento, and Drexciya's aquatic textures complete a palette of oscillators alone, no samples or vocals.

detroittechno.description: Detroit techno was born in the mid 1980s when Juan Atkins, Derrick May and Kevin Saunderson, suburban kids from Belleville, crossed the synthetic funk of Parliament with Kraftwerk and the futurist writing of Alvin Toffler. The result was both mechanical and melancholic, synthetic strings floating over drum machines against the backdrop of a deindustrialized city. The word techno itself comes from this scene, and the Detroit lineage remains the conscience of the entire genre.
detroittechno.production: Detroit techno runs 120 to 136 BPM, Cybotron and Model 500 around 120 to 128, Underground Resistance up to 136, with toms and hats nudged by hand rather than fully quantized, felt rather than seen. A TR-909 kick holds a straight four on the floor with a shortened decay, while three or four tuned toms placed across the beat are the real signature, closed hats grooving in sixteenths, open hat on the offbeats. The bass is often the toms themselves, tuned to the root and echoed, or a real line from a DX7, ESQ-1 or Operator playing staccato eighths on the tonic, or a sustained sub on the root, kick, tom and sub tuned to the same note. Synthetic strings carry the harmony, joined by an electric piano and a Juno pad, all pushed through light saturation for grain.

digitalhardcore.description: Digital hardcore was founded in Berlin in 1994 when Alec Empire started the label Digital Hardcore Recordings, welding together saturated breakbeats, screamed punk vocals and radical politics. Atari Teenage Riot became its commando unit, with the slogan riot sounds produce riot people. Closer to a riot than to a club, the genre passed its rage on to breakcore and its name on to an entire attitude.
digitalhardcore.production: Digital hardcore runs 160 to 200 BPM, often 170 to 180, though energy matters more than the exact number since this is punk played with machines, its grid a saturated breakbeat, often the Amen. The break is chopped roughly and pushed through heavy saturation and eight bit reduction, sitting under a distorted 909 kick on one and three, or every beat in hardest passages, and a doubled snare on two and four. There is rarely a written bassline, the low end coming from the distorted kick and sampled guitar power chords through a saturated amp, or a heavily distorted saw or square holding a short punk riff in the guitar's key. Screamed political vocals, sampled guitar riffs, speeches, sirens and eight bit noise fill out the mix, all distorted without exception, nothing meant to sound clean.

disco.description: Disco was born in New York's Black and Latino clubs in the early 1970s, turning soul and funk into music built for the floor: a steady four-beat pulse, hi-hats opened on the offbeats, strings and horns arranged like a full orchestra. It was the first music conceived for the DJ rather than the live band, and the 12 inch single was invented specifically for it. Everything this site maps traces back to that one decision: stretching the groove out as long as possible.
disco.production: Classic disco runs 110 to 125 BPM, centered around 118 to 122, played rather than sequenced, with 52 to 56 percent swing on the sixteenths and hats dragged 5 to 10 milliseconds late. The kick is round on every beat, the snare cracks on 2 and 4 doubled by a tambourine, and the hi-hat is the real signature: closed on the beat, open on the offbeat eighths, the Earl Young pattern heard on MFSB and the Trammps. Add sixteenth-note congas with simple tumbaos and a shaker. The bass is electric and finger-played, syncopated around the kick with octave jumps and muted notes in the style of Bernard Edwards for Chic. On top, staccato strings, horn stabs on the offbeats, wah guitar cut in sixteenths, and Rhodes or clavinet filling the middle.

discodub.description: Disco dub is the instrumental B-side of New York disco, the point where the sound engineer becomes the artist. Working under the direct influence of Jamaican dub, Walter Gibbons and later Larry Levan and Francois K stretched tracks out, cut the vocals, drowned the brass in echo and let the rhythm section breathe on its own. It marks the birth of the remix as a work in its own right, and it established the working method that all dance music since has followed: mute, reveal, extend, repeat. The mixing console itself becomes the lead instrument, turning a finished song into raw material for a new, extended journey.
discodub.production: Disco dub keeps the tempo of the song it reworks, generally 110 to 125 BPM as played by the original band, setting the project to the multitrack's tempo and using warp mode to lock played drums to the grid without stiffening them. Its rhythm is not new but the existing disco groove stripped bare, with silences the engineer carves out live at the console: time becomes elastic through echo rather than tempo. Start from a multitrack, or fake one from separate drum, conga, tambourine and bass tracks, then work by muting and revealing, congas alone, then the kick, then the hats, sending the snare into a tape echo on select hits. The original bass becomes the through-line, brought forward and compressed. The Roland RE-201 Space Echo and a plate reverb turning brass into distant pads are the real instruments here.

discohouse.description: House music that openly repays its debt to disco by sampling it outright: loops of strings and basses filtered open and shut with a lowpass, like a curtain being raised and lowered. New York practiced it from the 1990s onward, and the French touch turned it into a manifesto. Here the sample is never hidden but celebrated, reworked until it becomes a new chorus in its own right.
discohouse.production: Work between 122 and 128 BPM, faster than the 110 to 120 of the original records. Respect the loop's own swing, warped into place, but keep a straight, unswung 909 underneath, the contrast between the two is the groove. Filter the loop below 120 Hz so the 909 kick stays the only kick, letting the loop's own hats and shaker carry the feel, with a sampled conga on choruses. Fills are loop cuts or a filter slam, and on the break the 909 drops out to let the loop breathe. The bassline isolates the sample's own bass under a 200 Hz lowpass, or reprograms a funky line in eighths with octave jumps, backed by a sine sub and a light sidechain.

discopunk.description: Punk bands playing disco rhythms: a first wave in New York between 1978 and 1982, a second wave in the early 2000s. The rhythm section stays danceable and tense, played with punk's rage and economy, while the guitar scratches rather than sings. Liquid Liquid and ESG represent one wave, The Rapture and LCD Soundsystem the other, twenty years apart but sharing the same nervous energy.
discopunk.production: Disco punk moves fast and pushes forward, 120 to 135 BPM, usually 125 to 130, played with a slight rush, drummers leaning a few milliseconds ahead on the hats and snare rather than adding swing. Set the project at 128 BPM and nudge the hats a touch early, the signature is a disco four-on-the-floor played with punk's economy, few elements, all of them tense, a cowbell in eighths, and a bassline repeated to the point of hypnosis, nothing floats, everything stays tight and a little aggressive. Play the drums live wherever possible, with a dry kick on the four beats, a sharp snare on 2 and 4, closed hats in eighths, and a cowbell doubled by hand percussion like congas and claves, with clean cuts instead of long fills.

doomcore.description: Slow, funereal hardcore invented by The Mover out of Frankfurt: pads of apocalypse, cavernous kicks, and the atmosphere of an empty cathedral after the end of the world, running between 130 and 150 beats per minute. It has been an absolute cult favorite among connoisseurs of the PCP label, a style that was never mainstream and never tried to be. Its spiritual descendants run all the way to today's doomcore-wave revival.
doomcore.production: Doomcore slows hardcore down to 130 to 150 BPM, often 135 to 140 in The Mover's own tracks, the only branch of hardcore where the tempo drops below fast techno, and that slowness is the point, each kick has time to ring out and the space between hits becomes a place of its own. There is no swing, but a deliberate heaviness, delay pads by 20 to 30ms for a dragging effect, and program at 138 BPM, many tracks hold the same pattern for eight minutes, patience is the technique. The kick is a distorted 909 like in hard techno but treated with a long, dark reverb, unusual elsewhere in the family, sitting on all four beats or only 1 and 3 in the heaviest passages, with a distant, reverbed 909 snare or a long-plated clap on 2 and 4.

downtempogenre.description: Tempo brought down as a principle of pleasure: grooves between 80 and 110, round basses, jazz and soul samples, electronic music sitting back and relaxing. The term gathers what the 1990s variously called trip hop, chill or lounge depending on the angle. Kruder & Dorfmeister turned it into a Viennese art form, and it still fuels bar and lounge playlists worldwide decades after the style first appeared.
downtempogenre.production: Aim for 85 to 105 BPM and treat the groove like hip hop with time to spare. Swing is the key, 58 to 64 percent on the sixteenths, never fully quantized, with hats and percussion pushed behind the grid while the kick stays on the beat. The feel is often half time, the snare landing on beat three rather than two and four, which makes the track seem to float at half its actual speed. The kick is round and muffled, often a low tuned 808 or a sampled soul break kick with a short tail, while the snare is soft, a rimshot or a clap doubled with a filtered break snare. Hats play swung eighths alternating strong and weak velocities, joined by a humanised shaker, and a slowed, filtered jazz break often sits under the kit for dust.

dreamtrance.description: Italy between 1995 and 1997 turned trance into a stadium lullaby: a melancholic piano carries the hook, a house trance rhythm section does the rest. Children by Robert Miles, written to calm deadly rave traffic on Italian highways, became its planetary manifesto. The genre burned out in two summers but left a lasting mark on all of melodic dance music, proving that a piano melody could carry a whole dance floor.
dreamtrance.production: Sit between 130 and 140 bpm, but the feel is that of a song: the tempo serves the piano. Keep the grid straight, counting in 8-bar phrases that match the melody, with breaks where the kick drops and the piano carries the tempo alone. Soften the 909: low-pass the kick near 6kHz, a soft clap on 2 and 4, an open hat on the offbeat at low volume, and only a short roll before drops. For bass, follow the piano's root notes on a Juno-106 or filtered square, doubled by a sub sine, with a light kick sidechain. The piano lead carries everything: an 8-bar minor melody with held notes and silences, backed by string pads and a filtered choir, with a short delay and a long hall reverb.

drillnbass.description: The auteur hijacking of jungle in the mid 1990s: Squarepusher and Aphex Twin, around Rephlex and Warp, push break editing into absurd, virtuosic overdrive, IDM melody layered on top, humor and vertigo. This is not DJ music but a fireworks display of composition, one that would go on to shape breakcore and complex chamber electronics, prized more for listening than for mixing.
drillnbass.production: There is no club tempo here: sit anywhere between 150 and 200 bpm, often shifting mid track, with bars in 7/8 or 5/4 slipped in without warning, the feel of a virtuoso drummer who drank too much coffee. Build it by chopping an Amen or jazz break into dozens of slices per bar and writing each hit note by note in the piano roll, alternating two-step passages with bursts of thirty-second notes on the snare, pitch-shifting each slice. For bass, choose either a fast, played electric bass, slapped or walked, sampled note by note, or a TB-303 style acid line, running its own melody independent of the kick, with no sidechain. Layer soft IDM pads, music boxes and detuned pianos built through cascading resampling, a sound transformed until unrecognizable, then played back on a keyboard.

drone.description: The sustained note as a complete form: descended from La Monte Young and minimalism, carried forward by the guitars of Stars of the Lid or the amplifiers of Sunn O))). Drone works the raw material of sound over long duration, beating harmonics, suspended time. Sitting between ambient, metal and composed music, it is a transversal continent more than a closed genre, claimed by all three worlds at once.
drone.production: There is no tempo, and time is measured in minutes: a drone piece is a single note or chord held for ten or twenty minutes, with no events at all, since the movement lives entirely in timbre. Set a BPM of around 40 purely to sync LFOs, otherwise think in seconds. Beating between two close pitches produces a few beats per second, and changing that gap changes the pulse, the only metronome the genre has. There is no percussion: rhythm lives in the harmonics beating against each other, the tremolo of a tube amplifier, a bow crossing the string, or looping tape returning again. Stack two layers of the same sound slightly detuned to let a slow beating appear, and work intervals in just intonation, since a pure fifth does not beat while a tempered one beats slowly.

drumandbass.description: Jungle stylized and technicalized from 1995 onward: cleaner breaks, synthetic basses, jeweler's precision at 170 beats per minute. Goldie and Metalheadz turn it into a dark, futuristic club art, LTJ Bukem into floating elegance. Thirty years later the genre still turns, a global industry and an underground scene at once, a rare case of longevity in bass music, still built on the same two-step skeleton it invented.
drumandbass.production: Settle between 170 and 174 bpm, the break rebuilt step by step on a grid, groove coming from precise placement rather than swing.
