Build the two-step base, kick on 1, snare on 2 and 4, kick again on the and of 3, then layer a sub-heavy kick, a stacked snare, and a classic break, Amen, Think, Apache, high-passed underneath for hats and ghost notes. For bass, run two layers always: a clean sub sine between 40 and 55Hz, and a Reese on top, detuned saws in opposite directions, unison spread in stereo, filter moving by envelope then slow LFO, high-passed so it clears space for the sub. Add cold pads and saws for leads, white noise risers for transitions, and the signature heavily compressed parallel drum bus blended under the original.

drumfunk.description: The cult of the breakbeat taken to its furthest extreme: entire drum patterns recomposed hit by hit, living polyrhythms built from scratch, and a permanent homage to the session drummers of the 1970s. Paradox stands as the genre's guardian, with Photek preceding him as its aesthete. It remains a tiny and obstinate scene, but an essential one for understanding just how far the art of the break can be pushed.
drumfunk.production: Drumfunk sits between 165 and 172 BPM, a touch slower than standard drum and bass so the breaks have room to breathe, and the feel is entirely borrowed from the original drummer's playing, the swing is the one captured on a 1972 recording, not a setting. There is no fixed grid, patterns shift bar to bar with polyrhythms, three against two, from the breaks themselves, no quantization added. Source rare, whole breaks from funk, jazz-rock, and 1970s soundtracks, chop each one hit by hit at the exact start of its transient, then recombine a kick from one break, a snare from another, and a hi-hat from a third, preserving each hit's original timing.

drumstep.description: The 2010s hybrid: the tempo of drum and bass with half time drops inherited from American dubstep. Built for EDM festival stages and video games, where the doubled speed hits hard. More a production convention than a scene, it documents the moment drum and bass and brostep traded weapons and briefly shared the same festival main stage across an entire touring season.
drumstep.production: The grid runs at 174 BPM, but the drop sits in half time, the snare falling only on beat three, an 87 BPM dubstep feel. Intros and build ups stay in drum and bass two step, the drop switches to half time, and some tracks return to full drum and bass for a second drop, that switch between speeds being the whole point of the genre. Two step sections: kick on one and the and of three, snare on two and four, sixteenth note hats. The half time drop strips back to a kick on one and a snare on three, but that snare is huge and stacked: a 909 snare, a clap, a break sample and white noise with a short reverb. Hats keep running in sixteenths through the drop, and the bass wavetable wobbles on shifting LFO rates.

dub.description: Kingston, early 1970s: King Tubby and Lee Perry discover that a mixing console is an instrument. They gut songs, swell the bass and drums, drown everything else in echo: the version becomes a work in its own right. Dub invents the remix, and the sound system does the rest. Without it, there is no disco dub, no house, no jungle, no dubstep: it is the most fertile root on this map, alongside musique concrete.
dub.production: Dub carries reggae's tempo, felt as 60 to 80 bpm, built on the one drop: kick and snare land together on beat 3, beat 1 left empty, while a dotted eighth delay turns a single snare hit into a cascade. Program a dry acoustic kit, then treat it at the console: a spring reverb on the snare, a Space Echo delay with 60 percent feedback, and the defining dub gesture, cutting the whole drum bus and letting only the echo tail ring. The bass never disappears into the echo: a fingered electric line, deep and round, two-bar phrases with silences, compressed hard for constant sustain, mono and enormous. Build everything else around the console, tape echo pushed toward self-oscillation, and a reggae riddim of guitar skank, melodica and half-spoken vocal fragments.

dubstep.description: Croydon, 2002 to 2006: 2-step emptied of its vocals and slowed in spirit, hollowed out with physically felt sub-bass and dub-style space. Running at 140 beats per minute with sparse kicks, it plays like a meditation for the sound system. DMZ and FWD>> served as its churches, Rinse FM its radio station. Before its later, noisier American mutation, dubstep was a dark, contemplative music, and this entry documents that original strain.
dubstep.production: The tempo is 140 BPM without question, but the feel is halfstep: the snare lands only on beat 3, giving the sensation of a track at 70 BPM, a slowness its 2-step parent never had. Keep the swing light, 52 to 56 percent, and leave whole bars nearly empty, a two-bar loop is enough, with the bass and dub space carrying the variation. Place the kick on beat 1, sometimes a second on the off-beat of 2, and a huge snare on beat 3 only, layered with a clap under a long reverb, with sparse dub percussion run through a dotted-eighth delay.

dubstyle.description: Dubstyle was a brief hybrid from the early 2010s that crossed the kicks and structure of hardstyle with the wobbles of dubstep, played at half tempo against each other. It was more a production convention than a lasting scene, documenting the moment the hard festival world and the bass music world looked at each other. A handful of notable records marked the crossover, and then everyone went back to their own camp.
dubstyle.production: Dubstyle sits at 140 to 150 BPM, usually the hardstyle tempo of 150, doubling as dubstep speed in halftime at 70 to 75. Build two drum kits into the same track: a hardstyle mode with the kick on every beat, a reversed bass tail sucking into each offbeat, and a clap on two and four, alternating with a dubstep mode where the kick sits on one and the and of two, a huge snare lands only on beat three, the whole section feeling twice as slow. The kick itself stays the hardstyle kick, a tok with a tuned tail, even inside the dubstep sections, what separates dubstyle from real dubstep. Run two basses too, a reversed hardstyle tail on the offbeats, and a Massive wobble, a saw modulated by an LFO synced to eighths then sixteenths, hard-sidechained from the kick.

dubtechno.description: Berlin, 1993: Basic Channel applies the methods of Jamaican dub, echo, filtering, disappearance, to techno. Chords become misty pads that pulse inside the reverb, and the track becomes a state rather than a journey. Moritz von Oswald and Mark Ernestus almost never gave interviews: the music, reduced to its grain, speaks for itself. The style has become its own contemplative continent, one that still defines what a minimal, hypnotic techno track can be.
dubtechno.production: Work between 118 and 126 bpm, slower than Detroit, with a soft groove template at only 10 percent, since motion comes from delay rather than swing. Lock every delay to the tempo, dotted eighth or quarter, so it creates the sway. Build a soft, almost acoustic kick filtered above 1kHz, with faint ghost kicks before beats 3 and 4, a snare transposed far down and saturated, and alternating shakers with a closed hat on the offbeats. For bass, hold a dry mono sub sine on the root while everything else dissolves. The signature sound is a minor chord stabbed on an offbeat and sent into a Space Echo with 40 to 60 percent feedback, then a slowly moving resonant filter.

dungeonsynth.description: Born in the margins of Norwegian black metal in the early 1990s: cheap keyboards conjure the music of crypts and fortresses, deliberately lo-fi, steeped in the imagery of fantasy and role-playing games. Mortiis founded the lineage. Resurrected in the 2010s by Bandcamp into a teeming worldwide scene, cassettes included, it is, quite literally, the ambient music of dungeons.
dungeonsynth.production: This is the family's exception, a real meter and pulse, between 60 and 100 BPM, often in 3/4 or 6/8 like a medieval dance, sometimes a slow 4/4 for crypt pieces. The charm comes from stiffness: strict quantization to the quarter or eighth note, no swing, no humanization, this is a General MIDI keyboard's sequencer playing, not a musician, though tempos vary between tracks on an album. Drums are often absent, and when present come from cheap orchestral banks: timpani on beats 1 and 3, a roll ending each eight-bar phrase, a tambourine on the weak beats, fixed velocities throughout. The real rhythm comes from the keyboard's left hand, quarter or half notes marking the meter like a folk hymn on an organ, or a steady harpsichord arpeggio where there is no percussion.

earlyindustrial.description: The first industrial circle, active from 1975 to 1982: Throbbing Gristle, Cabaret Voltaire, and SPK, treating music as hostile information and the concert as a limit experience. This root entry documents the birth of that gesture, brutalizing studio technology to speak about industrial society itself. Its direct descendants sit in the wider industrial family, while its diffuse influence runs through nearly everything harsh that followed.
earlyindustrial.production: Early industrial refuses groove the way it refuses everything else: either a primitive drum machine looping monotonously between 100 and 130 BPM, or no tempo at all, as on Throbbing Gristle's United, pulsing around 120, or Cabaret Voltaire's 150 BPM Nag Nag Nag, both with no swing and no velocity nuance. Take a cheap preset rhythm, run it through a fuzz pedal and a lowpass closing off everything above 3 kHz, and dirty it further with 8-bit downsampling. Or record metallic impacts, sheet metal, cans, pipes, and loop them unevenly the way Einsturzende Neubauten and SPK did, no hi-hats or snares, only impacts and rattles. The bass is often absent or replaced by a drone, a single low note on an overdriven synth or an electric bass played by a non-bassist, or a modulated oscillator held for the whole track.

ebm.description: Electronic Body Music: Belgium and Germany between 1983 and 1989 militarize synth pop, square sequenced basslines, chanted shouts, disciplined pounding. Front 242 coins the term, DAF the posture. It is the first European electronic music built for a collective moving body, and the direct link to new beat and then hard techno. Its revival has never really stopped since 2010, and its rigid machine pulse still defines an entire strand of club music.
ebm.production: Keep it between 120 and 130 bpm with a perfectly straight groove, zero swing, everything sequenced in rigid sixteenths, never played by hand. Build the kick from a dry TR-808 with a short decay on every beat, an 808 clap on 2 and 4 through a short gated reverb, closed hats with strong accents on the beat, and sampled metallic percussion, drums, anvils, pipes, on the offbeats. For bass, sequence a single square wave note in tight sixteenths through a low-pass around 300 to 800Hz: the root sits on the first three sixteenths, the octave jumps on the fourth for the bounce, no portamento, no sidechain. Fill in with sequencer stabs, sampled brass and metal hits, and a doubled, shouted vocal with a short slapback and plate reverb.

electroacoustic.description: The academic formalization of sound experimentation: institutional studios from Cologne to Brussels, tape and synthesis, spatialization, scores made of sound itself. Stockhausen invents whole worlds there, Xenakis applies mathematics. It is the theoretical laboratory from which popular electronic music inherited its tools, often without knowing their names, and its methods still underlie granular synthesis, spectral processing and studio composition today.
electroacoustic.production: This music thinks in duration and form rather than pulse: a piece can run without tempo for minutes, then let a steady pulse surface as an event, the balance between smooth textures and impulses replacing the beat. Work at 60 bpm so the grid maps to seconds. Build rhythm from a very short click repeated at varying speeds, since under 20 repetitions per second you hear a rhythm, above it a pitch, a threshold crossed by automating repeat rate. For bass, build a held mass rather than a line: a low sine beating against a second oscillator detuned by a few Hz, plus ring modulation for metallic tones, pitch drawn as continuous automation. Layer pure oscillators, filtered noise, transformed voice, and spectral tools with granular delay and degraded tape echoes for texture.

electroclash.description: New York and Berlin, 1998 to 2003: electro and italo disco replayed with punk arrogance and fashion-world irony, spoken vocals, cold sex appeal, and smeared mascara. Miss Kittin and The Hacker, Fischerspooner, and Peaches turned a shoestring star system into art. The bubble burst quickly, but it permanently rehabilitated italo, EBM, and synth-pop within the contemporary club world.
electroclash.production: Sit between 125 and 135 BPM, Frank Sinatra and 1982 near 130, Emerge a touch slower, on a rigid grid with zero swing, just like the italo and synth-pop it reworks. The attitude is what changes: the feel is pop and almost lazy, with spoken vocals dragging slightly behind the beat, and a four-on-the-floor kick running the whole track, unusually steady for this family. Build it from a bare TR-808 or TR-606, or both mixed together: a short 808 kick, a thin 606 snare, and metallic 606 hats, with a clap on 2 and 4 barely touched by reverb, an 808 cowbell on even bars, and at most a short snare roll before a chorus, the sparseness is deliberate.

electrofunk.description: Electro funk is the Bronx and Detroit, 1982: Afrika Bambaataa's Planet Rock lays Kraftwerk over a TR-808 and invents the funk of machines. Vocoders, breakdancing and futuristic imagery: electro funk is the first entirely electronic African American music, a direct link between robotic Europe and Detroit. The 808 earns its everlasting credentials here. It fused Kraftwerk's cold European sequencing with the rhythmic drive of American funk and the emerging language of hip hop, and in doing so it laid the groundwork not only for Detroit techno but for decades of machine funk that followed on both sides of the Atlantic.
electrofunk.production: Aim for 110 to 130 BPM, Planet Rock's territory around 126, with a square, unswung feel: patterns came off a step sequencer, so quantize hard and keep any groove under 10 percent, since electro funk is robotic by choice. Build the kit from a TR-808: kick on beat one, on the and of beats two and three, avoiding four on the floor, an 808 snare doubled with a handclap on two and four, closed hats alternating velocity, cowbell in two bar patterns. The bass is a single sawtooth on a monophonic synth, filtered low near 400 Hz with a short, sustain free envelope, bouncing between root and octave, tucked between 80 and 300 Hz to leave the 808's low end alone. Finish with a vocoder chanting through a sawtooth carrier, an orchestra hit, and a monophonic melody with slow vibrato.

electrohop.description: The West Coast took up electro-funk in the mid-1980s: dry 808 drums, vocoders, breezy rap, and the block party culture of Los Angeles. Egyptian Lover and the World Class Wreckin' Cru, featuring a young Dr. Dre, were its stars. This is the electronic prehistory of California rap, before G-funk swapped out the machines for something warmer and funkier.
electrohop.production: Play slightly faster than its Bronx electro-funk parent, between 120 and 130 BPM, with Egypt, Egypt sitting around 125, everything quantized to the sixteenth with no swing. Keep the pattern dense throughout, driven by a continuous closed hi-hat, with the rapping sitting on the eighth notes for that breezy, almost sung feel. Program the 808 dry and bare: kick on beat 1, the off-beat of 2, and just before beat 4 with a short decay, snare on 2 and 4 with a snappy top, closed hats in steady sixteenths, open hats on the off-beats, and an 808 cowbell in eighths every other bar as a near-signature sound.

electrohouse.description: The 2000s house sound that swapped disco samples for saturated synthetic basslines played like riffs. The sound is aggressive, compressed and built for big rooms, from fidget to the Dutch style. It forms the bridge between late French touch and American festival EDM, the moment house became chart music again, trading the sample culture of the 1990s for the synthesizer as a lead voice.
electrohouse.production: Sit between 125 and 130 bpm, faster than the French touch it grew from, with an aggressive, swing-free feel: the bassline plays riffs like a guitar over 1 or 2 bar phrases, structured like a rock song, verse, riff, break, riff. Build the kick from a short, compressed 909 with a bright click and saturation, layered claps on 2 and 4, bright hats, and a sampled rock snare on the drops with rising rolls before each one. For bass, layer detuned saws, low-pass 500Hz to 2kHz with light resonance, then heavy distortion and compression, played as a riff with passing notes and octave jumps, backed by a clean sub sine, with a heavy, short sidechain on the kick.

electroindustrial.description: Electro-industrial is the studio-driven hardening of EBM at the end of the 1980s: denser structures, film dialogue samples, dark pads and layered production inherited from industrial music. Skinny Puppy in Vancouver acts as its laboratory, Front Line Assembly as its factory. It is the root of the dark electro and aggrotech scenes, and the bridge between the body-focused European EBM tradition and America's studio-based approach to the same sound. Where EBM relies on a live, danceable pulse, electro-industrial piles up layers in the studio itself, favoring dread and texture over the dancefloor's straightforward drive.
electroindustrial.production: Electro-industrial usually runs 110 to 130 BPM, slower than EBM, Skinny Puppy often under 120, on a straight groove made restless by syncopated kicks, half-time sections and tempo breaks, plus deliberate offsets on percussion for mechanical unease rather than swing. Build the drums as a stack: an 808 or sampled kick off the four-on-the-floor grid, a snare doubled with a metallic impact and dark reverb, sixteenth hats often swapped for looped machine noise, and rolls from retriggering a sample with rising velocity. The bass thickens a square EBM sequence with a sawtooth layer an octave up through overdrive, moving in minor seconds and tritones, its filter envelope pinching each note, lightly sidechained. Dark pads, sampled horror dialogue, a distorted vocal chain and metallic FM textures are bounced and reworked in layers.

electromodern.description: Modern electro is the genre's worldwide revival from the late 1990s onward: I-F and the Hague scene in a dirty italo vein, Anthony Rother in a more Germanic one, then a 2010s wave around Dave Clarke, Helena Hauff and CPU. The 808 and the vocoder become a living language again, moving between techno clubs and pure electro culture, answering Detroit's founders with a rawer, more European attitude.
electromodern.production: Modern electro plays in techno clubs, 128 to 140 BPM with I-F near 130 and Helena Hauff or DJ Stingray often past 135; the grid stays strict but the feel runs heavier and dirtier than Detroit, kicks carrying more sub and sounds pushed into saturation, many tracks alternating syncopated sections with straight four-on-the-floor ones for techno. An 808 or clone drives the kit, kick on 1 and the and of 2, run through a drum bus with drive, clap or snare on 2 and 4 with a transient shaper, and closed hats alternating velocities. The bass is a bigger analog sound than Detroit's, a sawtooth over a sine sub with a short filter-decay envelope and post-synth distortion for grain, jumping in octaves on the root. On top, the vocoder returns as lead voice, white noise rises marking the club transitions.

elektronischemusik.description: Cologne, 1951. Three years after Paris, West German radio opened a studio that took the exact opposite stance to musique concrete: where Schaeffer recorded the world and cut it up, Herbert Eimert and Karlheinz Stockhausen refused any preexisting sound and built every timbre from frequency generators. Stockhausen composed Studie I there in 1953, entirely in sine tones, then Gesang der Junglinge in 1955 and 1956, blending recorded voice with synthesis in what is considered the first work of spatialized electronic music. Its descendants are immense: Kraftwerk, formed an hour away in Dusseldorf, carried this heritage to Detroit techno, while its research into pure texture flows directly into ambient music.
elektronischemusik.production: What separates Cologne from Paris is the refusal to record anything: everything here is calculated, with durations fixed by number series rather than feeling, try a short Fibonacci sequence, 3, 5, 8, 13, turned into durations in seconds or sixteenth notes. There is no groove and no swing, rhythm is treated as structure, and Stockhausen's Studie II even published its score as a graph of durations and frequency bands. There is no drum kit either, rhythmic events are envelopes applied to synthesized tones: build a sound from four additive sine operators with a 0ms attack and an 80ms decay for a metallic impulse, or a 400ms attack and a long decay for a breath-like tone, alternating the two according to your duration series, then remove notes that land on strong beats so the pulse disappears while the order remains.

eurodisco.description: Euro disco was the European studio industry's answer to American disco, with Munich and Milan leading the way. Fewer musicians, more machines: Giorgio Moroder replaced the orchestra with sequencers and introduced the repeating electronic bassline that would announce the whole of dance music to come. Vocals were often sung in slightly approximate English, the production precise and cold, and that is exactly what audiences loved. Where American disco kept its live band warmth, the European studios pushed toward mechanical repetition and controlled arrangements, a shift that quietly rewrote the rules for everything that followed in club music.
eurodisco.production: Set the project at 126 BPM with full quantization and zero swing: Munich and Milan worked to the metronome, so eighth notes stay straight and groove comes from a repeating synth sequence rather than a drummer. Kick lands on all four beats, snare doubled with a clap on two and four, hi hats in even eighths or sixteenths, open on the offbeats but restrained, tambourine and cabasa standing in for congas. The signature is the sequenced bassline: a repeated eighth note through a dotted eighth delay, sawtooth wave, low pass filter near 300 Hz with light resonance, short 80 ms envelope, modeled on I Feel Love, kick and bass landing together on the beat. Add a modular style lead, an ARP Odyssey acid line, string synth pads, and a vocoder for the cold finish.

eurotechno.description: Euro techno is techno as continental Europe digested it in the early 1990s, forged between German raves, post new beat Belgium and Italian studios. More direct and harder edged than Detroit's original blueprint, it embraces the big gesture: rave riffs, rising breaks, and kicks pushed to the front. It stands as the common trunk from which trance, hardcore and continental club techno all branch off, a bridge genre that took Detroit's machine funk and reshaped it for the scale and intensity of the European rave floor.
eurotechno.production: Run between 128 and 140 BPM, faster than Detroit or Belgium, with Speedy J and the German raves pushing toward 135 or 140, with almost no swing: the groove is straight and martial, driven by hat velocities and rolling fills that push each 16 bar phrase forward. A sustained 909 kick, sometimes doubled for body, sits on every beat, with a clap on two and four, closed hats in sixteenths opening on the offbeats, and rising snare rolls tightening into thirty second notes before a drop. Bass is a simple sub on the tonic, or more typically a low sawtooth rave riff on an Alpha Juno filtered around 800 Hz, layered with a sub sine below 80 Hz. The defining sound is the Alpha Juno hoover, joined by sirens, pitched vocal snippets and sampled rave stabs.

eurotrance.description: Euro trance is the commercial dancefloor version of trance from the turn of the 2000s: simple choruses, pitched-up vocals, pumping kicks, three minutes calibrated for radio and compilation CDs. Scorned by purists but adored on provincial dancefloors across Europe, it became the matrix for German hands up and a reservoir of nostalgia for two generations. It is trance built for the mainstream rather than the initiated, unashamed of it.
eurotrance.production: Euro trance sits at 138 to 142 BPM, usually 140, on a straight, fully quantized grid, its pumping pulse coming from hard sidechaining on the bass and pads that replaces groove entirely; everything must arrive fast on the radio, a chorus by 45 seconds, counted in 8-bar blocks. A heavily compressed 909 kick carries an accented click, a loud open hat marks the offbeat like hard trance but brighter, and a 4-bar snare roll with a reversed cymbal leads into every chorus. The bass is a pumped kick-bass, an offbeat sawtooth sidechained hard at 10:1, sitting mostly on the root with a move to the fourth or sixth on the chorus. On top, a simplified supersaw lead plays a whistleable 4 or 8 bar hook in a minor key, and hard-compressed, pitched-up female vocals carry the chorus.

fidgethouse.description: Fidget house was a joyous accident of the years 2005 to 2009: house music chopped into hiccups, basslines twisted out of shape, and pitched vocals that skip and stutter, running the insolence of UK garage through the blender of blog house. The name started as a joke between Jesse Rose and Switch, and the style burned fast and bright, leaving its mark on bass house and on every producer who grew up on its twelve inch singles.
fidgethouse.production: Fidget house runs 125 to 130 BPM, usually 128, with an exaggerated 60 to 66 percent swing on the sixteenths, giving it a jerky, hiccuping feel borrowed from UK garage, percussion pushed far behind the beat and some bass hits landing early. A fat 909 kick, often layered with a tuned 808, plays every beat except one or two removed each four bars for the hiccup, with a big clap on two and four through a gated reverb, heavily swung closed hats jumping in velocity. The bass is the true center: detuned saws through a resonant filter with a fast pitch envelope dropping a few semitones on each note, modulated by a synced LFO sweeping the cutoff, syncopated and full of gaps. Pitched, chopped vocal syllables, often shifted up for a chipmunk effect, sit over bleeps and short stabs.

floridabreaks.description: 1990s Florida: Miami electro crossed with rave culture, funky breaks around 130 to 140, round 808 basses, beach town euphoria. Orlando and Tampa turned it into a full regional culture, with DJ Icey as its local hero. Rarely exported but durable at home, it stands as America's own school of club breakbeat, distinct from both the English rave sound and the rap leaning Miami bass around it.
floridabreaks.production: Florida breaks run between 130 and 140 BPM, often 135, faster than its English nu skool cousin. The feel comes from Miami electro, funky and bouncy, with a light swing on the sixteenths and a bouncing 808 bass. A sampled break, usually electro or funk, mostly kept whole, sits over 808 programming: kick on beat one, the and of two and the a of three, 808 snare or clap on two and four, 808 hats in sixteenths opening on the offbeats, and triplet hat rolls on the last beat every four bars. Add 808 cowbells in a clave pattern and scratches as percussion. The 808 kick itself, with a long decay tuned to the root, works as the bass on strong beats, while a funky synth line on the offbeats fills the gaps with the root and seventh.

folktronica.description: Folktronica is the folding of folk music into electronic production at the turn of the 2000s: acoustic guitars chopped up on a laptop, clicks and textures layered over chamber sized melodies. Four Tet's album Pause is its founding statement, with The Books offering a more collage driven version. The name has aged badly, and the approach it described became so common that nobody bothers naming it anymore, which may be the very definition of success.
folktronica.production: Folktronica runs 80 to 125 BPM with often irregular loop lengths, three bars, five beats, seven eighths, because the tempo is a consequence of the loop rather than a starting choice. The kit is built from noises and fragments, a table hit, a key, a finger snap, a soft kick from a low tom, a snare that might be a rimshot or chopped guitar hit, granular clicks standing in for hats. The bass stays discreet and often skips the sub range, a sampled double bass, gently played electric bass, or looped low guitar string, playing sparse root and fifth motifs, since the genre is meant for living room speakers. Sampled acoustic guitar is the raw material, chopped into slices that get reordered and pitched, joined by harp, banjo, toy instruments and domestic field recordings.

footwork.description: Born from Chicago dance battles at the end of the 2000s, footwork pushes juke into abstraction: 160 beats per minute, triplet toms set against offbeat kicks, vocal samples repeated into hypnosis, and brutal silences. It is functional music for dancers and a rhythmic vertigo for everyone else. Planet Mu introduced it to the world, Teklife keeps the house, and RP Boo followed by DJ Rashad stand as its architects. Its polyrhythms are so dense and its cuts so sudden that the music can feel disorienting on record even as it remains, for the dancers it was built for, a precise and functional tool.
footwork.production: Footwork runs almost always at 160 BPM, occasionally 155 or 165, battle speed, with a doubled feel: dancers count sixteenths at 160 while the track can equally be heard in half time at 80, and the best tracks exploit that ambiguity. An 808 kick plays irregular, often offbeat two bar patterns, sparse on beat one and busy on the ands and as, with brutal silences, while triplet 808 toms roll against the binary kick. Bass is often the kick itself, its pitch varied kick to kick between root, fifth and lower octave so the kick line doubles as the bassline, no sidechain, no filter, sometimes the only element left when the drums fall silent. On top, soul, R&B or rap vocal samples are chopped into syllables and repeated into hypnosis, alongside sampled Rhodes stabs and video game sounds.

forestpsy.description: Forest psy is the undergrowth of psytrance: dark but organic where darkpsy is digital and aggressive. It emerged at the turn of the 2000s around the Scandinavia-Copenhagen axis and the Parvati Records label, with Derango as a founding act. Its sound is a round, woody bass, textures that teem like leaf litter on a forest floor, humid night-time atmospheres and almost no melody, only a constant swarm of small details. It is danced barefoot in the mud, ideally among trees. The scene is global today, stretching from the Balkans to India, and remains fiercely underground despite its wide reach.
forestpsy.production: Forest psy sits at 148 to 152 BPM, a touch slower than darkpsy, on a straight grid, but let sampled percussion keep its natural imprecision and add a light swing on percussion only. Instead of building toward a drop, the track should swarm, 16-bar cycles overlaid with textures looping on odd lengths of 5, 7 or 9 bars so nothing repeats identically. The kick is warmer than darkpsy's, tuned to 55 to 60 Hz with a longer body and less click, joined by a wood-sampled snare, shakers and sliced acoustic percussion in varied sixteenths. The bass strips out acid distortion: a heavily filtered triangle or saw with gentle tube saturation, rolling in sixteenths with slightly longer, softer notes rooted in F or E. Field recordings through a granular sampler finish a sound built from almost no melody.

freestyle.description: New York, 1983 to 1987: Latino electro funk that becomes a love song, TR-808 and DX7 under the voices of Puerto Rican and Italian American teenagers. Let the Music Play by Shannon sets the formula. Freestyle is neighborhood pop before the house era, immense in its time, and its echo returns in every Latino synth pop revival, a genre built for singing rather than rapping.
freestyle.production: Sit between 110 and 122 bpm, no swing on the 808 but a singing feel since the vocal and chords carry the track. Use a Latin syncopated signature, the kick anticipating the beat by a sixteenth, cowbell and claves sketching a simplified clave, with room left for long vocal phrases. Build the 808 pattern with an 808 snare on 2 and 4 doubled by a plate-reverbed clap, closed hats in sixteenths, syncopated cowbell, and conga toms answering the kick, breaks stopping the drums before the chorus so the voice stands alone. For bass, recreate the bright, punchy DX7 FM tone: a modulator tuned an octave above the carrier, a short decay, playing eighths that follow the chords with octave jumps. Add a Fairlight orchestra hit, FM electric piano, and a melodramatic lead vocal doubled in thirds with long plate reverb.

frenchcore.description: France hardened hardcore in its own way at the end of the 1990s: a punched, bouncing, almost melodic kick around 200 beats per minute, rooted in free parties and the Micropoint sound. Frenchcore has since become an international style in its own right, with Dr. Peacock as its ambassador, yet its particular groove remains a national signature that other scenes have never quite managed to fully copy.
frenchcore.production: Frenchcore runs between 190 and 210 BPM, most tracks around 200, close to uptempo and terrorcore in numbers but with a unique bouncing feel built into the kick itself, which carries an offbeat inside it, a legacy of the tribe sound sped up from its original bounce. Build the kick as a hit on the beat followed by its tail alone, pitched the same but quieter with a shorter decay, so the whole thing bounces as a single sample repeated on every beat. Add a dry snare on two and four, discreet sixteenth note hats, and rising pitch kick rolls before each drop. The bass is genuinely melodic, unlike the nu style: the kick tail follows a real line, root, minor third, fourth, fifth, often doubled by a separate saturated bass on the offbeats.

frenchhouse.description: Paris, the second half of the 1990s: a generation raised on filtered disco turned sampling into a national signature. Breathing filters, compression pumping in time with the kick, and unashamedly pop melodies define the sound. Daft Punk carried it worldwide, but the scene ran from Motorbass to Alan Braxe, and its vocabulary, the French filter house sound, still stands as a production reference twenty five years later, studied by producers who were not even born when it first appeared on Parisian dancefloors.
frenchhouse.production: Stay between 120 and 128 BPM, as in the disco house it grew from. What changes is the breathing: the French touch feel comes from sidechain compression pumping on every kick, with a release landing just before the next beat, around 200 to 250 milliseconds at 125 BPM. The sampled loop keeps its own swing while the machine stays straight, and choruses are melodic, sung in phrases of four or eight bars. Drums stay simple, a sampled disco kick or a short 909, clap on two and four, hats from the disco sample, and the whole kit is caught in the same sidechain as everything else, so it pumps too. The bass is sampled or replayed in funky eighths with octaves, often through a talkbox, sidechained hard with a sine sub underneath.

fullon.description: Full-on is the most energetic and melodic branch of 2000s Israeli psytrance: galloping basslines in triplets or sixteenth notes, heroic leads and spectacular breakdowns, all built around 145 beats per minute. The label Hom-Mega was its historic factory and Astrix became its flag-bearer, carrying the sound worldwide through the 2000s. It is the psytrance of packed noon dancefloors, generous and straightforward rather than cerebral, made to lift a crowd rather than reward close listening.
fullon.production: Full-on runs at 145 BPM, sometimes 148, never below 142, and the real signature is the galloping bassline: a saw on Virus or Serum, lowpassed near 300Hz with a lively filter envelope and almost no release, programmed as kick on the first sixteenth, bass on the second, third and fourth, then kick alone on the next beat with bass on three and four only, or the triplet version, kick on the first triplet, bass on the other two. Kick and snare need to punch through a packed rig at noon, so layer a sharp click onto a synthetic kick body and compress hard at 8:1, with a big snare and long eight-bar snare rolls before every drop. Build a heroic lead from a detuned saw unison playing a natural minor melody with long upward bends, softened by saturation and delay.

funk.description: James Brown tightened soul onto the first beat, Sly Stone made it psychedelic, Parliament sent it into orbit: funk is the science of groove as a collective organism. On this map it stands as a major rhythmic root, disco descends from it, house inherits it, and the synthetic P-Funk of Zapp leads directly into electro funk and boogie, tying nearly every branch of the family tree back to one source.
funk.production: Funk lives between 95 and 115 BPM, centred around 105. The secret is not the tempo but the subdivision: everything runs in sixteenths with a light 55 to 58 percent swing, never straight, never triplet, with the weight landing on the first beat, James Brown's famous one, while the rest of the bar is a conversation of syncopations returning to that anchor. Program a dry acoustic kit with the kick on one and on syncopated spots, never four even hits. The snare sits on two and four with ghost notes filling the gaps, and hats run in sixteenths with occasional openings and varied velocities. The bass is the heart of it, slap or fingerstyle, a short staccato phrase built from the root, the octave and the flat seventh. Add clavinet, Rhodes and a talkbox.

futurebass.description: Future bass is the synthetic sugar of 2013 to 2017: supersaw chords chopped by an LFO, pitched-up kawaii vocals, and melodic drops that feel like a hug rather than an attack. Flume set the Australian template, and a wave of SoundCloud producers industrialized it into global pop. It is the bright, lighthearted side of post-dubstep, adored almost as quickly as it was diluted.
futurebass.production: Future bass runs 140 to 160 BPM in halfstep, feeling like 70 to 80 with the snare on beat three, 150 being a good center. The rhythmic signature is not in the drums but in an LFO chopping the chords into eighths or sixteenths, softer than trap. Build a supersaw chord in Serum, a seven-voice unison saw running a four-chord progression, chopped by a volume LFO synced to an eighth or sixteenth note. Layer in pitched vocal chops, a voice sliced into syllables and pitched up for that kawaii feel, with delay and reverb. Keep the kick on one, doubled on the and of two or four, a huge snare on three, building an eight-bar snare roll that accelerates into the drop then drops out for two bars. The bass is a soft sub sine, gently sidechained.

futuregarage.description: The lingering shadow of 2-step in the late 2000s: garage rhythms veiled in reverb, crackle and urban melancholy. Burial is its unwitting founding figure, Untrue its landmark record. The term gathers a sensibility more than a scene, the feeling of rainy nights after the club has closed, a memory of dance music rather than dance music itself, closer to a mood board than to a rulebook for producers.
futuregarage.production: Work between 130 and 140 bpm, using 2-step patterns but with a blurred feel: hits placed by hand off the grid, delayed slightly so the drums seem to stumble. Build a 2-step skeleton, kick on 1 and 2.5, snare on 2 and 4, but treat every sound as a found object, a scratched vinyl snare, a lighter click, a sampled street clap, pushed through reverb and a short delay with highs cut, plus continuous vinyl crackle. For bass, keep a soft sub sine in long notes in minor, no wobble, no Reese, a floor rather than a character. Layer pitched, ghostly R&B vocals, time-stretched with artifacts and drowned in reverb, field recordings of rain and streets, filtered pads, and a distant Rhodes playing two chords, everything gray and far away.

futurehouse.description: A label born around 2013 for melodic house built on plucked, metallic sounding basses, popularised out of the Netherlands. The sound is clean and instantly recognisable through its filtered sawtooth bass that seems to talk. A launching pad for the Spinnin' and Heldeep generation, it became the house sound of streaming playlists, efficient and precisely calibrated for headphones as much as for club sound systems.
futurehouse.production: Stay between 124 and 128 BPM, the clean Dutch house tempo, with a square, light feel, no swing, apart from a slight shuffle on the hats that separates it from heavier bass house. The pluck bass plays in eighths and sixteenths like a melody, and that melodic figure defines the track, with a marked but musical sidechain and a pop song structure built for streaming, a short intro and the drop around bar 33. Build a clean 909 kick with a click and moderate sustain, a layered clap on two and four with a snap and short reverb, closed hats in sixteenths with a light shuffle, and bright open hats on the offbeats. The bass itself is a filtered pluck, one or two sawtooths with light unison, a low pass filter and a moving phaser for the talk effect.

futurepop.description: Futurepop is the melodic turn the electro industrial scene took around the year 2000: trance style song structures, clearly sung choruses, and a dark, uplifting sound built specifically for gothic and industrial clubs. VNV Nation wrote its manifesto, with Covenant and Apoptygma Berzerk following close behind, softening the scene's earlier harshness into something people could sing along to. It was adored by newcomers and hated by purists for the very same reason, because it finally made the industrial scene sing.
futurepop.production: Futurepop runs 125 to 140 BPM, mostly 128 to 135, straight and steady with a trance feel, a regular four on the floor, open hats on the offbeats and snare rolls building into every chorus. A treated kick with a tight sub plays every beat under a layered clap and snare on two and four through a bright plate reverb, closed hats alternating velocities in sixteenths, an open hat on the offbeats. The bass sits between EBM and trance, a sawtooth through a lowpass filter playing sixteenths that avoid the kick for a rolling feel or run continuously with an EBM style accent. A supersaw built from detuned, unison saws carries the choruses, plucks carry the verses, and a clear, doubled vocal sits over wide cold pads and softened EBM sequences.

gabber.description: Rotterdam, 1992: pure Dutch hardcore, crushed kicks at 160 to 190, hoover stabs, shaved heads and Australian tracksuits. A massive working class, popular culture in the Netherlands, mocked then rehabilitated, it produced its own slang, its own dance, hakken, and a mainstream second life in the late 2010s. The kick is a national identity, and almost everything else in the mix bends around it.
gabber.production: Push between 160 and 190 bpm, most classic Rotterdam production around 170 to 180, with no swing, no nuance: the hakken dance follows every kick, so each one must sound identical. Build the kick by clipping a 909 hard until the waveform turns nearly square and its tail becomes a sustained tone, heavy saturation, EQ to strip the low end, then clipping again, paired with a forward snare or lone clap and near-absent, heavily saturated hats. There is no separate bass: the crushed kick's tail is the bassline, tuned so it lands on the track's key, matching hoovers and stabs to it. Layer the Alpha Juno hoover played high as a riff, shouted film and cartoon samples, sirens and fast-vibrato saws, all pushed through the same distortion as the kick.

garagehouse.description: Garage house is the New York, soulful side of house music, named after Larry Levan's Paradise Garage. Gospel vocals stay at the center, piano and organ chords carry the track, and the production aims for warmth rather than machine precision. Zanzibar in Newark and Tony Humphries on the radio built it as much as a DJ school as a style, and it is the direct root of UK garage, which keeps its name to this day.
garagehouse.production: Sit between 118 and 124 BPM, slower than Chicago house, with a swing of 55 to 58 percent on hats and percussion while the kick stays straight. Build the drums from a softened 909: a short kick doubled by a sampled acoustic kick, snare rather than clap on two and four, swung sixteenth-note hats, and a percussion layer of looped congas, shaker and tambourine that never sounds stiff. The bass should sound played: a round electric or Moog-style patch filtered toward 250Hz, following a real chord progression with chromatic passing notes, its first note often anticipating the beat by a sixteenth like a disco bassist. On top, plant a Korg M1 organ in chords, a percussive M1 piano, and a lead gospel vocal doubled and lightly reverbed, with a brass or string stab punctuating the changes.

germantrance.description: German trance is the historic heart of the genre, made in Frankfurt and Berlin between 1992 and 1996 when trance was still an exploratory music. Labels like Eye Q and MFS released long, hypnotic, cosmic tracks that were direct heirs to Tangerine Dream and to techno. It is the source that every revival invokes, the age before trance had settled into a formula.
germantrance.production: German trance sits between 130 and 140 BPM with an exploratory feel, straight pulse and no swing, tracks running eight to twelve minutes and counted in blocks of 32 and 64 bars, where a change can take a full minute. A 909 acts almost as an erased backdrop, kick on every beat with a clap or rimshot on two and four, an eighth note ride and an open hat on the offbeat, barely changing across ten minutes. The bass is often a sequence, a closed 303 or analog synth alternating the tonic and its octave in sixteenths with a short filter envelope, moving slowly with an accent shift every sixteen bars. Long, evolving analog arpeggios and pads, detuned oscillators with slow modulation, carry the real motion, filters automated to open gradually and sweep harder at the end of each block.

ghettofunk.description: The 2010s label for a festive breakbeat sound blending sampled funk, light dubstep bass and scratching, built for fanfare festivals and afterparties. The spirit is big beat gone more glitchy, unpretentious and effective. A DJ scene more than an album scene, somewhere between Bristol and summer tours, where a funk break and a wobble bass sit comfortably side by side.
ghettofunk.production: Play between 100 and 115 bpm, the slowest of the breakbeat family, with a party hip hop feel: MPC swing at 58 to 62 percent, a dragging funk break, and a bass that bounces in half time. Build it from a funk break, Funky Drummer style, played nearly whole, with a stacked hip hop kick and punchy snare on top, the break's own hats plus a programmed open hat, scratches, crowd claps and stutter fills from Beat Repeat. For bass, keep the wobble light and melodic: a saw with an LFO synced to a quarter on a resonant low-pass at modest depth, following the funk sample's riff in half time, backed by a sub sine. Layer reworked funk samples, brass, wah guitars, Hammond organ, shouted vocal phrases, and light glitch from Beat Repeat.

ghettohouse.description: Ghetto house is Chicago again, but from the South Side and West Side in the 1990s: raw, repetitive, obscene and joyful house music, pressed cheaply on the Dance Mania label. An 808 or 909, a chanted phrase looped over it, and a climbing tempo: dance music in the most literal sense, made for the footwork scene that would grow out of it. Its direct lineage runs through juke and then footwork itself. The records were made fast and cheap, often finished in an afternoon, favoring raw energy and functional repetition over polish, and that same rawness is precisely what later producers kept chasing.
ghettohouse.production: Ghetto house runs 128 to 140 BPM, climbing from 130 in 1994 to 140 by 1998 as juke emerges, with a raw, mechanical, unswung feel, an 808 or 909 looping without humanization, its groove from the syncopation of the kick and vocal phrase rather than the drums. Build a four-on-the-floor kick with an extra syncopated hit, a very dry clap on 2 and 4, closed hats opening on the offbeats, and syncopated 808 toms foreshadowing juke, programmed with no humanizing. The bass is usually an 808 kick with a long decay tuned to the tonic, playing a two or three note syncopated line, sometimes the same sound as the kick, with no sidechain since the two blend, lightly saturated for grain. A looped, obscene vocal phrase and a simple minor stab complete the track, deliberately raw.

glitch.description: The error promoted to raw material: skipping CDs, stuttering digital buffers, clicks and artifacts composed as music in their own right. Oval opened the way in the early 1990s by painting directly onto CDs, Fennesz added melody to the approach, and Alva Noto brought rigor. Glitch has since infused everything from pop music, in Bjork's post-Vespertine work, to advertising sound design, proof that even an accident can be tamed into a style.
glitch.production: Glitch splits into two poles: tempo-free in Oval and Fennesz, where artifacts drift over pads, and strict, rigid tempo in Alva Noto and Ryoji Ikeda, 120 to 130 BPM with clicks quantized to the sample. In both cases, the length of a looped buffer becomes a tempo of its own, repeat a fragment every 20ms and it becomes a pitch, every 200ms and it becomes a rhythm, this porous border between pitch and rhythm defines the genre. Build percussion out of errors: 1ms clicks, short noise bursts, sine blips, CD skips, and buffer stutters, made with Beat Repeat on a fine grid, buffer shuffling, or a Grain Delay pushed to a high spray, a short sample loop cut without crossfades does the job Oval got from a scratched CD.

goatrance.description: Goa, India, in the late 1980s: European DJs play psychedelic electronic music on the beaches, released on cassette and DAT, blending body music, acid, and sped-up new beat. The style crystallizes in the early 1990s with oriental arpeggios, braided acid lines, and spiraling builds around 140 beats per minute. It is the founding myth of the entire psytrance culture, and its 1994 to 1997 golden age remains a revered canon.
goatrance.production: Set the project between 140 and 145 BPM, fully quantized in straight sixteenths with no swing. The feel comes instead from layered arpeggios running at different speeds, eighths on one layer, sixteenths on another, triplets on a third, drifting against each other over 8 and 16 bar cycles, with tracks often running 8 to 10 minutes without slowing. Build a short, lightly saturated 909 kick, a clap buried in short reverb on 2 and 4, closed hats alternating strong and weak velocities, and synthetic percussion like 909 congas or sampled tablas. The bassline is a TB-303 or analog sawtooth, lowpass filtered near 300 Hz, playing sixteenths on the root with octave jumps and accents, often doubled an octave up with more resonance for the braided acid sound.

gqom.description: Gqom is a dark, stripped down club music from Durban in the early 2010s, built on droning triplets, cavernous drums and almost no round bassline, made on makeshift computers by teenagers in the townships. Emptiness itself is treated as an instrument. DJ Lag and Rudeboyz defined the sound, and the label Gqom Oh! documented it for listeners outside South Africa.
gqom.production: Gqom sits between 120 and 130 BPM, though it never reads as a straight four four: the kick is a triplet motif or broken pattern avoiding the downbeat, giving a heavy, lurching pulse with no swing. The kick is the real motif, heavy, cavernous, saturated and reverberated, playing triplet eighths over two beats before silence, often two or three differently tuned kicks answering each other, low toms or muffled snares standing in for a clap. There is almost no bass in the usual sense, the low end held by the kick's own decay and reverb, or a plain sine sub held on one note appearing and disappearing across whole bars. Saturated 808 kicks with long dark reverb, sampled Zulu chants pitched down and delayed, sirens and industrial noise complete a palette poor in elements and rich in space.

grime.description: Grime came out of East London between 2002 and 2004, where teenagers made their own rap over skeletal eight bar instrumentals at 140 beats per minute, produced on PlayStation consoles and FruityLoops and spread through pirate radio. Wiley called it eskibeat, but history settled on the name grime. It is MC music above everything, cold and fast, and stands as the true vocal descendant of garage and one of the major British sounds of the century.
grime.production: Grime sits at 140 BPM, the speed of the garage it came from, but square, cold and fast with no swing; two feels coexist, the common one placing the snare on two and four. A short digital kick with no sub, often on one plus a syncopated sixteenth, sits under a sharp, loud snare or clap on two and four, sometimes a sampled gunshot, hats kept low or absent. The bass is a blunt, monophonic square wave with a short decay and little filtering, playing a syncopated, memorable sixteenth note riff, often in minor with octave jumps. Cold digital strings, bells, orchestra stabs, sirens and video game bleeps fill out the sound, the mix pumping hard off the kick to imitate a pirate radio sidechain, the only voice being the MC rapping live.

happyhardcore.description: The smiling half of the 1993 hardcore split: euphoric pianos, helium-pitched vocals, sped-up breaks giving way to 4/4 kicks, teenage ecstasy at 170 beats per minute. England and Scotland turn it into a massive popular rave culture, the Netherlands cross it with gabber. Mocked, adored, it returns every time a new generation discovers that joy is a genre, and that a piano can be as heavy as a kick drum.
happyhardcore.production: Run between 165 and 180 bpm, 170 as the reference, with a light, bouncy feel: the 4/4 is there, but an offbeat bassline makes the track feel like it skips rather than pounds. The earlier UK period still blends sped-up breakbeats with the 4/4 kick, the later period moves to pure 4/4, with a light swing on hats for bounce. Build a clean, barely saturated 909 kick on every beat, a snare or clap on 2 and 4 with a bright reverb, prominent open hats, and a rising snare roll before every drop. The bouncing offbeat bassline is the real signature: a short note on every off eighth, filtered saw, an octave under the piano. Layer bright rave pianos in plucked chords, helium vocals, softened hoovers, and joyful sirens, all in major keys.

hardcoretechno.description: Hardcore techno formed between 1990 and 1992 across Frankfurt, New York and Rotterdam, as techno pushed its kick drum into distortion and its tempo past 150 beats per minute. We Have Arrived by Mescalinum United is the founding blast, championed by Marc Acardipane on one side of the Atlantic and Lenny Dee on the other. In the Netherlands, hardcore grew into an entire culture, with gabber as its dominant dialect.
hardcoretechno.production: Early hardcore techno sits at 150 to 170 BPM, faster than the Frankfurt and New York techno it grew from, still readable as techno, the kick a rhythm rather than a continuous vibration. There is no swing and no humanization, the brutality coming from the kick: layer a 909 sample and push it through repeated stages of light distortion, bouncing and distorting again for a chain-reaction crunch. Snare doubles a clap on two and four, closed hats sit in eighths, and a sixteenth-note snare roll closes out every eight-bar block. There is often no separate bass, the distorted kick's decay functioning as the note, and when a bass appears it is a short stab, a Juno or Operator saw at 300Hz. The signature sound is the hoover, three detuned saws through a chorus with a pitch glide rising twelve semitones.

hardhouse.description: Hard house is house music toughened up in English clubs of the mid 1990s, with Trade in London at its epicenter: faster, more percussive and more tense than classic house, without ever reaching the brutality of hardcore. It is built on pumping basslines, endless builds, and the hoover sound borrowed straight from rave. The style first spread through Britain's gay club circuit before feeding into the wider world of hard dance, where it eventually dissolved into a broader continuum of harder, faster genres that absorbed its energy and its tricks.
hardhouse.production: Program at 140 to 150 BPM, the fastest corner of house alongside footwork, and keep the feel tense and dead straight with no swing. The signature is offbeat bass, a short note on every offbeat creating a galloping kick bass kick bass pulse locked to the grid. A hardened 909 kick, short and saturated, sits on every beat, with a 909 clap on two and four and loud closed hats in sixteenths opening on the offbeats; long tom rolls with rising pitch drive 32 or 64 bar builds. The bass is a filtered sawtooth pumped hard by sidechain against the kick, ratio around 8 to 1, so it ducks on the tonic, with a sidechained sub layer underneath. On top, an Alpha Juno hoover, rising sirens, filtered noise sweeps and pitched vocal samples deliver the rave signature.

hardstyle.description: The Netherlands invented, around the turn of the millennium, a more accessible successor to gabber: the tempo dropped to 150, kicks grew huge and precisely tuned, and dramatic melodic breakdowns arrived alongside the reverse bass. It has since become one of the pillars of festivals worldwide, with Defqon.1 as its flagship event, complete with its own industry, yearly anthems, and a culture obsessed with the technical craft of the kick drum.
hardstyle.production: Hardstyle sits at a genuinely fixed 150 BPM, with the early years of 2002 to 2005 closer to 140 to 145 and modern hardstyle pushing to 155, unswung and built so every kick and reverse bass share exactly 400ms. Treat the kick as an instrument with two parts: a short, clicky tok of 30 to 60ms, often a clipped 909, and a saturated, pitch-dropping tail of 200 to 300ms that settles on the tonic, when the harmony changes only the tail gets repitched, never the tok, or the attack loses its shape. Place the kick on every beat, a clap well back on 2 and 4, hats in eighths, and pitched kick rolls before the drops.

hardtechno.description: Techno pushed to extremes of speed and pressure, running from 140 to well over 160 beats per minute, built on distorted kicks and percussive function above all else. It has had its own ages: the warehouses of the 1990s, the schranz of the 2000s, and a 2020s revival that has brought it back to the center of Europe's biggest clubs, faster than ever before. Melody is a rare luxury here, the kick drum is the raw material to be sculpted.
hardtechno.production: Work between 140 and 160 BPM, centered on 150, straight and unswung since any humanization turns to blur at this speed. Build a three-layer kick: a sub sine near 41 Hz, a pitch-modulated body sine a semitone above it for a slow internal beating, and an air layer above 15 kHz, with its tail kept under 300ms. Add an electronic tom just after kicks 1 and 3, a metallic impact at the same spots, a clap locked to the kick with varied velocities, an off-beat snare, and hats on every off-beat with quiet ghosts before 2 and 4. The kick's sub often is the bass, boosted with Drum Buss, or add a rumble by sending the kick into a long, filtered, saturated reverb sidechained to it.

hardtrance.description: Hard trance is trance on steroids, born in German and Dutch raves: hardened kicks flirting with the nascent hardstyle sound, hoover leads, abrupt build-ups and aggressive euphoria around 145 beats per minute. Between 1993 and 1998 it was the soundtrack of the big continental raves, before hardstyle absorbed its energy and commercial trance absorbed its melody. Everything is loud and squared off, built for a crowd that wants maximum impact rather than subtlety. Artists such as Kai Tracid and DJ Scot Project defined its uncompromising, driving sound before the scene split into the genres that followed it.
hardtrance.production: Hard trance runs 140 to 150 BPM, the fastest of the trance family, usually settling at 145, on a straight, unswung grid where the energy comes from compression and offbeat accents, moving through 16-bar blocks with abrupt build-ups: eight bars of rolling drums, then the drop. The kick is hard and heavily compressed, a distorted 909, sitting alone at the centre, matched by an open hat on the offbeats pushed almost as loud, a dry clap on 2 and 4, and accelerating snare rolls. The bass is an early reverse bass, an offbeat note with an inverted, rising attack sucking toward the next kick, or a pumped, sidechained synth tone, static on the root for whole sections. On top sits the hoover, a detuned, PWM sawtooth with a descending pitch sweep, plus fast arpeggios and white noise risers.

hinrg.description: Disco sped up and toughened for the gay clubs of San Francisco and London at the turn of the 1980s. Octave-pumped eighth-note bass becomes the genre's signature, tempos climb toward 130, and the vocals stay big and dramatic. Hi-NRG is the missing link between disco and house, and the production school of Stock Aitken Waterman grows directly out of it. The style pushed disco to its fastest, most euphoric edge, paving the way for the dance music that followed.
hinrg.production: Set the project at 134 BPM, fully quantized with straight eighths and zero swing. The pumping octave bass carries the pulse, creating an illusion of extra speed. Build the beat on a LinnDrum: a firm, short kick, a Linn snare doubled with a clap on 2 and 4, hi-hats in sixteenths opening on the off-beat, tambourine doubling them. Syndrum fills mark every eighth bar with a four-note descending tom run, an Operator sine with a fast falling pitch envelope works well. The bassline alternates a low root and its octave on every eighth note, a Juno-60 or 106 sawtooth with the filter wide open, short envelope, and a 50ms release for a clean staccato, following a four-chord minor progression. Keep it between 80 and 200 Hz, no sub.

hiphop.description: Hip-hop is a root, not a branch, of this family tree. Born in the Bronx, it invented the isolated, looped break, sampling as a form of composition, and the DJ as an instrumentalist in their own right, the foundations that every electronic genre here borrows from. SONAA does not trace this lineage in depth, since its scope is electronic music, but hip-hop appears here as the parent of everything it passed on to machines, from breakbeat hardcore to footwork. Its early sound, built from funk breaks, drum machines and turntables, laid the groundwork that sampling-based dance music would run with for decades.
hiphop.production: Early hip-hop lives between 85 and 105 BPM, the tempo of the funk breaks DJs looped, from Rapper's Delight at 110 to Paid in Full at 97, its feel from sampler swing: the SP-1200 and MPC60 add a shuffle and slight quantization drift that make boom bap, snare landing late, kick slightly early. Build drums from a looped two-bar break chopped and reordered, or an 808 pattern, long deep kick, dry snare, sixteenth hats, kick on 1 and the and of 2, snare on 2 and 4, quantized only lightly. The bass is sampled with the break and low-passed, doubled by a sine an octave down, or an 808 kick with a long decay tuned to the key. A short sample, transposed by ear, resampled for grit, and a dry, central MC vocal complete the sound.

hiphouse.description: Hip house paired rap directly with house rhythms in Chicago and New York in 1988, running around 120 beats per minute. The phrasing was chanted, the choruses built for the dancefloor, and the crossover was claimed from both sides: house producers like Tyree and Fast Eddie, and rap groups like Jungle Brothers. The wave was short lived, but its underlying idea, rapping over whatever club music was current, resurfaces every generation, from UK garage to grime.
hiphouse.production: Hip house runs 118 to 124 BPM, fast for a rapper, kick staying a straight four on the floor while the rap phrasing reads in eighths with hip-hop syncopation, locked to the kick rather than a breakbeat. A 909 or 808 kick plays four on the floor under 808 snare or clap on two and four, often doubled with a breakbeat snare sample, sixteenth 808 hats accented on the offbeats. The bass stays synthetic and simple, octaves or repeated eighth notes on a filtered sawtooth or a cut funk sample, at most two bars long so the vocal stays legible. The real instrument is the sampler, an Akai S900 or SP-1200, chopping a cappella rap into syllables alongside horn stabs, crowd noise, sirens, a house piano and organ stabs.

hitech.description: Hi-tech psy is the speed extreme of psychedelic trance, born from Russian darkpsy at the turn of the 2010s, when Kindzadza and the Osom Music scene pushed tempos past 170 and started cutting sound with a digital scalpel. Everything here is precise, bright and ultra-edited: bursts of micro-sounds sparkling like an overheating circuit board, over dry, machine-gunned kicks. It is less dark than the darkpsy it grew out of, maniacal and playful rather than menacing. The name says exactly what you hear: technology showing off.
hitech.production: Hi-tech psy starts at 170 BPM and commonly climbs to 190, a speed where a sixteenth note lasts just 80 milliseconds, so the genre often shifts to eighths, kick then bass, or keeps sixteenths but shortens notes to 40 milliseconds for a machine-gun feel, with no swing at all. The kick is very short, about 60 milliseconds of body tuned near 70 Hz with a sharp click, built with a fast pitch envelope and heavy compression, while the hats are micro FM sounds rather than cymbals; percussion arrives in bursts of dozens of different micro-sounds sequenced in thirty-seconds for that overheating-circuit sparkle. The bass comes from FM8 or Serum, an FM wave with a ratio-1 modulator for a metallic attack, notes of 40 to 60 milliseconds changing root every two bars with fast glissandi over a separate sine sub.

hypnotictechno.description: Deep techno is a techno of patient repetition, an heir to minimalism and dub, carried through the 2010s by the Italian scene around Donato Dozzy and Neel. Its variations are minute, its textures organic, and time stretches until it becomes genuine trance. It is the techno of afterparties and forest clearings, the kind that unfolds over hours. Deep techno and hypnotic techno are the same current under two names: labels say deep, dancers say hypnotic, and this atlas counts them as a single genre. Its patience runs directly counter to the drop driven logic of much modern club music, rewarding long, undivided attention rather than a series of peaks.
hypnotictechno.production: Deep techno sits between 124 and 132 BPM, often 127 or 128, with a very light groove, around 10 percent, since motion comes from turning sixteenths and near invisible variations across long, 32 or 64 bar sections. A kick built from filtered white noise, self oscillating near 39 Hz, sits under a low acoustic tom playing sixteenths in the gaps left by the kick and an organic sixteenth click randomized in timing and velocity, felt rather than driven. The bassline stays a dark, continuous sixteenth pattern filtered low on the tonic, or a single sine undulating through an LFO modulated filter, almost never changing, mono, free of reverb. Above it, slowly realigning modular sequences, sustained drones, filtered field recordings, and felted percussion through echo and reverb create a cavernous space, no stabs, no hoover.

ibizatrance.description: Trance filtered through Ibiza in the late 1990s: sunny melodies, balearic guitars, and wide, open production sitting somewhere between the club and a postcard. Cafe del Mar compiled its softer side, while Chicane and Energy 52 wrote its enduring classics. This is the trance of summers people miss, embraced openly as nostalgia rather than fought against.
ibizatrance.production: Ibiza trance runs 128 to 136 BPM, between the balearic sound it grew from and the club trance it courts, on a straight grid with only a light 5 to 8 percent swing on the percussion. The feel is sunny and wide, built for a set's closing moments on a big terrace, with the kick present throughout, unlike its balearic parent, and breaks that stretch over 32 bars without building tension, only opening up. Soften a 909 kick with an 8 kHz filter, add a soft clap on 2 and 4, an off-beat open hat, a ride in eighths, and gentle shakers and congas with ghost notes, keeping the same base pattern through the track while the synths and guitar carry the variation.

idm.description: IDM, Intelligent Dance Music, got its name from a 1993 mailing list built around the Warp Records catalog, and the label has been contested from day one, including by the artists themselves. The music is clearer than the name: club electronic rewritten for home listening, breaks twisted into knots, melancholic melodies, constant sonic research. Aphex Twin, Autechre and Boards of Canada form its three canonical poles.
idm.production: IDM has no typical tempo, the first difference from club music, ranging from 80 BPM at Boards of Canada to 170 at Squarepusher, with a grid that exists but is broken: micro-offsets, triplets against straight time, bars in 7/8 or 5/4 at Autechre, tempo changes mid-track. The edited break is the central gesture: chop a break to the sixteenth or thirty-second, reorder it, reverse a slice, pitch each one differently, so the pattern never returns identical. The bass has no standard, a clean sine sub under a chaotic break, a detuned analog line, or a real electric bass played jazz-fusion, always melodic, following minor chords with sevenths. Weathered analog synths carry the melodies, sometimes run through a worn cassette for wow and flutter, staying simple and a little sad.

illbient.description: Illbient is ambient music filtered through hip hop, born in Brooklyn in the mid 1990s: urban synth pads, slowed down breaks, spectral scratches, and the aesthetic of a New York loft after midnight. DJ Spooky acted as its theorist, and the label WordSound as its world in miniature. The name is a pun on ill and ambient, and the scene itself was short lived, but its blend of concrete and haze left a lasting trace.
illbient.production: Illbient runs 75 to 95 BPM, the tempo of slowed down hip hop rather than reggae, its feel coming from an MPC style swing of 54 to 58 percent and sampled breaks dragging slightly behind the grid. Hip hop breaks get slowed, filtered, pitched down a few semitones, chopped and reassembled, with the turntable treated as an instrument, a slowed scratch, a vinyl rumble. The bass is an urban dub bass, a long, distorted 808 sub held on the root, crushed harder and left dirtier than in ambient dub, a pressure rather than a line, deliberately overlapping with the break's kick. City field recordings, subway noise, sirens, conversations, recorded on a phone and pitched low, along with stretched vinyl chords and radio voices, give illbient its identity.

indiedance.description: Indie dance is where independent rock meets the dancefloor, first activated in the mid-2000s and reshaped in the 2010s into a darker, more melodic sound. Darlyn Vlys describes his own music as somewhere between rock, indie dance and synthwave, and that's the right key to it: round, italo-derived basslines, treated guitars or vocals, and a tempo that stays under techno's. The label itself is something of a streaming-platform catch-all, but the real scene plays out in the clubs and festivals that claim it as their own.
indiedance.production: Indie dance stays under techno tempo, 110 to 122 BPM, often around 115 to 118. The feel blends drum-machine stiffness with band energy: straight eighths, little swing at 50 to 53 percent, while the guitar and vocal accents push and pull. A TR-8 or 808 clone holds a round four-on-the-floor kick, a rock snare or clapped 808 cracks on 2 and 4 with short reverb, and open hats mark the offbeat of 4. The bass is a Juno-106 sawtooth with chorus, round and slightly warbly like the italo it descends from, playing an eighth-note riff that falls with the kick and fills the gaps, sidechained lightly at 3:1. On top, cut guitar chords and arpeggios with dotted-eighth delay, chorus-treated vocals, Juno pads, and a rising sawtooth lead for the chorus.

industrial.description: Industrial was born in Sheffield and London between 1975 and 1980, when Throbbing Gristle founded Industrial Records and treated the studio as a factory and the social body as a subject for experiment. It works through tampered tape, mistreated synthesizers, noise and documentary-style provocation. It was not yet dance music, it was the raw material that EBM and the whole machine-music lineage would later turn into a dancefloor track.
industrial.production: There is no fixed tempo, many pieces sit around 90 to 120 BPM, often without a clear grid, built from tape loops that drift, so disable Warp on audio loops and let a sample fall wherever it lands rather than on the bar. Build rhythms from recordings of struck objects, sheet metal, a pipe, a garage door, a chain, in a simple unvarying pattern, then push through Saturator drive and 8-bit Redux, with a tape loop drifting alongside, never locking to the pattern. The bass is often a drone: a held note on a saw synth with its filter creeping slowly, or a recorded electric bass through fuzz, with no sidechain, the bass and pulse meant to overlap. Field recordings, a contact mic on a radiator, a coil picking up interference, become instruments nobody else has.

industrialrock.description: The American fusion of the 1990s: industrial vocabulary poured into the rock song format, sampled guitars, drum machines and stadium choruses. Nine Inch Nails is its author's version, Ministry its assault version, Marilyn Manson its spectacle version. This is the door through which industrial music entered mass culture, MTV included, turning a niche studio aesthetic into arena rock built for guitars as much as machines.
industrialrock.production: Sit between 90 and 140 bpm across two feels, a heavy mid-tempo with a snare that lands like a hammer, and a fast one in the Ministry mold with double kick drumming, the groove rock at heart but stiffened by the machine, zero swing, sampled and played drums blended together. Build a hybrid kit, acoustic drum samples played with machine rigidity plus electronic elements, a tight, dry kick, an enormous snare through a room reverb, and crushed breakbeats sliced and retriggered on top. For bass, layer a sampled guitar riff, sliced and requantized for robotic rigidity, under a synth bass following the riff an octave down, or a fuzzed electric bass instead. Layer distorted, resequenced guitars, aggressive synth basses and leads, film dialogue samples, and a whispered verse vocal turning to a distorted, delayed scream in the chorus.

industrialtechno.description: Industrial techno is techno that fully owns its industrial heritage: wasteland textures, hangar-sized reverbs, and kicks that land like hydraulic presses. Birmingham sketched the style in the 1990s through the Downwards label, and Berlin hardened it in the 2010s around Berghain and labels such as Perc Trax. It is a music of raw matter and negative space, where noise itself is treated as a noble material rather than a flaw to be cleaned up.
industrialtechno.production: Sit between 128 and 140 BPM, Birmingham leaning toward 135 to 140, Berlin closer to 130 to 135, with no swing, the groove coming instead from reverb tails spilling into the next beat. Build the kick as a hydraulic press: route it to a reverb at full wet, a nine-second decay and a 70Hz highpass, then sidechain-compress the tail against the dry kick so the wash breathes between hits. Build percussion from found objects, struck canvas, a metal plate, a coil picking up electromagnetic interference. The bass is a rumble rather than a line: a dark reverb fed by the kick and lowpassed at 150Hz, or a modular drone on the tonic, mono below 120Hz without exception, free to vanish for sixteen bars. Treat noise as a noble material, running field recordings through heavy distortion and hangar reverb.

isolationism.description: Isolationism is a British label from 1994, forged around a Virgin compilation: hostile ambient music drawn from the margins of metal, industrial and dub, built on frozen drones, empty spaces and a refusal of new age comfort. Thomas Koner and Lull, the project of Mick Harris, stand as its two poles. The word itself barely survived, but the sensibility it named has spread through all of today's dark ambient music. It rejected the soothing intent of most ambient music outright, treating silence and stasis as ends in themselves rather than as a backdrop for relaxation, and that refusal is what later dark ambient inherited most directly.
isolationism.production: Isolationism has no tempo and fewer events than even dark ambient: this music installs a frozen landscape where nothing happens, change measured in minutes rather than seconds. Work without a grid, in real time, in three to five minute blocks, with the only motion coming from a slow low pass filter sweep or a reverb whose size grows, no audible LFO, since any perceptible modulation is too fast. Rhythm is replaced by the ten second attack of a slowed gong or the barely perceptible swell of a mass of sub bass, drawn from feedback and tape noise but stretched until it freezes. The bass is a static sub between 25 and 40 Hz, a pure sine with a higher drone moving by a few cents over minutes. Source gongs, tape hiss and decaying digital reverb, avoid anything warm.

italodisco.description: In the 1980s, Italy built a fully synthetic, melodic and sentimental strain of disco, often sung in a dreamed up English. Bright synthesizer arpeggios and dry drum machines replaced everything American disco still had that was organic and played by hand. Despised at the time as cheap and derivative, Italo disco has since become one of the most plundered sources in dance music, feeding everything from Chicago house to the synthwave revival. Few genres balance a cold, quantized machine pulse against such warm, romantic melody, and that contrast remains the style's defining trick.
italodisco.production: Set the tempo around 118 to 120 BPM and let a strict drum machine grid carry the track: straight sixteenth and eighth notes, no swing. Motion comes from sixteenth note synth arpeggios and a sequenced bass, while a four chord minor progression, often i, VI, III, VII, loops through the whole song. Program a LinnDrum or TR-808: a dry kick on every beat, a clap on two and four doubled by a snare through a gated reverb, closed hats in sixteenths with an open hat on the upbeat of beat four, and a quiet cowbell on the chorus.
