The bass is a sawtooth Juno-106, sequenced with octave jumps following the chord, a short release and a low pass filter near 400 Hz. Add a Korg Poly-61 for the arpeggios and a vocoder for the robot voice.

italohouse.description: Italy answered Chicago with what it did best: melody. Bright, chord-stabbing piano, inherited from italo disco, became the style's emblem, dubbed dream house by some and spaghetti house by others. Between 1989 and 1993 these euphoric pianos defined the sunlit side of European raves, before falling out of favor and then returning to grace among crate-diggers in the 2010s. It is house music with a pop heart, built for arms in the air rather than the after-hours.
italohouse.production: Italo house sits between 118 and 124 BPM, slower than the UK house it feeds, with an almost swing-free, joyful feel where a stabbing piano in eighths carries the pop pulse, the groove coming from the bounce between piano offbeats and bass on the beat. A clean, simple 909 holds kick on every beat, clap on 2 and 4, closed hats in eighths opening on the offbeat; fills are snare rolls or silence before the chorus. The bass moves in octaves like the italo disco it descends from, bright and present around 500 Hz to sit with the piano rather than dig for sub. On top, the Korg M1 piano preset plays major chords with light chorus and bright reverb, a sped-up sampled diva vocal, and crowd noise on the buildups.

jcore.description: J core is Japan's hardcore: happy hardcore and gabber digested by otaku culture, anime melodies, vocaloid voices and the speed of a rhythm game. It was born in the doujin circles of the 2000s, distributed at Comiket, and globalized through music games and osu!. Camellia became its worldwide superstar, DJ Sharpnel its founding legend. The genre packs far more melodic incident per bar than its European ancestors, treating every few beats as an opportunity for a new hook or a new tempo shift, a density that maps directly onto the note charts of the rhythm games that helped spread it worldwide.
jcore.production: J core spans a wide tempo range, 170 to 200 for its happy hardcore strain, up to 220 or 250 for the gabber and speedcore strain of DJ Sharpnel, and Camellia often shifts tempo mid track. What sets it apart is density: very fast sixteenth melodies, section changes every four or eight bars, note detail written for rhythm games like osu! where every hit counts, no swing anywhere. The kick swings between a clean tuned kick and a crushed gabber kick, backed by clap on two and four, dense hat rolls, and busy fills, snare rolls, pitched kicks and glitches stacked at each block's end. Bass shifts identity constantly, an offbeat sawtooth following J pop chords, a gabber kick tail on harder sections, or a Serum growl on bass passages. Layer in chiptune leads, vocaloid chops and video game sounds.

jerseyclub.description: Jersey club is Newark's inheritance of Baltimore club sound in the 2000s, reshaped into its own identity: bouncy, triplet-feeling kick patterns, sampled bed squeaks, vocals chopped into hiccupping fragments, and a teenage dance culture that spread first on YouTube and later on TikTok. DJ Tameil and the Brick Bandits crew are its pioneers, Cookiee Kawaii its viral breakthrough. It has become the most influential American club music style of the 2020s. The tracks are short, functional and built around a single recognizable trick, the layered, rebounding kick pattern, rather than melody or long-form arrangement.
jerseyclub.production: Jersey club runs 130 to 140 BPM, with 137 or 138 a common start, and its bounce comes entirely from the kick pattern rather than swing: on a sixteenth grid, place kicks on steps 1, 5, 9, 12 and 15, beats 1 to 3 plus the a of 3 and the and of 4, layering sub, mid and click kicks. Add a clap or snare on 2 and 4, the bed squeak playing against the kicks, eighth-note hats, and kick rolls in thirty-seconds for fills. The low end is usually just the kick, a short 808 with a brief tail, or a short sine sub following the kick on beats 1 and 3 so the bounce stays legible, sidechained fast. Chopped vocal hiccups, the bed squeak, water drips and crowd sounds finish the track, kept short and dry.

juke.description: Juke is Chicago ghetto house accelerated at the turn of the 2000s, up to 150 or 160 beats per minute, built for the south side's dance battles. Triplet toms, 808 basslines and vocals chopped into syllables create a permanent sense of syncopation. It sits as the intermediate step between ghetto house and footwork, and where exactly the border falls remains a debate among connoisseurs.
juke.production: Juke runs between 150 and 160 BPM, the zone where ghetto house turns into juke, with a nervous, syncopated feel: the kick no longer sits on a regular four beats but plays sixteenth-note motifs with rests, while 808 toms roll in triplets on top to create a second grid, a constant sense of three against two. Kick and bass are often the same 808, decayless for the kick and long-decay for the bass, playing a two or three note line with glides and no sidechain needed. The 808 toms are the real signature, three different pitches rolling in triplets in answer to the kick, with a clap on 2 and 4 or half-time on 3. On top, vocal samples chopped into syllables and stuttered in sixteenths or triplets, and simple monophonic square-wave leads.

jumpstyle.description: Belgium and the Netherlands, around 2007: a simplified, bouncing form of hardstyle at 140 to 150 BPM, built for a codified jumping dance that YouTube turned into a European teenage phenomenon. Patrick Jumpen became its face, with millions of views as proof. The wave receded quickly, leaving the dance itself as a generational memory, still revived at reunion parties by fans now well into adulthood.
jumpstyle.production: Jumpstyle plays between 140 and 150 BPM, often 145, a little slower than the hardstyle it comes from. This tempo matches the dance itself, each beat a jump and each offbeat a landing, so kick and offbeat bass must stay regular, with no swing and no velocity variation anywhere. What sets it apart from hardstyle is simplicity: no breakdown, no screech, just kick, bass and a plain melody. Build a shortened, drier hardstyle kick with a clear tok and a short tail, on every beat with no rolls or variation, since the dancer counts on it. Add a fairly dry clap on two and four, discreet open hats on the offbeats and closed hats in eighths. The bass is a light reverse bass on every offbeat, shorter than in hardstyle, sitting on the root and following the chords.

jumpup.description: Jump up is Saturday night drum and bass: a trampoline bassline that does all the work, simple breaks, and DJ friendly hooks. It was born in the mid 1990s around the Ganja and True Playaz labels with DJ Hype and Zinc, then revived in an even more exaggerated form during the 2010s. Purists tend to look down on it, dancefloors keep demanding it, and the argument between the two camps is now thirty years old. Its formula stays deliberately narrow, built around one bouncing bass idea and one straightforward beat, favoring immediate impact over the intricacy that much of drum and bass prizes.
jumpup.production: Jump up runs at 170 BPM for the classic Ganja and True Playaz era or 174 to 175 for the 2010s revival, with no swing and a bouncing feel built around the bass leaping from beat to beat. Keep the break simple: kick on beat one and the and of three, snare on two and four, hats in steady eighths or sixteenths, with a hip hop break sometimes playing underneath, and a snare roll before each drop. The bass, monophonic and doing almost all the work, is a Nord Lead square or filtered saw with a fast envelope, or an FM or wavetable bass with an LFO synced cutoff for a modern wobble, backed by a separate sub sine. Layer in hip hop vocal samples, sirens and crowd noise, and keep it lean: one bass idea, one beat.

jungle.description: Jungle emerged in London between 1993 and 1995: breakbeats cut apart with surgical precision, sped up toward 160 beats per minute, over soundsystem bass and ragga vocals. It was the first authentically Afro-British music of the electronic era, built on the science of chopping the Amen break and the pride of pirate radio. Its refinement would lead into drum and bass, but its spirit keeps resurfacing with every revival.
jungle.production: Jungle sits between 155 and 165 BPM, with 160 as the center of gravity for 1994, and the groove lives in two speeds at once, a break running in sixteenths against a reggae bassline falling in dotted quarters as if at 80. Chop the Amen break into sixteen slices per bar: kick on beat one, snare on two and four plus an extra snare a sixteenth before beat four, pairs of fast kicks on the and of three, changing every two bars as Remarc or Shy FX did. The bass is a pure soundsystem sub, forty to fifty five hertz, playing the root for a dotted quarter, a silence, then dropping to the fourth below, with a downward pitch bend for that dub wobble. Grainy vocal chops and sirens fill the top, built from records rather than keyboards.

kosmische.description: Kosmische Musik is the synthetic branch of krautrock, the Berlin School: Tangerine Dream and Klaus Schulze stretch analogue sequencer patterns across entire album sides, arpeggios turning like slow-moving stars. It is the direct ancestor of trance, ambient music and anything that thinks in pads and sequences rather than songs. Tangerine Dream's Phaedra, from 1974, marks the milestone: a Moog sequencer becoming a landscape in itself rather than a backing track. The music trades verse-chorus structure for patient, cyclical motion, built almost entirely from synthesizers and tape rather than conventional bands, and it changed how electronic music thinks about time.
kosmische.production: Kosmische Musik drops the drummer entirely: the pulse comes from an analogue sequencer, often set to a slow-seeming 60 to 90 BPM while running in sixteenths for a felt pulse closer to 120 to 180. Following the Moog 960's eight-step layout, program short eight-note sequences and let them run with a machinal feel, no swing, though tempo can drift slightly over minutes. Build the rhythm from the sequence itself, an eight-note line through a resonant filter automated open and closed over 32 bars, layered with a second sequence at a different subdivision for crossing patterns. The bass is a low, repeating sequence with a Moog-style sawtooth tone, sliding by minor thirds every 32 bars, sharing its clock with the percussion. A Mellotron, a Farfisa organ and sweeping modular textures fill out the sound, tied by a tape echo.

krautrock.description: Krautrock is West Germany's refusal of Anglo-American blues in the 1970s and its invention of a trance all its own: motorik, the straight, obstinate pulse driven by bands like Neu! and Can, built in community studios alongside a nascent electronic sound. It became the school of European repetitive groove, and Detroit techno would later cite it as an obvious ancestor.
krautrock.production: The motorik pulse runs 120 to 140 BPM, straight and without swing but played by a human drummer, what makes it hypnotic being its constancy over ten minutes with only micro variations in intensity, never a spectacular fill. The pattern is simple: kick on every beat plus an extra hit on the upbeat of four, snare on two and four, hats in continuous steady eighths. The bass is an electric bass playing one or two notes for minutes, holding a steady eighth note pulse with an occasional rise to the fifth or minor seventh every eight bars, blended with the kick rather than sidechained. An organ held in open chords, a modular synth producing sliding tones, and a tape delayed guitar complete the sound, colored with plate reverb and short echoes.

latinfreestyle.description: Latin freestyle is the explicitly Latin, Miami branch of freestyle, where clave rhythms and percussion inherited from salsa color the electro pop, running from the mainstream sound of Miami Sound Machine to the club records of TKA and the New York Latin scene. Its distinction from New York freestyle is more a matter of degree than of nature, a line that collectors still draw carefully.
latinfreestyle.production: Latin freestyle shares its tempo with New York freestyle, 112 to 126 BPM, but what changes is the clave: the track organizes around a son clave, three two or two three, played on 808 claves or a woodblock. An 808 keeps the kick, snare and hats while congas in a tumbao pattern, timbales with a cascara ride and cowbell fills, and 808 claves playing the clave throughout take the top layer. The bass follows the salsa tumbao rather than the kick, anticipating by playing the root on the upbeat of two and the fifth or root on beat four while often leaving beat one empty, over a minor progression with dominant chords. Synthetic brass, trumpet and trombone lines, carries the main color, answered by a montuno piano part and bilingual, doubled vocal choruses.

latinhouse.description: Latin house is house music spoken in Spanish and played in clave: Afro Cuban percussion, montuno piano and sampled or live brass. Chicago and New York began producing it in the 1980s within their Puerto Rican and Mexican communities, and Masters At Work later gave the style its noble credentials. It keeps returning in waves, whenever a dancefloor wants some warmth.
latinhouse.production: Latin house sits between 122 and 128 BPM, though the tempo matters less than the clave: everything locks to a son clave, two three or three two, that the montuno piano, congas and often the bass all respect. A 909 supplies the kick, clap and hats, while an Afro Cuban layer carries the character, congas in a tumbao pattern, timbales with a cascara ride, bongos, guiro and cowbell. The bass alternates between a tumbao and a house feel, in tumbao anticipating the next chord on the upbeat of two and beat four while leaving beat one empty, or switching to octave eighths for the choruses over a simple progression. A montuno piano arpeggiating a two chord figure, sampled or played brass stabs, and bilingual call and response vocals complete the sound.

lentoviolento.description: Lento violento is Gigi D'Agostino's own invention: hardstyle and Italian dance music slowed down to 100 or 120 beats per minute, heavy slow-motion kicks, and simple melodies repeated until they become hypnotic. The name says it all, slow and violent. It remains an Italian cult sound above all, regularly rediscovered whenever a slowed-down edit spreads across social media, decades after its first run of records.
lentoviolento.production: Lento violento sits between 85 and 115 BPM, most of D'Agostino's own tracks around 90 to 105, essentially hardstyle and Italian dance slowed almost by half, so each kick becomes an event lasting over 600 milliseconds. Build a distorted hardstyle-style kick with a long tuned tail, on every beat or sometimes only on one and three with a softer kick on two and four, since a slight ten to twenty millisecond delay on the melody gives everything a trailing feel. A real dance bassline can sit underneath, a filtered saw or square around 400Hz playing a simple eighth-note motif, tonic, tonic, fifth, tonic, like in italo dance, lightly saturated and sidechained with a long release so the pump is felt. On top, write simple minor-key saw leads with portamento, repeated unchanged, alongside sampled accordions, a D'Agostino trademark, and pitched-down vocals.

liquiddnb.description: Liquid drum and bass is the side of the genre that breathes: soul chords, sung vocals and round basslines, reviving Bukem's legacy in the early 2000s when Fabio named it liquid funk. Hospital Records turned it into a mainstream-facing label without betraying the tempo. For most listeners it is the genre's entry point, and its own unabashed embrace of softness.
liquiddnb.production: Liquid keeps drum and bass tempo at 170 to 174 BPM but softens the feel, with real swing of 55 to 58 percent on the hats and ghost notes; where neurofunk counts in sixteenths, liquid counts in two-bar phrases, chords changing every two or four bars like soul, so the fast tempo becomes a treadmill under a song at 87 BPM. The break is a softer two-step, kick on 1 and the and of 3, snare on 2 and 4 but rounder, over a jazz or funk break played whole underneath with light swing. The bass is round, never distorted, a sine or triangle sub playing a melodic line that follows the chords, sidechained lightly just so the kick can breathe. The Fender Rhodes carries the genre with seventh and ninth chords, joined by sung soul vocals and warm pads.

lofihiphop.description: Lo-fi hip hop is dusty instrumental hip hop that became, through YouTube and its lofi hip hop to study radios, the background soundtrack of an entire generation. Its roots are noble, running through J Dilla and Nujabes, with their human swing and hazy jazz samples. The current scene has turned into a playlist industry, but the original idea, the beauty of an imperfect beat, still holds true among the best producers working in it.
lofihiphop.production: Lo-fi hip hop runs 70 to 90 BPM with a human feel above everything, deliberately dequantized the way J Dilla turned off his MPC's quantization so the kick lands early, the snare late, and the hats hesitate. The kit is short and muffled, a kick from a soul break or tuned 808 through a gentle filter, a snare blended from a break hit and a clap until it is almost a dull thud. The bass stays round and short, an 808 or saturated sine playing just a few notes, usually the tonic and minor third, sometimes gliding, cut around 250 Hz so it stays under the sample. A hazy jazz sample, piano, Rhodes or guitar, slowed slightly through a low filter and cassette style wow and flutter, is the heart of the sound.

lofihouse.description: Lo-fi house is house music deliberately degraded, soaked in hiss and tape noise, born on YouTube and Bandcamp in the mid-2010s. The machines run slightly out of tune, the compression crushes everything flat, and a VHS aesthetic and joke pseudonyms are part of the gesture. Behind the irony sits a genuine return to the sentimental house of Chicago and New Jersey, recorded like a memory rather than a document.
lofihouse.production: Lo-fi house sits at 118 to 126 BPM, slower than the deep house it descends from, and deliberately a little off: the machines slightly detuned, the tempo allowed to float, the hat swing pushed to 56 or 60 percent, so everything lands early or late like a found cassette. Build the drums from saturated 707 and 909 emulations, a kick with a long decay filtered above 8kHz, a clap softened by sampler reverb, and sixteenth-note hats, run through a cassette chain, tape saturation, a bitcrusher and a lowpass filter. The bass is a supple deep house line on minor seventh roots, slightly detuned and saturated, its low end blurring into the kick rather than a clean sub. Layer veiled pads on top, a Juno preset holding minor chords through chorus and wow, plus a stretched vocal sample from 90s R&B.

lounge.description: Lounge is the 1990s recovery of 1950s and 60s easy listening: cocktails, exotica and bossa nova run through the sampler, equal parts irony and genuine comfort. Vienna's dZihan and Kamien, the Paris scene and the Hotel Costes compilations turned it into a soundtrack for a lifestyle. The kitsch is a conscious material here, and the craft behind it is entirely real.
lounge.production: Lounge runs 95 to 120 BPM, livelier than the chill-out it descends from, groove drawn from bossa nova, mambo and slow samba: a regular sixteenth pulse with a 3-2 clave motif shifting the accents, swing kept to just 52 or 54 percent since bossa stays straight and the sway comes from accents rather than lag. The kit stays clean, unlike downtempo: a dry short kick with no sub, snare swapped for a rimshot or brushes, and clean closed hats in even eighths. Latin percussion, bongo, cabasa, shaker, guiro and a clear clave, sits on top for the genre's blend of precision and hand-played warmth. The double bass is the instrument, sampled or played pizzicato with real wood and finger noise, walking a bossa or tumbao line, mixed quieter than trip-hop. Vintage exotica samples and a Hammond fill out the palette.

lowercase.description: Lowercase turns extreme discretion into an aesthetic, an approach that took shape around the year 2000: tiny sounds, mostly silence, and listening pushed right to its threshold. Steve Roden formulated its manifesto with Forms of Paper, a piece commissioned by a library. A cousin of reductionism and Japanese onkyo, lowercase is the quietest room on this whole card, a music that asks for near total silence around it.
lowercase.production: There is no tempo, the silences themselves are composed, ten seconds, forty seconds, a minute of almost nothing, so disable the grid and work the way you would edit a film. Build rhythm from tiny strikes rather than percussion, the friction of a page, a finger on a contact mic, a relay click, amplified and placed rarely, one or two events every thirty seconds, leaving the rest to background noise. A cheap piezo taped to paper, wood or glass into a clean preamp is enough to start, alongside a field recorder capturing empty rooms and fans. The low end is almost absent, and when it appears it is a pure sine around 25 to 40Hz, felt rather than heard. Generate plain sines, isolate resonances with a narrow bandpass filter, and use a long, low-feedback delay to space out repeats.

makina.description: Northern Spain, Valencia then Catalonia in the 1990s: local hardcore between Barcelona's makina and Valencian bakalao, hard kicks, simple epic melodies, a culture of the ruta and giant clubs. Exported to Newcastle, where it strangely becomes the soundtrack for Northeast English MCs, a unique double life on this map, and a rare case of a Spanish club sound crossing borders wholesale.
makina.production: Sit between 150 and 180 bpm, no swing, with a stronger link to hard trance than to hardcore techno, epic melodies, long breaks and builds, and darker minor key melodies than happy hardcore's childlike ones. Build a hard, saturated 909 kick with light clipping on every beat, a snare on 2 and 4, prominent open hats, and the makina signature, long rising snare rolls plus kick rolls before every drop. For bass, use the same offbeat pattern as happy hardcore but pitched higher and sharper, a saw filtered around 700Hz with more resonance, following the melody's minor chords, no sidechain. Layer the Alpha Juno hoover as a full melodic lead, epic stacked supersaws, breakdown pianos, and Spanish or English vocals drenched in reverb, everything dramatic and rising.

melodictechno.description: The 2010s label for a slow, grandiose strain of techno built on minor-key arpeggios, emotional builds, and polished production, sitting somewhere between the progressive house heritage and festival pop. Afterlife and Tale of Us turned it into a worldwide staging. Its border with melodic house is more a matter of marketing than of music, and this entry flags it as a genuinely debated category.
melodictechno.production: Keep the tempo between 120 and 126 BPM, the slowest in the techno family alongside dub techno, with a light swing on the hats and a soft sidechain running through the mix for its characteristic pump. The feel is cinematic, built for a festival stage, so each 16-bar section should announce the next, with sixteenth-note arpeggios creating perceived speed even at 122 BPM, and delays synced to the dotted eighth to widen them. Layer a clean, calibrated 909 kick with a sub and a click, a plate-reverbed clap and snare on 2 and 4, closed hats alternating velocities, and a discreet shaker, keeping the rhythm sparse so it serves the melody, with a snare roll and crash before every drop.

miamibass.description: Miami, 1985: the 808 tuned for the trunk of a car, sub bass reaching below the threshold of hearing, rising tempos, raw lyrics and sweaty parties. 2 Live Crew turned it into a national scandal and a free speech court case. Bass is as much a car culture as a musical one, and the acknowledged ancestor of the whole booty and Southern club lineage that followed decades later.
miamibass.production: Faster than its parents, 120 to 135 BPM, with a sweet spot around 128 to 132 for club tracks. There is no swing on the grid, but nervous energy comes from sixteenth note hats and shouted vocals landing on every beat, and unlike electro hop the kick is no longer percussive but sustained, each hit a dotted eighth note or longer, giving the fast tempo a heavy feel. The 808 kick is the centrepiece, decay pushed to a second and tuned under 40 Hz, kick and bass essentially the same sound: a long decaying 808 sampled and played chromatically as a bass line, root, fourth and fifth in a low key. Dry 808 snare on two and four, often swapped for a 12 bit clap, closed hats, open hat on the and of four, with triplet rolls before changes.

microhouse.description: House music examined under a microscope, around the year 2000: clicks, fragments of voice, and tiny grains of sound assembled into silky grooves. Germany, through labels like Perlon and Kompakt, meets the glitch scene here, and Luomo writes entire songs in this pointillist style. It is a jeweler's music, sensual despite its miniature vocabulary, and the direct ancestor of the following decade's minimal techno.
microhouse.production: Set the tempo between 120 and 126 BPM with a marked shuffle, around 58 to 62 percent on the sixteenth grid, applying the same groove to every track so everything sways together. Use a short, dry kick around 150ms, from a filtered 909 sample or a sine with a fast pitch envelope. Replace the snare with clicks and noise fragments of 30 to 80ms on 2 and 4, and swap the hi-hat for sliced noise: cut a loop into thirty-two slices and keep only the first 20ms of each. Program a dozen or more micro-sound tracks, each playing two or three notes per bar, never all at once, since the placement of these tiny hits is the groove itself. Keep the sub round and soft, often on the off-beat, almost singing.

microtechno.description: Micro techno reduces techno to its smallest grains, a current that applies the precision of micro sound to techno's own structures, somewhere between Thomas Brinkmann's mathematical variations and the duo SND. It favors bare digital textures and millimeter precise rhythms, with absolutely no fat left on them. It is laboratory music built from clicks and sine tones, and yet it keeps a real groove, austere but still physical, precise rather than cold.
microtechno.production: Micro techno runs 125 to 135 BPM, faster and straighter than microhouse, with a bare grid and no swing, its movement coming from motifs of five. The kick shrinks to a short fifty to eighty millisecond sine on every beat or just one and three, with no snare, replaced by digital clicks generated from a filtered impulse on beats two and four. The bass is a pure forty five or fifty five Hertz sine with no harmonics, playing a pulse with a very short envelope, joined by a second sine an octave up playing its own step cycle for a low polyrhythm. Built with DSP and granulation rather than traditional synths, the palette adds crackling granular textures and static harmonic sines, reverb avoided except as a deliberate choice.

minimalprog.description: Minimal prog is progressive house passed through a minimal sieve between 2005 and 2015: melody shrinks to two or three note motifs, a round bass line carries the track, dub-style delays carve out space, and the music evolves over ten minutes by subtraction rather than addition. It is the soundtrack of warm-ups and after-parties, hypnotic, patient and never spectacular. The South American school around Hernan Cattaneo is its living home, with an acknowledged kinship to Scandinavian psy-prog, which explains this graft on the family tree. Nothing rushes: the pleasure lies in slow, repeated cycles rather than in build-ups or drops.
minimalprog.production: Minimal prog sits at 120 to 124 BPM, the slowest of the family, with little or no swing since movement comes from delays and automation rather than note placement, and nothing changes before 16 or even 32 bars. Build a round 909 kick with no click on every beat, a soft rimshot on 2 and 4, closed hats in eighths and, the genre's real signature, tiny ghost percussion sounds sitting quietly on isolated sixteenths, mostly heard through their own delays. The bass is a round, sustained saw or square tone on the root, near legato, filtered low, changing one note every 4 to 8 bars while its cutoff opens gradually over 64 bars in place of a build-up. A soft pluck feeds a synced dub delay, joined by a filtered pad and a sustained lead rising across half the track.

minimaltech.description: Minimal tech is the club minimal of the 2000s, the sound of Berlin's after-parties: a reduced but fleshy groove, round basslines, and small details that circle the stereo field across ten-minute stretches. It sits between the austere dogma of Robert Hood and the pop instincts of Kompakt, a supple middle ground that built the reputation of venues like Bar 25 and Club der Visionaere.
minimaltech.production: Sit at 124 to 127 BPM with the heaviest swing in the family after microhouse, 58 to 62 percent on the sixteenths, applied to hats, percussion and often the bass. Add timing randomness, five percent in Ableton's Groove Pool, so nothing falls the same way twice. Build a round kick with a slight boost near 46Hz, and surround it with micro-percussion: a low tom in sixteenths with gaps where the kick lands, a click filling all sixteen steps at randomized velocities, a wood block ticking three steps every two beats, and a rimshot for the clap. The bass is a round sub, sine or triangle with soft saturation, playing a single note like F1 with gaps, ducked by a hand-drawn volume automation dipping six decibels after each kick.

minimaltechno.description: Minimal techno strips the genre down to the bone. Robert Hood laid out the manifesto in 1994 with Minimal Nation: a loop, a groove, almost nothing, and somehow everything holds together. Germany turned it into a dominant club aesthetic over the following decade, from the Berlin click to the Cologne groove. It is the art of subtraction applied to the dancefloor, where every element left standing counts double.
minimaltechno.production: Minimal techno sits between 128 and 130 BPM, the Hood and Hawtin zone, with groove coming not from swing but from machine offset, an Ableton MPC groove at 60 percent that delays and softens certain sixteenths; the real movement lives in micro-variations and a sample starting a touch late. Think in one-bar loops, never below 126 BPM. A four-on-the-floor kick lands on steps 1, 5, 9 and 13 of the sixteenth grid, cut above 1 kHz with body boosted near 160 Hz, joined by a wood block, a low 808 tom on a single step, and duplicated hats offset for sway. The bass is a sub pulsing between the kicks rather than a melodic line, tuned to a single note that merges with the kick, with a slow sine LFO on volume for breathing tremolo.

minimalwave.description: Minimal wave is the posthumous rediscovery of obscure, cold synth-pop recorded between 1978 and 1985 on cassettes and tiny private pressings: primitive drum machines, monophonic synths, blank vocal delivery and bedroom production. The name comes from Veronica Vasicka's Minimal Wave label, which began exhuming this lost continent of music from 2005 onward. It is placed here by convention: a cousin of the synth-pop roots rather than a true descendant of minimal techno, sharing only a name. The music itself is intimate and modest in scale, made by isolated bedroom artists with a handful of cheap machines rather than by any organized scene.
minimalwave.production: Minimal wave sits between 100 and 130 BPM, usually 110 to 125, closer to chamber pop than club music, and its stiffness is part of the charm since period drum machines could not swing: play synth lines live and unquantized, or quantize lightly, to recreate a hand-played synth over an unsynced drum machine. Build the beat from one primitive drum machine, a thin analogue kick with no sub, a short noisy snare on 2 and 4 widened with echo, and closed hats in eighths or sixteenths. Unlike the rest of the minimal family, the bass is a melodic line carrying the song: a monophonic synth, resonant low filter, simple root, fifth and minor-third patterns, no sub below 60 Hz. Cheap synths for chords, blank vocals, and a cassette recorder for natural hiss finish the sound.

morningfullon.description: Morning full-on is the sunrise version of psytrance's full-on style: major-key melodies, floating vocals, euphoria fully embraced as the sun returns to the floor. Slower and brighter than nocturnal full-on, it flirts with uplifting trance without adopting its production codes. Its anthems are recognizable from the very first build, and festivals reserve it for the hour the sun comes up.
morningfullon.production: Morning full-on sits between 138 and 143 BPM, slower than nocturnal full-on, the grid staying straight while a classic rolling bass often replaces the galloping pattern for something gentler that lets the track breathe. The kick is rounder and less punchy than its nocturnal cousin, around 55 Hz with a moderate click, soft snare or clap on 2 and 4 with longer reverb, and the build is the genre's central moment, an 8 to 16 bar snare roll with an opening highpass filter and rising velocity. The bass keeps the classic full-on kick-then-three-sixteenths pattern but with less distortion and more roundness, and, unusually for psy, it actually follows the pad's chord changes. On top, a Sylenth1 lead plays bright, singable major-key melodies climbing to the third and fifth, wide chorused pads, and ethereal reverb-drenched vocals in isolated words.

musiqueconcrete.description: Musique concrete began in Paris in 1948, when Pierre Schaeffer recorded trains, cut the tape, reversed it, looped it, and declared that recorded sound itself was material for composition. It invented sampling forty years before the sampler existed and turned the studio into an instrument in its own right. Everything gathered on this card descends, through one route or another, from that founding gesture.
musiqueconcrete.production: There is no dance tempo, this music thinks in durations and gestures rather than BPM, though Schaeffer invented the loop with his closed groove, and a loop has a duration that becomes a pulse. Set the grid to an arbitrary tempo, 100 BPM say, only to keep loops aligned, and let irregularity do the rest, a 1.7 second loop against a 2.3 second one, creating a cycle repeating after minutes. Build rhythm from the sound objects themselves, a locomotive, a creaking door, a sigh, recorded on a phone and dropped into Simpler in Slice mode. Slow any recording two or three octaves with Warp off, like tape run from 38 to 9.5 centimeters per second, for a manufactured bass. The essential gesture stays the scissors: cut recordings into fragments and glue them end to end.

ndh.description: Neue Deutsche Harte: 1990s Germany welded industrial metal to declaimed German lyrics, low tuned guitars over electronic sequences, and a deep, spoken vocal delivery. Rammstein became its global monument, but the scene runs from Oomph! to its current heirs. This is the stadium sized branch of the industrial lineage, pyrotechnics included, built as much for arenas of thousands as for underground clubs of a few hundred fans.
ndh.production: Tempos run from 90 to 130 BPM, with many tracks around 100 to 120 in a heavy, near half time feel, the groove square and locked to the grid like modern metal. The drums are metal drums, real or sampled, kick on quarter notes or doubled sixteenths, a huge snare on two and four through a long room reverb, eighth note hats, ride on the choruses and a crash on the strong beats. Under the acoustic kick, layer a saturated 909 kick for electronic weight, with a constant sixteenth note synthetic sequence running throughout. The bass follows the guitar in unison: low tuned guitars play palm muted eighths on the root, doubled exactly by a slightly distorted electric bass, with a square synth bass an octave below adding the machine edge underneath.

neogoa.description: Neo goa is a studious revival of the 1994 to 1997 goa sound, led since the 2000s by devotees who reclaim its machines, its scales and its art of layering. Suntrip Records serves as its parent label. This is not lazy nostalgia: the best neo goa productions rival their models in complexity, and the scene releases as much new material as it reissues old. Its practitioners treat the original goa records as a technical discipline to be mastered rather than a mood to be sampled, painstakingly recreating period hardware and arrangement techniques with a level of precision the genre's original producers rarely had the studio time to achieve.
neogoa.production: Neo goa reuses 1995's tempos, 142 to 148 BPM, a touch faster than original goa since its producers grew up on psytrance, on a straight, unswung grid but distinguished by real precision, arpeggio layers quantized to the sample, over 9 to 12 minute tracks counting 16 bar blocks while layering 3, 5 and 6 bar phrases against them. A better produced kick, tuned near 55 Hz, sits under a 909 clap, alternating velocity sixteenth hats, and synthetic congas, tablas and bells, snare rolls kept moderate since real lifts come from arpeggios not drum fills. The bass is continuous sixteenth acid, a TB-303 style sawtooth or square with resonant filtering, accents and slides like the real hardware, sometimes layered with a second, higher line. Arpeggiator lines, a phrygian lead, and period effects like slow phasers finish the picture.

neurofunk.description: Neurofunk is the systematic refinement of techstep from 1998 onward: constantly modulating basslines, surgically precise mixing and a cold, functional groove. The term itself came from criticism, coined by Simon Reynolds, before the scene adopted it as its own. Through the 2000s, Noisia turned this approach into a worldwide production standard, admired and imitated far beyond drum and bass, reaching into metal and video game soundtracks. It favours engineering precision over emotion: every element is mixed and processed to a near-forensic degree, with the bass treated as a constantly evolving sound design problem rather than a simple melodic line.
neurofunk.production: Neurofunk sits at a fixed 172 to 174 BPM with no swing, and the word funk is key: the beat stays a rigid two-step, kick on beat 1 and the and of 3, snare on 2 and 4 with a ghost hit, but the bass syncopates in sixteenths like a funk line played by a robot, its groove from the contrast between static drums and a bass that bounces and changes timbre note to note. Layer the kick from a short click and a 909 body, stack the snare from several sample-aligned hits with no reverb, program hats with tiny variation. The signature bass is a multiband-resampled Reese, two detuned oscillators split into three bands and processed separately, clean lows, distorted mids, FM'd highs, then bounced back and reworked. Serum supplies the Reese, FM8 the metallic, talking basslines.

newage.description: New age is the wellness music of the 1980s: soft synth pads, harps, ocean recordings and a sonic promise of healing. Commercially it was enormous and critically it was mocked, yet it also produced genuine contemplative masterpieces, from Iasos to Laraaji, that the ambient revival of the 2010s rehabilitated through compilations such as those on Light in the Attic. The line between new age and ambient is really a matter of intention rather than sound: new age wants to soothe and resolve, while ambient is happy to simply exist in the room. Both share soft synths and long reverbs, but new age always points somewhere gentle and warm.
newage.production: New age usually sits at 60 to 90 BPM, or drifts fully rubato with no grid, close to a resting pulse, which suits relaxation, with eighth-note arpeggios rocking gently in 4/4 or a soft 6/8. Unlike ambient there is a clear pulse and an advancing melody, but everything is rounded off, no swing, a slight lag of the chords behind the beat, and rallentandos at phrase ends. When there is a drum part it stays muted, a soft drum machine, kick on 1 and 3, gated reverb-drowned snare, or world percussion like shaker and tabla. The bass, when present, is soft and sustained, barely audible as a line, with the harmony doing the work through bright major chords and a tonic pedal that resolves. Period presets, pan flutes, choir voices, harp and nature recordings complete a crystal-clear sound.

newbeat.description: New beat was a Belgian accident from 1987: a DJ played an EBM record at 33 RPM instead of 45, and the resulting slowness became a style in its own right. New beat drags along at 105 to 115 beats per minute, with rubbery basslines, deep voices and a laboratory kind of eroticism. Two years of national madness and dozens of opportunistic studios followed, before the wave dissolved into the emerging techno and hardcore scenes, leaving them the distinctly Belgian taste for a heavy kick.
newbeat.production: New beat drags along at 105 to 115 BPM, sometimes 100, roughly 20 percent slower than the EBM it comes from, heavy and almost lazy but perfectly straight. A TR-909 dominates, slowed and pitched down, kick on every beat with a long decay, snare on two and four through a big reverb, and an open hat on the offbeats giving the sway. The bass is a relaxed EBM bass, a square or sawtooth note in eighths through a closed lowpass filter with marked resonance and a long release so it bounces, a slight glide between notes, lines often descending through the minor scale. New beat lives on samples, moans, erotic phrases, slogans, sirens, a deep voice pitched down and spoken slowly, with the era's rule that anything too bright gets pulled down three semitones and filtered.

nitzhonot.description: Israel's heresy against Goa, 1997 to 2000: nitzhonot means victories in Hebrew, and the sound goes for it, near-hardtrance kicks, grand oriental melodies played without irony, euphoric builds made for Tel Aviv beaches rather than Himalayan plateaus. The international psy scene despised it at the time, precisely because it was popular, local and sentimental. It burned fast, left a handful of anthems, and its direct descendant is the Israeli uplifting sound that fed commercial full-on, a genre now extinct but rehabilitated by nostalgia.
nitzhonot.production: Push a bit harder than the Goa it comes from, 145 to 155 bpm, with a square, near-hardtrance feel: tight 8-bar phrases, one main rhythm, one heavy kick, one melody taking up all the space, with short breaks returning every 32 or 48 bars. Build the kick as a fast pitch-dropping laser kick, sine from 200Hz to 50Hz, then hard saturation on every beat, paired with a loud open hat on the off eighths and a clap doubled with a 909 on 2 and 4. For bass, choose an off-eighth line, sawtooth filtered near 250Hz, or the Goa-style sixteenth motif, following the melody's chord changes. The lead is a supersaw played on phrygian or harmonic minor scales with long singing melodies, stacked with grand strings and a discreet acid line underneath.

nudisco.description: Nu-disco is the unabashed return of disco within 2000s production: part reissues, part edits, part brand new tracks played with today's tools. It keeps the format's core disco elements, sweeping strings, chicken-scratch guitars and round basslines, while adding sequencer precision and modern mastering. The edit scene, running from DJ Harvey through the blogs of the 2010s, drives the sound as much as the labels releasing it. It is disco remade with contemporary ears: the same warmth and swing, but tightened, cleaned up and built for today's soundsystems and dancefloors.
nudisco.production: Nu-disco runs 112 to 125 BPM, usually 118 to 122, with 55 to 58 percent swing on the sixteenths inherited from a played disco loop, a solid default being 120 BPM at 56 percent while the kick stays locked to the grid. Layer a chopped, replayed disco break over a clean 909 or 808 kick on all four beats, a modern clap doubling the snare on 2 and 4, open hats on the offbeats, plus congas, shaker and tambourine. The bass, played or sampled and transposed, moves in syncopated sixteenths with octave jumps, its filter opening from intro to drop, sidechained to the kick. Filtered disco samples, a Juno-106 for pads, a Rhodes for chords and a real chicken-scratch guitar complete it, tied together by filtering and a dotted-eighth delay on the stabs.

nuitalo.description: Nu italo is italo disco reread by producers born after it, from the mid 2000s to today. The machines are the same ones, or faithful emulations of them, the melodies keep the original's unashamed sentimentality, but the production is clean and the wink to the past is constant. Sweden and Italy answer each other across the style, somewhere between sincere homage and studious reconstruction. It treats italo disco less as a museum piece than as a living vocabulary, one that later generations can polish, slow down and soften without ever losing the emotional directness that made the original records so beloved in the first place.
nuitalo.production: Nu italo keeps italo disco's tempo, 115 to 125 BPM, though melancholy producers like Johnny Jewel or Sally Shapiro lean lower, 112 to 118, sitting perfectly on the grid with no swing but softer attacks than the originals. A sampled LinnDrum, kick on every beat, clap and snare on two and four through a shorter, gentler gated reverb than 1983's, and sixteenth hats opening on the offbeat of four, sits under light bus compression. The bass is a Juno 106 or emulation, sawtooth with light chorus, filtered near 500 Hz, playing octaves through a sentimental four chord minor progression, gently sidechained to the kick and doubled by a quiet sub sine. The Juno 106 also supplies chorused pads and sixteenth arpeggios with dotted eighth delay, doubled whispered vocals in long reverb, DX7 bells, and a restrained sawtooth lead.

nujazz.description: Jazz reread through machines around 2000: broken beats, house and hip hop placed under extended harmonies, spanning Viennese studios, the clubs of Saint-Germain and the Scandinavian scene. St Germain sold millions, Jazzanova refined the formula, and The Cinematic Orchestra brought real emotion to it. It became the door through which jazz returned to clubs, well before today's London wave of young jazz musicians reclaimed the same ground.
nujazz.production: Nu jazz lives on two tempos, jazzy house around 120 to 128 BPM as with St Germain, and broken beat around 100 to 110 BPM as with Jazzanova, with accents falling off the grid onto syncopated sixteenths rather than a simple late feel. On the house side keep the four on the floor straight and leave the swing to hats and percussion: a 909 or sampled kick on every beat, open hats on the offbeat, a jazzy rimshot and sampled brushes swinging over the top, plus congas. On the broken beat side syncopate the kick itself, with the snare and hats in shifted accents. In both cases layer a real, sampled or played jazz kit with ride and brushes over the programmed drums, the mix of machine and drummer being the true signature.

nuskoolbreaks.description: Nu skool breaks is breakbeat taken back in hand at the end of the 1990s: house tempo, tense electro basslines, precise production, with neither rave nostalgia nor big beat's heaviness. Adam Freeland and Rennie Pilgrem codified its sound, and the scene held English and Australian clubs until the mid 2000s. Its synthetic bass would go on to anticipate melodic dubstep and electro house, making it a quiet but direct ancestor of much of the bass music that followed, even as the scene itself faded from view once those descendants took over the clubs it had once defined.
nuskoolbreaks.production: Sit at house and progressive tempo, 125 to 135 BPM with 130 as the standard, and keep the feel clean and precise, closer to techno than to rave nostalgia or big beat weight, with swing at zero. Program the break: a 909 kick on beat one, the and of two and the sixteenth before four, snare on two and four, closed hats in alternating velocity sixteenths, plus an 808 cowbell on the offbeats. The bass, a saw or square on a Nord Lead or Analog, runs a resonant low pass filter modulated by a fast envelope and a slow LFO, playing syncopated eighths on the root and minor seventh with an octave glide at phrase ends and a light sidechain against the break kick. This restless bass points toward electro house and melodic dubstep.

nustylegabber.description: Nu style gabber is hardcore reborn at the turn of the 2000s in a slower, heavier form: long, sculpted kicks around 150 to 160 BPM, modern mixing, and MC choruses. Angerfist became its worldwide mask, Masters of Hardcore its cathedral. This is the hardcore of today's big venues, a Dutch industry fully embraced with its own stars and anthems. Where old-school gabber prized speed and chaos, nu style prizes weight and polish.
nustylegabber.production: Nu style gabber sits between 150 and 170 BPM, slower and heavier than 1990s gabber, and at that speed a beat lasts 375 milliseconds, long enough for the kick to carry a real tuned tail. The kick is built in layers, the genre's key difference from classic gabber: a short, clipped 909 attack, then a separate tuned, saturated tail lasting 250 to 300 milliseconds, glued together and bounced repeatedly, with snare or clap sitting back on 2 and 4. The bass is essentially the kick's tail, built from a sine or triangle with a pitch envelope dropping an octave over 100 milliseconds; chord changes come from pitching the kick's tail rather than adding a separate bassline. On top, the screech, a distorted resonant sawtooth lead through a bandpass filter, sits alongside shouted MC hooks and reverse cymbals.

orchestraltrance.description: Trance written like a score: sampled strings, classical harmonic progressions, breakdowns that unfold like a symphonic movement. Tiesto carried it to stadiums with Elements of Life, and Andy Blueman turned it into fine craftsmanship. This is the point where uplifting trance meets film music, with all the grandeur and unashamed kitsch that implies, sitting somewhere between a club anthem and a concert hall score.
orchestraltrance.production: Play at 136 to 140 BPM, the uplifting tempo, but think in movements rather than blocks, as if writing a score, over a straight grid. A breakdown can run three minutes and include a key change, a slowing of the harmony, or a section built entirely in whole notes, with full tracks stretching to ten or twelve minutes. Count in eight bar phrases that match melodic lines, and plan a key change up a tone for the final drop. On the drop, use uplifting style drums, a clean kick, clap and snare on two and four, and add orchestral percussion on top, timbales on the first beats of eight bar blocks, a big bass drum reinforcing the kick, and a fanfare snare roll. The bass is an offbeat sawtooth doubled by sampled cellos and double basses for warmth.

peaktimetechno.description: The retailer's genre tag turned into programming reality: big room techno of the 2010s and 2020s, builds, drops, clean kicks and maximum efficiency between 128 and 135 beats per minute. More a shelf label than a scene, and a debated one in the corpus, it nonetheless describes exactly what headline acts play at midnight. Drumcode is its obvious reference point, the label most associated with the sound.
peaktimetechno.production: Run from 128 to 135 BPM, most often 130 or 132, with at most a light swing on the hats and everything else straight, built for efficiency and clarity in a big room at midnight, with every gesture clearly announced. Layer the kick carefully: a short sine sub tuned to the key, a 909 or synthesized body, and a click for definition. Add closed hats on the offbeats, an open hat on the last offbeat, ride on the peaks, a clap on two and four with a short reverb, and descending tom fills at the end of phrases, building into snare rolls before the drop. The bass is often FM, built from a carrier and a modulator through a low pass filter, played as a jumping octave pattern, joined by a processed bass lead that becomes the real hook.

phillysoul.description: Philly soul came out of Philadelphia in the early 1970s, where Gamble and Huff industrialized orchestral soul: silky strings, the MFSB house band, love songs and songs of social conscience. The Philly sound is the direct matrix of disco, the same orchestra and the same studios, needing only an opened hi-hat to cross over. Love Is the Message is literally the founding record of both worlds.
phillysoul.production: Ballads sit at 65 to 80 BPM, while uptempo dance sides that prefigure disco, songs like Love Train or TSOP, run 110 to 125, with a light 52 to 55 percent swing, the drums leaning slightly ahead of the beat. Build the drums from Earl Young's MFSB template, the one that invented the disco beat: kick on four beats, snare on two and four, hats in eighths opening on every offbeat for that pshh. Layer discreet ghost snare notes, sixteenth-note congas, tambourine and cabasa. The bass is a fingered Fender line, walking through the chord changes with passing tones, a third or fifth as an approach note, kept warm with gentle compression. Write real orchestral string parts rather than block chords, a rising violin motif answered by a descending cello line, plus soft horns and a wah guitar.

postdisco.description: Post-disco is New York between 1979 and 1983, after the Disco Demolition Night made the word disco commercially toxic while the music simply kept going under other names. The groove strips down, the strings disappear, bass and drums take over the whole space, and the studio becomes more experimental. It is the shared matrix of boogie, garage and house, the densest hinge in this whole map.
postdisco.production: Post-disco slows slightly and strips down, 105 to 120 BPM, the feel still played but drier and tenser than disco, with light swing around 53 to 55 percent. The signature is space: fewer elements, each one louder, the kick not necessarily on every beat, the snare cracking alone on 2 and 4, the whole groove resting on just drums, bass and one keyboard. The drums are dry and close-mic'd, sometimes doubled or replaced by an early drum machine like the LinnDrum or CR-78 for a machine edge. The electric bass sits up front as the main element, minimal, a two-bar motif on one or two notes, slapped or picked and repeated without variation, compressed hard to snap. On top, a Prophet-5 replaces the strings with minor chord stabs, and the vocal is often treated as an instrument.

powerelectronics.description: The fully embraced extremity of noise: feedback, treated screams, hostile frequencies, and deliberately unbearable subject matter. Whitehouse named the genre in 1982, and the scene has remained a restricted circle ever since, caught between theatrical transgression and radical sound art. Nobody dances to this, they endure it, and its place here is as a boundary marker, the furthest point from the rest of the industrial family.
powerelectronics.production: There is no tempo. Power electronics plays in free time, with no grid and no regular pulse, refusing even the machine pulse of the industrial music it descends from, the only real measure is duration, blocks of noise running 2 to 15 minutes. Turn off the metronome, work with the snap grid disabled, and think in seconds rather than bars, if a pulse does appear it should come from a low-frequency square oscillator chopping a drone at 2 or 8 Hz, not a drum machine. There is no drum kit: rhythmic events come from a square LFO gating a drone, feedback oscillating in bursts, or a voice screaming in salvos, a fast auto-pan at full amount gets close to the genre's mechanical pulse.

progpsy.description: Psy prog was born at the end of the 1990s in Scandinavia from the meeting of progressive trance and psytrance, not from goa alone: psytrance slows down and hollows out, while progressive trance supplies its long trajectories. The bass is offbeat, round and rolling, builds stretch over minutes, and sound design replaces the melodic assault of full on psytrance. It is sunrise music, not a peak time assault. The Swedish school, Atmos, Ticon, Vibrasphere, defined the sound, while the 2010s Israeli wave, Ace Ventura, Liquid Soul, made it more melodic and mainstream. What sets it apart from psytech and zenonesque is that offbeat bass and melodic light.
progpsy.production: Sit around 138 BPM, between 134 and 140, with the bass shifting from rolling to offbeat: kick on the beat, bass on the eighth note offbeat, giving a sway rather than a wheel, with only light swing, 51 to 53 percent, allowed on percussion and never on the bass. Phrases stretch to 32 or 64 bars, over 8 to 10 minutes. The kick is round and deep, tuned near 50 Hz, since the bass never crowds the following sixteenth; percussion stays discreet, softly swung shakers and spaced wood blocks rather than snare rolls. The bass opens its filter envelope on every note and releases quickly for the bounce, sidechained gently to the kick. Above it sit evolving Virus and Nord Lead pads, soft plucked leads with dotted eighth delay, and slow filter sweeps rather than acid squelches.

progressivebreaks.description: The long, rising trajectories of progressive house laid over breakbeats instead of a four-on-the-floor kick: swelling pads, round basslines, and an end-of-night melancholy around 130 beats per minute. Hybrid writes its symphonies here, Way Out West its anthems. The style lives somewhat in the shadow of the progressive house it grew from, cherished mainly by connoisseurs of its 1999 to 2004 heyday.
progressivebreaks.production: Play at 128 to 134 BPM with a long, drifting feel, no swing, breaks kept clean and understated so attention goes to pads that rise over 32 or 64 bars, changing roughly every 32 bars rather than the 8 of nu skool breaks, so a build can last two full minutes. Program a mid-tempo break from clean 909 or soft samples: kick on beat 1 and the off-beat of 2, snare or rimshot on 2 and 4, gentle sixteenth hats, shakers, and low tribal percussion looped over two bars, with rare fills like a reversed cymbal every 32 bars.

progressivehouse.description: Progressive house is the English sound of 1990 to 1992 that stretches house music into long tracks, built in layers that rise in stages rather than through verses and choruses. Round basslines, discreet tribal percussion and stacking pads turn the record into a journey rather than a song. The label Guerilla and the sets of Sasha and Digweed fixed the aesthetic, which ruled the clubs of the 1990s before diluting into the mainstream of the 2010s.
progressivehouse.production: Work at 126 to 128 BPM, dead-straight kick, only a light 52 to 55 percent swing on the percussion. Think in long forms: 32-bar phrases, 64-bar builds, tracks running 8 to 10 minutes with a single peak two-thirds through. The rhythmic core is a tribal percussion layer, congas, bongos and sampled shakers looped over two bars and doubled by dotted-sixteenth delays, entering one instrument at a time, under a round 909 kick and a discreet clap on one and four. The bassline is a filtered saw or square turning like a wheel, its two-bar motif changing one note every eight bars, lightly sidechained, cutoff automated open across 32 bars. Stack two or three pads in held chords, each opening its own filter at a different speed, washed in delay and reverb.

progressivetrance.description: Trance learning the patience of progressive house: fewer shouted choruses, more long trajectories, rolling basslines and layers that assemble themselves over ten minutes. It began in the 1990s on Platipus, reached its golden age around 2000, then found a melodic rebirth through Anjunabeats. This is the side of trance that club purists have always preferred to its stadium sized anthems and hands in the air hooks.
progressivetrance.production: Work between 128 and 134 BPM, barely faster than the progressive house it borrows its patience from. The grid stays straight, but the groove comes from a rolling bassline in eighths and sixteenths rather than from the drums. Think in ten minute tracks built from 32 bar blocks, each changing one element, with transitions by filter fades rather than hard cuts. The kick is less dominant than in uplifting trance, a short 909 or a drier sampled kick, and the snare is often a thin clap kept low. Closed hats run in sixteenths with alternating velocities to create a rolling feel, joined by discreet shakers and a filtered conga. The rolling bass is the signature: a sawtooth around 350 Hz, eighths on the root with added sixteenths, sidechained from the kick, doubled by a sine sub below 60 Hz.

prototechno.description: Proto techno is Kraftwerk, in Dusseldorf between 1974 and 1981: the man machine, the robotic melody, the electronic beat embraced as a total aesthetic. Trans Europe Express would cross the Atlantic to help spawn Bronx electro and Detroit techno, both of which unanimously recognize it as point zero. Moroder, working from Munich at the same time, supplied the other half of the genetic code: the looped, sequenced bassline. Together these two strands, one German and conceptual, the other Italian by way of Munich and disco, gave the coming decades of electronic dance music both its machine rhythm and its rolling low end.
prototechno.production: Keep tempos between 110 and 130 BPM, fully quantized with zero swing, since the man machine embraces the grid; Trans Europe Express sits near 112, Moroder's The Chase around 125. The feel comes from repeating a two bar motif for six minutes with tiny variations, so disable groove and let the machine dictate. Build the kit from bare synthesized sounds, a sine kick sweeping down in pitch, a bandpass filtered noise snare, and short noise hats, kick on every beat, snare on two and four. Bass follows two paths: a short, round Minimoog note per chord, or Moroder's sequenced sixteenths alternating root and octave through a short dotted eighth delay, kick and bass landing together, no sidechain. Finish with a vocoder singing through a sawtooth carrier, a detuned Minimoog lead, and chorused synth strings.

psybient.description: Psybient is the ambient wing of psytrance culture: cosmic pads, dub basslines, fractal textures and ethnic instruments, the chill zone of festivals grown into its own continent. Shpongle is its baroque flagship, Carbon Based Lifeforms its crystalline Swedish counterpart, and Ultimae the label that built it a cathedral. The near-synonymous names psybient and psychill both describe roughly the same territory.
psybient.production: Psybient sits between 70 and 100 BPM when there is a beat at all, many passages dropping it entirely, treating tempo as a frame for syncing delays across tracks running eight to twelve minutes. Build a round, deep kick with a long decay, and a dub snare or rimshot on beat three washed through a Space Echo at high feedback. Layer sampled ethnic percussion, tabla, udu, djembe, frame drum, sliced and replayed in humanized two-bar motifs, letting the beat enter only after two minutes. The bass is a round dub tone, an Operator sine or Moog with soft saturation and a long release, holding the tonic and minor seventh with slow glides, rolling rather than pulsing. Above it, stack long evolving pads with slow LFOs on wave position, changing so gradually nobody hears the transition.

psybreaks.description: Psybreaks applies the sound design of psytrance to breakbeats: precise, shifting basslines and psychedelic textures running around 135 to 140 beats per minute. Hedflux gave the style its clearest form in the late 2000s, sitting between the English breaks scene and the psychedelic festival circuit. It is a narrow but real zone that shows the two cultures share more than people tend to assume.
psybreaks.production: Psybreaks runs 135 to 140 BPM, a touch faster than nu skool, with a precise, rolling feel: the break stays clean with no swing while the bass follows a continuous sixteenth note pulse. The break uses short, precise sounds, kick on beat one and the upbeat of two, a very dry snare on two and four, closed hats in alternating velocity sixteenths, and synthetic percussion, clicks, blips, pitched rimshots, following a triplet motif every other bar. The real center is the bass, a Serum saw or wavetable through a fast, resonant lowpass filter playing very short sixteenth notes on the root that roll continuously and rest where the kick lands. Classic psytrance effects, long feedback delays, synced phasers, resonant squelches and panning sweeps, finish the psychedelic texture in a production kept surgically clean.

psychedelictrance.description: The globalised form that succeeded Goa in the late 1990s: cleaner digital production, a continuous rolling bass, liquid textures, and a tempo between 140 and 148. Israel became its second home, and festivals its central institution, from Boom in Portugal to Ozora in Hungary. Every branch this map details, from full on to dark, grows out of this single common trunk, precise and globally recognisable wherever it is played.
psychedelictrance.production: The core tempo sits between 140 and 148 BPM, with 145 as a common reference point, everything quantized dead straight with no swing: movement comes from the rolling bass and delays, not from groove. The whole track leans on a one bar pattern repeated with digital precision, kick on the beat, bass on the three sixteenths that follow. Keep the kick short and round with a marked click and a tail under 150 milliseconds, with a dry snare or layered clap on two and four, closed hats on the offbeats, and an open hat on the and of four. The rolling bass defines the genre: the kick plays the first sixteenth, the bass the following three, each note short, built from a filtered sawtooth with a fast decaying envelope. Add liquid FX from resonant filter sweeps.

psycore.description: Psycore is the point where psychedelic trance stops negotiating: tempos beyond 180 beats per minute, sometimes reaching 250, shattered song structures, noise and black humor, and an openly claimed junction with hardcore and speedcore. It is a tiny, international scene, radical by definition, that treats trance as an experience of total saturation rather than release, pushing the whole idea of psychedelia to its breaking point.
psycore.production: Psycore starts around 180 BPM and climbs to 200, 220, sometimes 250, where the grid becomes almost abstract, and the genre exploits that by changing tempo mid-track, doubling or halving it by section, or layering a kick at 200 over a bassline at half speed. Build a hybrid kick, a tuned psy kick layered with a distorted speedcore kick, a saturated sine pushed until it turns square, playing in bursts of eighths or sixteenths rather than on the beats, while the snare is clipped white noise and the hats are replaced by glitched micro-sounds. The bass is a pierced, ultra-fast tone, an FM wave or saw with sharp distortion and a bandpass filter, notes lasting 30 to 40 milliseconds with zero release, often fused with the kick, while a clean sub stays separate below 60Hz.

psydub.description: Psychedelic music laid over dub bass: mid tempo, endless echoes, oriental and organic textures, the legacy of Shpongle and the psytrance festival chill scenes. It is the music of the rest areas turned into its own genre, complete with dedicated producers and labels, somewhere between a journey and a waking nap, played as the sun rises over a festival field once the main stage falls silent.
psydub.production: Psydub sits between 70 and 100 BPM, with many tracks around 85 to 95. The feel is half time, the snare landing on beat three rather than two and four, which reads as deep slowness even when the hats run in sixteenths. Swing is welcome on the percussion, and played instruments add their own natural micro delays. Dotted delays build long cycles over the slow tempo, and a track can run seven to twelve minutes without rushing. The kick is deep and long, tuned low with a 300 millisecond body, often a dub sample doubled with an 808. Hats are thin and swung, often replaced by shakers and ethnic percussion, tabla, udu, dumbek, through a tape delay. The bass is a sine or triangle with a soft attack, a long decay and a low pass filter, following dub tradition.

psytech.description: Psytech is a crossroads between techno and psytrance rather than a straight line out of psy prog: the kick turns dry, the groove turns club oriented, and the bass no longer bounces on the offbeat but rolls straight, techno style. Its roots sit in Hamburg in the early 2000s, when X Dream and The Delta hardened their sound, and today it is carried by the netlabel scene, Digital Diamonds foremost, and by Techgnosis. What separates it from its two neighbors is that straight kick and club function, since psy prog keeps an offbeat bass and melody while zenonesque slows down for texture.
psytech.production: Psytech runs 130 to 138 BPM, a club techno tempo rather than a psytrance one, with a straight, unswung grid where the groove comes from a bass rolling in regular sixteenths, slower than psytrance but built the same way. A dry techno kick, tuned around 55 Hz with a sharp, compressed attack, plays four per bar under a short reverbed clap on two and four, closed hats on the offbeats, an open hat on the upbeats. The bass rolls straight, a kick on the first sixteenth followed by three bass notes with short releases, a less aggressive tone than psytrance. Modular style step sequences, dub style tape delays, and sparingly dosed psychedelic effects, a squelch, a filter sweep, a background drone, round out a sound built never to saturate the spectrum.

raggacore.description: Raggacore is breakcore that chooses dancehall over dread: the Amen break and hard kicks driven under sped-up ragga toasts, sound-system culture run through a grinder with humor and speed intact. Aaron Spectre, Bong-Ra and FFF held the scene together across European squats and netlabels in the mid-2000s. It stands as ragga jungle's illegitimate, joyful offspring, where satire matters as much as studio precision.
raggacore.production: Raggacore runs between 160 and 220 BPM, usually 175 to 190, pushing ragga jungle's tempo further, the grid a chopped Amen breakbeat rather than a regular four-on-the-floor, with gabber kicks falling wherever the producer wants. The Amen is sped to tempo and reordered over two bars with displaced snare hits and sixteenth retrigs, then crushed gabber kicks replace the break's own kick on certain beats, sometimes bursting in fours like a punch, while dancehall rimshots sit on the offbeats and sections drop to half-tempo for the skank. The bass draws from dancehall and jungle, a sine sub or a Reese filtered around 300 Hz playing a short, syncopated minor-key motif on the offbeats, sidechained hard by the gabber kick so it can cut through. On top, sped-up ragga acapellas turn into a machine-gun toast, joined by sirens and dub delays.

raggajungle.description: Ragga jungle is jungle with the microphone up front: dancehall and reggae vocals, soundsystem bass, and the Jamaican culture of London asserted front and center rather than sampled in passing. Its golden age ran from 1994 to 1996, with Congo Natty as the keeper of the flame ever since. It is the most directly dub-descended branch of jungle, and the most festive.
raggajungle.production: Ragga jungle sits at 160 to 170 BPM, the jungle tempo of 1994 and 1995, but the voice leads here, dictated by a deejay's flow counting in at 80 to 85, half the actual tempo. Play the Amen or Think break fairly whole, with cuts timed to the end of vocal phrases: break kick on one, snare on two and four, plus an extra snare on the and of four, a rimshot on three for the dancehall feel. The bass is the slowest sub in the family, a sine or filtered square between 40 and 55Hz playing a real reggae line, root on one, fifth on the and of two, back to root on four, then silence, like a slowed Sly and Robbie bassline. Build the top from ragga a cappellas, sirens, foghorns and a guitar skank on the offbeats.

reggae.description: Reggae is a root here, not a branch. Jamaican reggae gave the world the sound system, the bass as foundation, the instrumental version and a remix culture before the word even existed: dub descends directly from it, and with dub, half of British bass music. SONAA does not develop this lineage further, since its scope is electronic music; reggae appears here as the parent of everything it handed down, from dub to UK funky.
reggae.production: Reggae plays at a felt 60 to 90 BPM, often notated 120 to 180 by electronic producers, the feel resting on two things: the one drop, weight on beat 3 rather than 1, and the skank, guitar and organ chords struck on the offbeats, played with a light swing, ahead of the beat and behind on the 3. Three drum patterns matter: the one drop, kick and rimshot together on 3 with nothing on 1; the rockers, kick on all four beats with rimshot on 3; and the heavier steppers. The bass is the foundation, a muted, deep fingered Fender playing a two-bar riff that defines the whole riddim, with long silences and a held note on the 3. On top, offbeat skank guitar doubled by a bubbling organ and short spring reverb on the snare.

rhythmicnoise.description: Noise brought to heel: massive distortion organised into danceable rhythms, crushed four on the floor beats, textures of scrap metal. Esplendor Geometrico announced it in the 1980s, and the scene structured itself in the 1990s around Ant-Zen and Hands, with the Maschinenfest festival as its cathedral. This is the dancefloor of hard industrial music, physical and cathartic, built for bodies as much as for ears.
rhythmicnoise.production: Hold between 120 and 150 BPM, four on the floor, dead straight, no swing at all, though some tracks sit at 90 BPM with a double time pattern that reads the same. What separates rhythmic noise from the power electronics it descends from is that the grid has returned, and it is unforgiving. The kick is a product of distortion, not a drum sound: take a 909 kick and stack three or four stages, overdrive, hard curve saturation, fuzz and heavy bit reduction, until it becomes a buzzing square wave with a droning tail. Program four beats, plus syncopated sixteenth note kicks for a galloping feel, a snare built from a burst of distorted noise, and clicking noise hats, with looped, saturated metal samples as texture. There is usually no separate bass: the distorted kick fills the low end alone.

riddim.description: Riddim is the minimalist reduction of brostep that took hold in the mid-2010s: a single hammering bass motif repeated in triplets, almost without variation, built for hypnosis in the pit. The name borrows from dancehall, though the actual kinship is distant. It belongs to a North American festival scene with a devoted audience, mocked and thriving in equal measure, dubstep's answer to gabber.
riddim.production: Riddim sits at 140 to 150 BPM, often 150 today, with a kick that is frequently a straight 4/4 or on one and three, snare on two and four, closer to heavy techno than to dubstep. The signature is the triplet feel: the bass plays eighth or sixteenth triplets on a hard-quantized grid, and a two-bar motif repeats up to thirty-two times, hypnosis replacing the brostep rollercoaster. Build the bass in Serum as a square oscillator with a touch of FM, a short decay and an instant pitch envelope, playing one or two notes, doubled by a sub sine, varied only by a filter change every eight bars. Drums stay short, dry and minimal, a kick with a pronounced click and no sub, a sharp snare with a clap, hats nearly absent, the bass itself functioning as the main percussion.

rominimal.description: The Romanian school of minimal, born in Bucharest in the mid 2000s around Arpiar: endless loops, tiny organic sounds, a clean swing, ten-hour sets where time dissolves. Villalobos is its outside godfather, Rhadoo, Petre Inspirescu and Raresh its local masters. The scene insists on its difference from Berlin minimal, and vinyl remains a religion there, played in sets built to last an entire night.
rominimal.production: Sit between 123 and 126 bpm with a clean, discreet swing applied with clockmaker precision to the percussion only, organic percussion sitting slightly after the grid while the kick stays on it. Extract a groove from an old house record and apply it lightly to everything but the kick, since ro-minimal is built for ten-hour sets that must stay mixable throughout. Build a very round kick, no clap, just a muted rimshot or wood tap on 2 and 4, and organic, felted percussion, congas, bongos, shakers, programmed over several bars so nothing repeats identically. For bass, keep it almost subliminal, a pure sub sine on the root in long notes, occasionally joined by a shorter second bass on an offbeat. Layer intimate field recordings, tiny organic sounds, and dub delays synced to the percussion.

schranz.description: German hard techno of the 2000s, named by Chris Liebing: saturated, rolling percussion loops planed down until they become a single block of friction, around 150 beats per minute. Melodic events are scarce, replaced by a trance of pure texture and pressure, built for long, physical sets. The hard techno revival of the 2020s owes it almost everything, while rarely crediting the debt it owes to these earlier German producers.
schranz.production: Hold between 145 and 155 BPM with no groove at all: schranz is a trance of matter, and the tempo is a wall nothing should stray from. The feel comes from loops grinding against each other and moving filters, not from drum programming. Build a three part kick group: a main kick, a quieter offbeat kick with a faded attack, and sidechained sixteenth note kicks filling the gaps, together creating a constant pulsation. Above that, a noise blanket of claps, low closed hats, open hats and doubled rides, all saturated. Percussion comes from loops: take a chunk from an eight bar sample, roll it under an automated bandpass filter, and saturate it. There is no separate bass: the treated kick group owns the low end alone.

skweee.description: Scandinavia, 2006 to 2010: a minimal, twisted synthetic funk with round, squelching basses, naive melodies and a hip hop tempo. The name comes from the gesture itself, squeezing every last drop from simple synthesizers. A tiny scene between Stockholm and Helsinki became an instant cult favourite among diggers, with an obvious kinship to wonky and a shared taste for slow, gondoled hip hop tempos.
skweee.production: Skweee sits slow, 80 to 105 BPM, hip hop tempo, with a marked swing on the sixteenths. It is one of the few styles in the family that leaves so much air between hits, letting the kick and snare breathe while the bass stretches into the space. Use a dry drum machine, kick on one and the and of two in a boom bap pattern, never four on the floor, with a thin, slightly late snare on two and four, swung closed hats with gaps, and only one extra element such as a bell or a filtered percussive hit. Restraint is the rule, four or five bare drum tracks, variation created by muting a hat rather than adding a fill.
