The bass is round and detuned, a simple monophonic synth playing fifth or octave slides in naive minor keys.

soulfulhouse.description: House that keeps gospel at its center: big voices, choirs, piano chords and written arrangements, a direct inheritance from New York garage. Masters At Work are its major craftsmen, working between house, Latin and jazz. The style has its churches, its standards and its faithful performers, and it ages like soul music: slowly, and well, always favoring musicianship over machine precision.
soulfulhouse.production: Sit between 120 and 126 bpm with a live band feel: swing on hats and percussion, a straight kick, but keyboards and bass played by hand keeping their small human shifts, the vocal phrasing freely over the top. Build a softened kit, snare and clap together on 2 and 4, swung hats, and essential Latin percussion, congas in tumbao, bongos, shaker, guiro, dropping the kick on breaks so percussion and vocal carry alone. For bass, play a funky, melodic line following a jazz progression, walking between roots, chromatic passing tones and ghost notes, on electric bass or a fingered synth. Layer played Rhodes and piano jazz chords, written strings and horns, and a lead gospel vocal with choir harmonies and call and response, finished with hall reverb and chorus.

spacemusic.description: Space music is the mainstream cosmic electronic sound of the 1970s: clear melodies floating over planetary pads, somewhere between science popularization and pop reverie. Jean-Michel Jarre filled stadiums with it, Vangelis wrote it for film, and Space made planetariums dance. It was the door through which millions of ears first walked into the synthesizer, grand and accessible at once, turning it from a laboratory curiosity into a household sound.
spacemusic.production: Space music keeps the kosmische pulse but pops it up, 100 to 125 BPM with eighth or sixteenth sequences built around a melody you remember; Oxygene Part IV sits near 120 with a discreet drum machine and a slight human lead on the main melody to keep it alive. The drum machine stays in the background, modeled on Jarre's toy-like Korg Mini Pops: a simple kick on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4, eighth-note hats, all near subliminal. The real rhythm comes from arpeggiated sequences, sixteen notes on a minor chord run through an up-down arpeggiator. The bass is a held or eighth-note line following the chord progression with slow portamento. The signature comes from the ARP 2600, the Eminent 310 and the Yamaha CS-80, wrapped in long, wide reverb.

spacesynth.description: Spacesynth is the instrumental, cosmic branch of italo disco, built on space imagery and science fiction album covers. Melodies play like film themes, with laser sounds and cascading arpeggios standing in for a singer, who is almost entirely absent. Laserdance and Koto set the genre's grammar in the mid-1980s, giving it a repertoire of heroic instrumental themes and arpeggiated basslines. A loyal scene of fans has kept spacesynth alive ever since, still trading records and playing that mid-1980s sound today.
spacesynth.production: Rule of thumb: 126 BPM, fully quantized, no swing, with a constant sixteenth-note pulse running through the bass arpeggios. Build the drums around a Roland TR-707: dry digital kick, short cracking snare doubled by a clap on beats two and four, closed hats in sixteenths opening on the offbeats, and Simmons-style tom fills descending every eight bars, with a short gated reverb for that 1986 sheen. The bass is a relentless sixteenth-note octave arpeggio, a sawtooth with a little square wave and a 500Hz filter, built with Ableton's Arpeggiator, always locking with the kick on beat one. Layer a JX-8P or virtual Juno for the heroic lead theme, a DX7 emulation for snappy FM basses and bells, and laser sweeps, a sine or saw pitched down 36 semitones with delay trailing behind.

speedcore.description: Speedcore pushes beyond 250 beats per minute, sometimes past 1000, until tempo itself becomes the subject of the music rather than just a setting. It grew out of the extremes of hardcore in the mid-1990s, between Australia's Bloody Fist label, Germany and Japan, and it is as much a production challenge as a piece of music, somewhere between conceptual performance and pure release valve. Moby unintentionally founded the concept with Thousand and its Guinness World Record for fastest tempo. At its outer edges the genre stops functioning as dance music altogether and becomes closer to an extreme listening experiment or endurance test.
speedcore.production: Speedcore starts at 250 BPM and climbs past 1000, where tempo becomes a frequency: at 600 BPM the ear hears a drone rather than distinct hits, and the genre lives on the transition between fused bursts and isolated strikes rather than swing. Keep the kick extremely short, 60 to 120 ms, mostly attack, heavily distorted, then build bursts in eighths, sixteenths and thirty-seconds over one to four bars, often accelerating; snare is nearly absent, breaks are clean cuts of silence then an abrupt return. There is effectively no bassline: the kick burst becomes the bass, since chaining kicks at a steady rate creates a low pitch, or a held white noise layer fills the low end. The few sounds that fit are short and sharp, film samples, sirens, swept noise, crushed for tracker aliasing, each with a clean transient.

speedgarage.description: Speed garage is 1997 London: New York house doped up on jungle basslines, warbling sub lines, garage organ stabs and ragga vocal samples. Double 99's RIP Groove is its founding act, and the summer of 1997 its commercial peak. Brief but foundational, it was the airlock between house music and everything the UK would go on to make from bass, periodically resurrected ever since.
speedgarage.production: Speed garage runs between 130 and 135 BPM with a squarer four-on-the-floor kick than the UK garage that follows it, the energy coming from the bass rather than the swing, though a moderate 909 shuffle still sits on the hats. A full TR-909 kick holds every beat, snare or clap cracks on 2 and 4, and each 8-bar phrase closes with a snare roll or a timbale build. The real DNA is the warp bass inherited from jungle: a Reese built from two detuned sawtooths in opposite directions, mono with glide, through a lowpass filter with slowly modulated cutoff, sliding a semitone or a fourth under a sine sub an octave below. On top, Korg M1 organ stabs, sampled ragga and dancehall vocal phrases, sirens and vinyl spin-backs, kept direct and simple.

suomisaundi.description: Finnish freeform psytrance, born in the late 1990s around the Texas Faggott crew: a joyful refusal of every rule in the genre. Twisted melodies, absurd samples, hidden funk under the kicks, and deliberately homemade production where you can hear the studio and the jokes shared between friends. The name literally means Finnish sound, and the scene owns that: local, self-produced music that gently mocks Goa's cosmic seriousness. Cult everywhere, understood nowhere, and still alive today in the forests of Finland.
suomisaundi.production: Suomisaundi sits between 140 and 150 BPM, but tempo is the one rule this branch of psy breaks freely, some tracks shift tempo mid-track or drop into half-time. The groove hides funk underneath, so a swing of 54 to 58 percent on percussion and bass is welcome, and the structure feels like a jam, count in eights but allow six or ten when the joke calls for it. Keep a proper psy kick but let it share space with sampled drum breaks and absurd extra percussion like a car horn or a spoon on a glass. Fills are tricky: triplet rolls that land a beat too early, or Beat Repeat chopping up a whole bar.

synthfunk.description: Synth funk is 1980s funk run entirely through machines: Zapp and the talkbox, Cameo and the Linn drum, Prince floating above it all as a free electron. Dry drum machines, slapped synth basslines, robotized voices, yet the groove stays intact throughout. It is the direct source of G funk, electro funk and boogie, and proof that a machine can sweat just as hard as a live band. Where much electronic music of the era chased coldness for its own sake, synth funk kept the swagger and the pocket of live funk playing while replacing nearly every instrument in the room with a machine.
synthfunk.production: Synth funk is the slowest of the family, 96 to 115 BPM, More Bounce to the Ounce near 108, the only genre here with real swing: the LinnDrum's shuffle calls for 54 to 58 percent swing on the sixteenths, a heavy, laid back feel where the snare falls just after the beat. Program a kick on beat one and the and of three, a huge Linn snare on two and four doubled with a clap and gated reverb, swung closed hats opening on the and of four, several hat velocities plus ghost notes. The bass imitates slap technique on a Minimoog, two layered tones, a closed low sawtooth for the thumb and a brighter tone for the pop, in swung sixteenths. Top it with a talkbox as the genre's voice, a DX7 electric piano, and Oberheim brass in rich chords.

synthpop.description: Synth pop rewrote pop music entirely on synthesizers in England and Germany between 1978 and 1984: unstoppable melodies played on visibly artificial machines, a cold kind of romanticism, and the song format kept intact. Bands like Depeche Mode, Human League and Soft Cell were the generation that proved machines could make people cry. Synth pop is the melodic root of italo disco, freestyle, minimal wave and everything in dance music that has stayed sung rather than instrumental.
synthpop.production: Synth pop kept the pop song format at 100 to 135 BPM, centered near 120, the beat machine quantized while the sung melody carries the expression, and the verse chorus structure forcing an energy shift every eight bars. A LinnDrum or TR-808 supplies the beat, kick on one and three or every beat for dance tracks, snare or clap on two and four, eighth note hats with an open hat on the last upbeat. The bass is played on synth, usually a Juno, a sawtooth plus sub oscillator through a filter with a fast envelope, changing note every two to four bars to follow the chords. A DX7 supplies snappy FM basses and bell like electric pianos, joined by chorused pads, plaqué chords, dotted eighth delays on the leads, and a bright plate reverb on the vocal.

techhouse.description: Tech house is the London compromise of the 1990s between the groove of house and the pull of techno, embodied by the Wiggle and The End club nights. It trades in round basslines and dry percussion, keeping neither house's soul nor techno's hardness, but achieving a formidable dancefloor efficiency instead. By the 2010s it had become the best selling style on streaming platforms, though at the cost of a standardization that its pioneers do not always recognize as their own creation, the genre having drifted far from its original London club roots.
techhouse.production: Sit between 124 and 128 BPM, where house meets techno, and unlike minimal techno, embrace the swing: 55 to 58 percent on the sixteenths for hats and percussion while kick and bass stay square. A round 909 kick with a short tail holds every beat, with clap or snare on two and four doubled by an offset rimshot, and closed hats alternating velocities 100 and 60. What sets tech house apart is its layer of dry percussion, congas, shakers and blocks with no reverb filling the free sixteenths, plus a swung shaker driving the groove. The signature bass is round and looped, sine and square mixed, filtered low around 300 Hz, playing short notes on the offbeats and sidechained to the kick. On top, chopped and repeated vocal hooks, short minor stabs, and filtered noise risers keep things lean.

technobass.description: Techno bass is Detroit's answer to Miami bass: electro-funk hardened by the city's own techno culture, fast 808 patterns, vocoders, and a ghetto strain of science fiction. Aux 88 and DJ Assault hold its two poles, one cosmic, the other obscene, and ghettotech would be born from this crossing with Chicago's ghetto house. The name comes from both the label and the sound: bass treated as a vehicle.
technobass.production: Techno bass runs 130 to 150 BPM, tipping to 155 or 160 once it crosses into ghettotech, with a strict grid, no swing, and the 808 quantized to the sixteenth. Two kick patterns split the genre: the classic electro pattern for the Aux 88 side, and a four-on-the-floor borrowed from Chicago ghetto house for the ghettotech side. Two basses coexist, a tuned 808 kick playing fast eighth-note motifs like Miami bass, and an electro synth bass, a saw or square with a fast-enveloped 300Hz lowpass filter jumping octaves in sixteenths, taking on the role of melody as much as bassline, usually in a minor key. Alternate the two, holding the 808 through the chorus and switching to the synth bass for the verses. The vocoder returns front and center, voices chopped into one-syllable fragments and played in rhythm.

technobodymusic.description: Techno body music is the return of EBM inside the body of techno, forged in Berlin during the 2010s: distorted sequenced basslines inherited from DAF and Nitzer Ebb, techno kicks, shouted vocals drowned in reverb, and an aesthetic of leather and cold neon. The term took hold around 2017 through the Berlin club scene and labels like aufnahme + wiedergabe and Fleisch, and through a compilation that literally carries the genre's name. It is music of sweat and living machines, played as often live as in DJ sets, that brought industrial new wave back onto techno dancefloors, closing a loop between two scenes that had drifted apart for decades.
technobodymusic.production: Start around 130 BPM, straight, with techno's drive and EBM's weight. Hardware sequencers like the MC-202 and SH-101 give the genre its slight timing drift and per step accents, imitated with a lightly swung groove. A big layered techno kick, a saturated 909 plus a long, sidechained reverb tail, holds every beat, with a clap on two and four, closed hats in sixteenths opening on the offbeats, and repitched metal hits for industrial percussion; the pattern stays simple, complexity sits in the bass. That bass, an SH-101 or MC-202 style sawtooth sequenced in sixteenths with an accented step pattern, pushed through fuzz or overdrive and filtered near 3 kHz, sits nearly as loud as the kick. Shouted vocals are driven into distortion and drowned in a long metallic reverb, the shared space for everything but the kick.

techstep.description: Techstep is the cold turn drum and bass took between 1996 and 1998: industrial two step breaks, twisting basslines and dystopian science fiction imagery. Labels like No U-Turn and Virus were its factories, with Ed Rush and Optical as chief engineers. Techstep shifted the genre's center of gravity from the sound system to the laboratory, and it paved the way for neurofunk, which would later systematize its methods.
techstep.production: Techstep runs at 170 BPM, colder than classic drum and bass because everything sits on a square grid: kick on the one, snare on two and four. There are only two real drum layers, a very short kick with no sub around 80 to 120 Hz and a dry, unreverbed snare, often an isolated Think or Amen hit compressed hard. The bass is a Reese built from two detuned saws in mono, recorded to audio and run repeatedly through overdrive, a slowly moving lowpass filter and further distortion until it vibrates on its own. A Nord Lead supplies the raw Reese material and an Akai S3000 resamples and refilters it in series, while dystopian film dialogue, machine noise and metallic drones sit low in the mix around a single melodic synth.

techtrance.description: Tech trance is the hard zone between techno and trance: the massive kicks of the former, the arpeggios and tension of the latter, and very little melodic sweetness. It was born in the German and Dutch raves of the 1990s and remains the backbone of the toughest trance sets, and the crossing point where techno and trance DJs trade records with each other.
techtrance.production: Set the grid at 136 to 142 BPM, dead straight with no swing, letting the kick lead rather than the melody and holding a high energy plateau instead of rising and falling like uplifting trance. Layer the kick from a 909 and a longer, saturated, distorted kick tuned to the tonic, add a dry loud clap on two and four, and harden the open hat into something metallic. Keep the bass on the offbeat, a Virus-style saw with distortion, staying on the tonic or alternating with the fifth every eight bars, doubled by a saturated sixteenth-note line close to a closed 303, hard-sidechained at 8:1. Melodic content stays sparse and tense: an acid arpeggio with high resonance, dark two-bar minor stabs, and a four-note motif transposed once per section rather than any wide supersaw pad.

terrorcore.description: Terrorcore is the hardest wing of 1990s hardcore, faster and darker than gabber, built on horror movie samples and New York nihilism at labels like Industrial Strength, with an equally extreme Dutch scene on the other side. It sits in a zone of deliberate radicalism between gabber and speedcore, where the kick stops functioning as rhythm and becomes a continuous, openly claimed assault.
terrorcore.production: Terrorcore starts where gabber leaves off, running 190 to 250 BPM, often 200 to 220; at these speeds a beat lasts under 300 milliseconds so the kick never finishes before the next. The kick is the gabber kick with its decay cut shorter and its distortion pushed further until each hit is almost white noise, the snare often swapped for a second, higher pitched kick, with rolls stretching into fast thirty-second notes. The kick's tail is too short to carry a bass note, so terrorcore substitutes distorted noise, a low sawtooth drone, or a second, slower kick with a long decay acting as a bourdon. Horror movie samples, screams, laughter, killer dialogue pitched down and distorted, sit alongside a faster hoover, resonant saw pads and industrial noise, degraded to eight bit to match the era's trackers.

trance.description: Trance emerged in Frankfurt at the very start of the 1990s, at the crossing of techno and Germany's cosmic musical heritage: a music of repetition and build, turning arpeggios, opening chords, programmed ecstasy. The name says exactly what it does, putting the floor into a trance through accumulation. Underground at first on labels like MFS and Harthouse, it became by decade's end the mass music of European raves.
trance.production: Trance holds between 130 and 138 BPM on a dead-straight, fully quantized sixteenth grid with no swing, the feel built from accumulation rather than groove; count in 8 and 16 bar blocks, pick one tempo and stay there. A long, round 909 kick sits on every beat, snare and clap on 2 and 4, open hat marking the and of each beat, and a continuous 909 ride from the first drop for the rave feel. The bass falls on the offbeats, a short note in the gap between kicks, sawtooth or square with cutoff around 300 Hz, staying on the root for eight bars before opening to the sixth or fourth. On top, a sawtooth arpeggio on a three or four note minor chord, a wide detuned pad, and a softened TB-303 line.

trapedm.description: Atlanta trap translated for festivals around 2012: triplet hi hats and 808s from Southern rap, married to rave drops and EDM build-ups. Harlem Shake by Baauer turns it into a planetary viral phenomenon. The style permanently installs rap's grammar into festival electronic music, and vice versa, welding the 808 and the festival drop into a single, durable vocabulary that both worlds still use.
trapedm.production: Run between 140 and 150 bpm in halftime, felt as 70 to 75 bpm, snare on 3, kick on 1 plus syncopations, a heavy, slow Atlanta trap feel where triplet hi hat rolls create the bounce. Build the kick from an 808 varying every 2 bars, a layered snare on 3, 808 hats rolling into triplet bursts at phrase ends, and a riser or snare roll building to the drop, where drums can drop out to leave a horn alone. The 808 is the bass itself, a decaying sine tuned to the key with a short pitch envelope for click and saturation for harmonics. Layer huge synthetic brass hits, supersaw festival leads, pitched-down rap shouts, sirens and white noise risers, contrasting a melodic build with a brutal drop.

tribalhouse.description: House reduced to percussion: congas, timbales and toms layered into polyrhythms, harmony almost absent, tension built entirely through the drum. New York carried it into its after hours clubs of the 1990s, with Danny Tenaglia as its great architect. The style then travelled between Spain, Italy and the international gay scene, where it remains a dancefloor language decades after its original New York after hours heyday.
tribalhouse.production: Work between 125 and 130 BPM, a touch faster than classic house so the percussion can run. The feel is a drum circle laid over a straight kick: the kick itself stays even, but every percussion layer has its own placement, some slightly ahead, others a few milliseconds behind, and that friction creates the groove. Use hand played loops where possible, or humanise timing slightly. Tracks run long, eight to ten minutes, with tension building through accumulated layers rather than synth risers. The kick is a dry, strong 909 on all four beats, with little or no clap, the backbeat role instead taken by a tom or timbale. Layer syncopated tom patterns tuned to different pitches, sampled congas in a tumbao loop, bongos in sixteenths, accented timbales, a shaker and a bell, each a short pattern stacked in cross rhythms.

triphop.description: Trip-hop took shape in Bristol between 1991 and 1995: hip-hop slowed under the English rain, dub basslines, ghostly soul vocals, and a melancholy built from concrete. Massive Attack opened the door, Portishead carved the canon, and Tricky scrambled all of it. The name, coined by the press, has irritated its own makers ever since, but the music came to define the 1990s so thoroughly that it turned into a cliche, and later a treasure again.
triphop.production: Trip-hop drops further than downtempo, to 65 or 90 BPM, and drags rather than swings, delaying the snare behind the beat so it lands like something heavy falling, while the kick stays locked to the grid. Take a funk or soul break and slow it without clean time-stretching so the pitch drops and the sound darkens, filtered to 8kHz, with a heavy kick and a dry, plate-drenched snare on beat three. The bass is dub, bigger and darker than downtempo, dropping below 50Hz on held whole notes, often the tonic and minor seventh, with a silence on beat one every other bar, and no sidechain, kick and bass meant to overlap into one mass. On top sits a colder Rhodes with a slow phaser and a fragile female soul vocal sung close to the mic, drowned in plate reverb.

twilightpsy.description: Twilight psy is the South African school of hard psychedelic trance, sitting between full-on and dark psy at 145 to 150 beats per minute: massive basslines, mean leads and a sense of end-of-night humor. The name refers to its time slot, the dawn and dusk hours of Cape Town's festivals. It is a tight, close-knit scene that has become a major export, from the Vortex festival to European lineups. It keeps full-on's readable drops and structure but trades its heroic melody for weight and aggression, aimed at a crowd that is tired but still wants to dance hard.
twilightpsy.production: Twilight psy sits between full-on and darkpsy at 145 to 150 BPM on a straight, unswung grid, distinguished from full-on by sheer weight, a bass that gallops less and hits harder, and leads aiming for aggression rather than heroic melody, while staying more readable than darkpsy with clear drops and breaks. Build a kick longer and more compressed than darkpsy's, around 55 Hz with a marked click, layered with a heavy, distorted snare on 2 and 4, saturated open hats on the offbeats, and metallic percussion in varied sixteenths, closing each section with short, brutal snare rolls. The bass hardens full-on's kick-plus-three-sixteenths motif with a heavily filtered, distorted sawtooth, each note shorter and meaner, rooted on F sharp or G with a clean separate sub. Aggressive resonant acid leads and metallic FX from comb-filtered impacts complete a hard, precise sound.

ukbass.description: The umbrella label for the post-dubstep years, from 2009 onward: everything London produced between house, garage, techno, and grime without fitting neatly into any of them. Hessle Audio, Night Slugs, and Hemlock were its home labels, with bass as the only true common denominator. Less a genre than a moment of formal freedom, its inaugural anthem was signed by Joy Orbison with Hyph Mngo.
ukbass.production: UK bass does not have one tempo so much as a range, 125 to 135 BPM with 130 most common, often a 128 house grid carrying garage swing at 56 to 60 percent, or a halfstep feel at 130 with the snare on beat 3. The feel is dry, precise, and syncopated, with silences that matter as much as the hits, tighter than the dubstep it grew from. Build dry, short percussion with no reverb, rimshots, woodblocks, muted claps, pitched 808 toms, and a syncopated house or saturated 909 kick, placed on beat 1, the off-beat of 2, and beat 3 with a gap, plus a snare on 2 and 4 or alone on 3. Keep hats rare, replaced by syncopated sixteenth percussion with widely varied velocities and occasional polyrhythms.

ukfunky.description: UK funky is 2008 to 2010 London: a soca and Afro-inflected house sound born on pirate radio, built on tribal percussion, female vocals and a rolling 130 BPM swing. A brief, bright genre sitting between UK garage and South African house, its percussive motifs still run through UK bass today. Kyla's Do You Mind, later covered by Drake, remains its best-known pop trace.
ukfunky.production: UK funky sits between 128 and 132 BPM with a tropical feel borrowing from soca, dembow and South African house; the kick is not always straight four-on-the-floor, often syncopated, and the groove comes mainly from stacking three or four sixteenth-note percussion patterns, the 3+3+2 dembow rhythm turning up often in the congas or the bass. Snare or clap sits on 2 and 4, or a rimshot on 3 for a broken feel, with congas playing a tumbao motif, bongos, offbeat cowbell and shakers, dry and panned wide. The bass is round and short, between a sub and a house bass, playing a syncopated pentatonic minor line that follows the kick on some hits and contradicts it on others, no wobble, no Reese. On top, sung female lead vocals and sampled marimba or steel drum for tropical color.

ukgarage.description: UK garage took shape in London in the mid-1990s: New York garage sped up and run through the filter of pirate radio, with swollen basslines, chopped and pitched vocals and a tight, rolling swing. It became Britain's first great mutation of house music, a whole culture built around clubs, MCs and dress codes rather than just a sound. From its restless, shape-shifting coastline came 2-step, grime, dubstep and much of what is now called bass music. The genre bridges American club sensibility and British street culture, taking a smooth import and roughing it up until it sounded unmistakably local.
ukgarage.production: UK garage sits at 128 to 135 BPM, with 130 the classic starting point, and swing is the whole story: apply a groove of 58 to 62 percent to the hats and percussion, much less to the kick, so sixteenths pull back while eighths stay nearly straight. Build a short, dry four-on-the-floor kick, a clap or snare on 2 and 4 layered with a pitched-up 909 snare, swung closed hats with uneven velocities and an open hat on every offbeat, plus shakers, leaving some percussion unquantized so the loop breathes. The bass is a round sub, sine or triangle, played in short syncopated notes, root, fifth, octave, flat seventh, answering the kick rather than doubling it, lightly sidechained. The Korg M1 organ, chopped R&B vocals, string stabs and pirate-radio sirens complete a short, midrange-heavy sound.

ukhardcore.description: UK hardcore is the modern continuation of British happy hardcore after 2000: polished trance-style production, supersaw leads, fully sung vocals rather than pitched-up snippets, and a tempo around 170 beats per minute. Artists such as Styles and Breeze and Darren Styles, and later the Monstercat label, have turned it into a surprisingly durable genre, sitting somewhere between rave nostalgia and accelerated pop. Kandi bracelets and light-up gloves come included in the price. It keeps happy hardcore's tempo and offbeat bounce but swaps its cheap piano stabs and chipmunk vocals for a bigger, cleaner, radio-friendly wall of sound.
ukhardcore.production: UK hardcore keeps happy hardcore's tempo, 170 to 175 BPM, usually at 172 with no swing, but applies trance-level polish: fully quantized, clean and wide. The real change from the original is the sound, a supersaw replacing the piano, a fully sung pop vocal replacing the pitched-up snippet, and a longer, more tuned kick with gentle saturation, between hardstyle and trance. Build clap and reverbed snare on 2 and 4, an open hat on every offbeat mixed lower than classic happy hardcore, alternating closed hats, and accelerating snare rolls into a crash on each drop. The bass keeps happy hardcore's offbeat placement but grows fatter, a detuned unison sawtooth following a four-chord minor progression, backed by a sidechained sub. The supersaw, detuned saws through a wide filter and reverb, carries the drops, joined by plucked arpeggios and the sung vocal.

ukhouse.description: UK house is Britain's reception of Chicago house, filtered through acid house and the raves of 1988 before settling in as the common language of English clubs. It runs faster and harder than its American source, absorbing the Italian piano sound, breakbeats and the culture of pirate radio stations. From this mix come hardcore, UK garage and, later, most of British dance music. It is a hybrid built by samplers as much as by DJs: American house grooves crossed with homegrown breaks, played loud and a little rough around the edges, made for packed clubs rather than polished record collections.
ukhouse.production: UK house runs faster than Chicago, 122 to 128 BPM around 1988 to 1990, with an energetic, slightly rough feel since everything passes through the sampler: breakbeat loops layered over a 909. Use light machine swing but let sampled loops keep their own groove against the grid, in 16-bar structures that change every 8 bars like a pirate radio set. Build a four-on-the-floor 909 kick and clap on 2 and 4 under a chopped, tempo-matched funk breakbeat filtered above 150 Hz and mixed low, sometimes standing alone on breakdowns, plus open hats on the offbeats. The bass is a single-note disco or funk sample, or a driving sawtooth line, while harmony comes from a bright Italian piano, sampled brass and string stabs, chopped vocal samples, sirens and crowd noise, run through an Akai S1000 or Simpler in slices.

upliftingtrance.description: Uplifting trance is the genre at its emotional peak: enormous breakdowns, major-key melodies climbing in steps, and resolution as euphoric release. Formalized at the end of the 1990s between the Netherlands and England, it became the genre's canon, the sound the word trance evokes first. Ferry Corsten and Armin van Buuren industrialized the formula without ever quite wearing out its effect.
upliftingtrance.production: Uplifting trance sits at 138 BPM almost as a rule, tolerance 136 to 140, on a straight, fully quantized grid with no swing; the feel comes from tension and release, built around a breakdown lasting 90 seconds to two minutes that everything else leads into or out of. A clean, punchy 909 kick holds every beat with clap and snare stacked on 2 and 4, and the signature snare roll runs through the last 16 bars of the breakdown, moving from eighths to sixteenths to thirty-seconds as volume rises and a highpass filter opens. The bass is a sawtooth on the offbeats, short and filtered, following a vi-IV-I-V progression, sidechained hard at 6:1 for the characteristic pump. On top, a supersaw lead, wide reverberant pads, and a climbing major melody carry the euphoria.

uptempo.description: Uptempo hardcore is the acceleration of the 2010s and 2020s: nu style pushed past 200 beats per minute, kicks riddled with rolls in the frenchcore tradition, Dutch festival culture, and memes embraced without embarrassment. Partyraiser stands as its patriarch, and the TikTok generation has become its fuel. Hardcore proves once again that it can always find a way to outrun itself. What began as a niche extension of nu style hardcore has turned into a self aware, festival scale phenomenon, one that treats speed itself, along with its own absurdity, as the central joke and the central thrill.
uptempo.production: Uptempo hardcore runs from 190 up to 230 BPM, much of it around 200 to 210, with no swing and a party rather than terror feel: kicks stay tuned and long like nu style or frenchcore rather than crushed gabber, tails shortened since a beat lasts 300 ms at 200 BPM. The signature is pierced or rolled kicks, short bursts in sixteenths with rising pitch acting as fills, offbeat kicks playing just the tail for bounce, and kick patterns cut and rearranged every two to four beats like fast video editing. Bass mostly comes from that kick tail, replayed on offbeats or doubled by a separate saturated bass, hard sidechained so it ducks under every hit. On top sit harsh Serum screeches, stacked sawtooth leads, and meme and crowd samples, edited into a bright, compressed sound.

usdeephouse.description: In 1986, Larry Heard laid down the deep house formula with Can You Feel It: sustained, jazzy synthesizer chords, a supple bass line, discreet drums and a gentle melancholy. It is house built for listening as much as dancing, introspective and harmonically rich. New York and New Jersey dressed it in vocals, while Chicago kept it instrumental, and for forty years it has quietly run through everything tender in house music, shaping how producers everywhere treat chords and space.
usdeephouse.production: Aim for 118 to 123 bpm, never faster, with moderate 54 to 56 percent swing on the hats, a straight kick, and chords sitting 10 to 20ms behind the beat, held over one or two bars. Build a muted 909: short kick decay, a soft clap or rim instead of snare, closed hats at low velocity, a quiet open hat on the offbeats. For bass, use an SH-101 style sawtooth, filtered around 200 to 400Hz with light glide, a melodic line with passing notes and sevenths like a jazz bassist. The heart is the chord: Juno voicings held over a slowly opening filter, answered by a Rhodes and a distant string pad, everything soft, never bright.

vocaltrance.description: Vocal trance is trance turned into song: a female voice floats over the arpeggios, the breakdown carries the verse, and the drop stands in for the chorus. From the anthems of 1998 to 2004, running from Delerium to Above & Beyond, all the way to the online radio stations that play almost nothing else, this is the genre's most mainstream face and its greatest vehicle for nostalgia. It softens trance's harder mechanics into pop songcraft, built around a singer rather than a build, and it remains the version of trance most people outside the scene actually remember and still return to.
vocaltrance.production: Sit between 132 and 138 BPM, a touch under uplifting trance so the vocal has room to breathe, on a straight grid, with the vocal's natural tempo deciding the track's. Arrangement follows song structure, verse, pre chorus and chorus, rather than plain 16 bar blocks; during the verse drums drop back to little more than kick and hat so the voice can lead, a clean 909 kick, clap and snare on two and four, open hat on the offbeats returning in full for the chorus. The offbeat bass follows the song's chord changes, sawtooth filtered around 400 Hz with a fast sidechain, simplifying to sub whole notes in the verse and disappearing on the breakdown for the piano. The lead vocal, doubled with harmonies, sits over two stage compression with a dotted eighth delay and plate reverb.

wonky.description: The 2008 to 2010 label for deliberately unhinged beats: synths sliding off the grid, detuned basses, instrumental hip hop warped into video game colours. Glasgow, through Rustie and Hudson Mohawke, and Los Angeles, through Flying Lotus, answered each other across the ocean. The word has aged, but the sensibility won: half of modern pop now slides off the grid too, gondoled just enough to feel alive.
wonky.production: Tempos follow hip hop logic, 70 to 90 BPM or its double, 140 to 180, depending how you count. The rule is off grid: strip out quantization or apply a loose groove, then nudge hits further by hand, 15 to 40 milliseconds. Let the snare land late, the kick sometimes early, and the hats stagger, so the feel is drunk but still held by a constant pulse. Build the kick from an 808 placed on shifted spots, never quite on the grid, and the snare on two and four but late, layered with a rimshot or snap. Hats run in swung eighths or sixteenths with gaps and ghost notes. The bass is a detuned sub that slides, a sine in mono with long glide, overlapping notes so the portamento does the work, written in a minor pentatonic with bends.

zenonesque.description: The sound of the Australian label Zenon Records, mid 2000s, now used as an adjective the scene prefers to progressive psy dark. It does not descend from psy-prog: that link is a common error born from a similar tempo, the sound actually coming from slowed dark psy crossed with hypnotic techno, with a glitchy edge from downtempo. Sensient set its grammar: rubbery mid-tempo basses, granular textures, muffled industrial atmospheres, a slow tribal groove. There is no lead melody, tension coming from the sound material itself. The scene claims it as its own thing; others call it a branch of psy-prog, a debated lineage this entry keeps open.
zenonesque.production: Play between 126 and 132 bpm, the slowest of the dancing psy genres, with a slow tribal groove, swing on percussion, ghost notes, patterns shifting by texture every few bars rather than by melodic build, the bass bouncing rather than rolling. Build a round, deep kick with little click, often with no snare at all, replaced by a dull rimshot or wood hit through a dark reverb, plus sampled skin drums and shakers in swung sixteenths, and granular micro FX, clicks and drips with random pitch, standing in for extra percussion. For bass, build the rubbery sound on a saw, low-pass with raised resonance for bounce, an elastic offbeat pattern of varied note lengths, soft saturation and a slow filter LFO. Layer granulated field recordings, filtered industrial drones, and a few short, dark stabs in place of any lead.
